1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways on the observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and
Ninety Third Report on Demands for Grants (2013-14) of Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways, which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 3 rd May, 2013.
2. The Action Taken Replies received from the Ministry in respect of all the observations/
recommendations contained in the Report have been categorized as follows:–
(i) Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry:
Paragraph Nos. 9, 13, 18, 19, 34, 36, 50, 56, 61, 62, 63, 68, 71, 73, 85, 90, 99,
111, 112, 116, 119, 122, 127, 132, 135, 137 and 140
(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Ministry replies:
Paragraph Nos. 35, 37, 138 and 139
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not
been accepted by the Committee:
Paragraph Nos. 94, 95 and 104
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry are
still awaited:
Paragraph Nos. 34, 36, 62 and 63
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of these recommendations/
observations, which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be
furnished to it at the earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee
contained in the One Hundred and Ninety Third Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry and
recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the
succeeding paragraphs
ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
5. The Committee finds that funds under both plan and non-plan outlays have seen substantial
reduction at RE stage for the year 2012-13. The Committee is not convinced of the reasons for
such drastic reduction of funds especially under plan head from Rs. 23000 crores at BE stage to
Rs. 17773.54 crores at RE stage. The Committee found that reduction of funds at RE stage is
happening every year due to one reason or the other. The Committee feels that the Ministry should
strive to utilize the allocated money. The Committee also feels that major modification of allocation
at the stage of revised estimate should be avoided as it delays the implementation of sanctioned
projects.
(Recommendation at Para 9 of 193 rd Report)

2
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6. The total GBS outlay for Central Sector Roads at BE stage was Rs. 23,000 crore, which
was reduced to Rs. 17,773.54 crore at RE stage, i.e., there was reduction in GBS outlay for
Rs. 5,226.46 crore during RE. To accommodate this drastic reduction, release to NHAI for
Rs. 1,878.95 crore and Rs. 1,777.03 crore under NHAI investment and remittance of toll receipts
cannot be made. Otherwise, these amounts would have been spent. Perhaps M/o Finance reduce
the BE allocation keeping in view the expenditure pattern during the first three quarters of the
financial year.
7. As far as road work is concerned majority of expenditure is incurred during the last quarter
of the financial year due to favorable weather condition. Whereas, M/o Finance imposed restrictions
for ceiling of expenditure by 33% and 15% for the last quarter and last month of the financial year
respectively, which is a main impediment in incurring expenditure for this Ministry. This Ministry
has taken this issue with M/o Finance for relaxing these norms. However, the 33% ceiling was not
relaxed during 2012-13. Even, Parliamentary Standing Committee also recommended relaxing these
ceilings for this Ministry on a number of occasion.
8. This Ministry agrees with the fact that modification of allocation at RE stage delay
implementation of sanctioned projects. However, this aspect is not within the purview of this
Ministry. We are bringing recommendation of the committee to the notice of Ministry of Finance
and Planning Commission.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
9. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and hopes that it will pursue the
removal of restrictions of 33% ceiling of expenditure for the last quarter with Ministry of
Finance seriously. The Committee may also be apprised on the reaction of Planning
Commission to committee’s recommendations in this regard.
TWELFTH PLAN (2012-17)
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
10. The Committee notes that the total GBS outlay provided during the Twelfth plan is
Rs.1,44,769 crore including central transport sector as against the projected requirement of
Rs.2,64,080 crore excluding central transport sector. The Committee feels that this reduction in
allocation will certainly deter the Ministry in taking-up the new projects/schemes envisaged for the
Twelfth plan period. Projects like connectivity to 50 minor ports, connectivity to 24 airports and
implementation of special packages for J&K and North-Eastern Region have to be dropped by the
Ministry for want of funds from the Government. The Committee also notes that Rs. 6,400 crore
has been allocated against the requirement of Rs. 37,540 crore for works NH(O) for the entire plan
period, which is unsustainable considering the length of roads taken-up for improvement under this
scheme. This reduced allocation for the NH(O) will affect the NH (O) works adversely and
ultimately result in diversion of cess towards development of non-NHDP projects from NHDP
projects. The Committee is concerned to note that such diversion of cess meant for NHDP projects
has been taking place for the last three years which is alarming. The Committee feels that the
Ministry should take up the enhancement of GBS during mid-term plan review so that new
projects/schemes apart from the on-going ones do not suffer.
(Para 13 of ibid)

3
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
11. This Ministry vide d.o. letter No. NH-22023/1/2011-P&M dated 31.08.2012 has taken up
the issue for enhancement in allocation during the Twelfth Five Year Plan with Planning
Commission and M/o Finance. However, the same has been turned down citing overall resource
constraints. Accordingly, all the new schemes/projects envisaged to be taken up during Twelfth
Plan have been dropped. Further to mention that if the level of Annual Plan outlay (about
Rs. 23,000 crore) is maintained for the entire Twelfth Five Year Plan then we will not even able
to reach the total outlay provided for the entire Five Year Plan (Rs. 1,44,769 crore).
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
12. The Committee reiterates its concern about the fact that road sector, one of the
important segments of country’s infrastructure, will not be able to meet the targets with
the current allocation.
ANNUAL PLAN 2013-14
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13. The Committee finds that the GBS component for the Ministry has seen only a marginal
increase of Rs. 500 crore, from Rs. 23,000 crore in 2012-13(BE) to Rs. 23,500 crore for
2013-14 (BE). As against the projected requirement of Rs. 26,450 crores, the Ministry has been
allocated Rs. 23,500 crore only as GBS for 2013-14 which is about 88% of the projected
requirement. The Committee feels that static allocation forces the Ministry not to take up new
projects/schemes and it also affects the progress of the sanctioned projects adversely. The
Committee finds that Rs. 3,024 crores meant for financing of NHDP will be diverted to NH(O)
works resulting in various schemes under NHDP being delayed. The Committee feels that the
Ministry should find ways to check such diversions in consultation with the Planning Commission
so that major national highway projects are not delayed for want of funds. Implementation of our
road transport Schemes/programmes are not visible/felt at the ground level at all and, therefore,
these may be supported in a big way.
(Para 18 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
14. As stated earlier, regarding poor allocation recommendation has been forwarded to Ministry
of Finance and Planning Commission. The diversion of cess from NHAI to NH(O) was necessitated
due to Gross Budgetary Support 2013-14 being less than what was projected. The shortfall will
be made good by National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) through increased market
borrowings. Further to mention that the projected requirement for 2013-14 (BE) is based on the
criterion specified by the Planning Commission, whereas, the actual requirement was much more.
Diversion of funds has been done in consultation with the Planning Commission.
15. Ministry also agrees with the recommendation of the Committee to take up more projects
through budgetary support. Accordingly, Ministry has decided to take up more projects on
Engineering Procurement Construction (EPC) mode through budgetary support.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
16. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and hopes that it will get adequate
budgetary support for EPC road projects.

4
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17. The Committee also expresses its concern over the reduction in allocation of funds for
Road Transport Sector from Rs. 400 crore in 2012-13(BE) to Rs. 200 crore for 2013-14 (BE).
(Para 19 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
18. The reduction in allocation for road transport sector has been done based on the overall
resource constraints.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
19. The Committee notes the reply and feels that reduction in allocation of funds for
road transport sector will definitely have a negative impact on the schemes and projects
particularly pertaining to road safety related matters.
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
20. The Committee, in view of the complicated and long procedure involving multiple agencies
at different levels coupled with strict norms, legal, administrative, financial etc. that are required
to be followed at different stages, appreciates the constraints under which highways projects have
to be executed. Then there are problems with land acquisition and environmental clearances that
are time taking. But, the Committee feels that such infrastructure projects as highways have to be
taken up and completed in this setting only; there in no escape from the constraints as these are
built into the system. Real challenge, therefore, before the Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways is to expedite the projects in minimum time and to maximum possible extent, by having
a robust monitoring and coordination mechanism at different level/stages. Every important agency
involved in the process like financial institutions such as Banks and RBI, State Governments, other
Ministries and particularly Planning Commission will have to realize the urgency and importance of
faster development of Highways and will have to make it a joint effort.
(Para 34 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
21. Observations have been noted. A copy of the recommendations is being sent to Ministry of
Finance and Planning Commission for appropriate action.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
22. The Committee notes the reply and it may be appraised about observations of the
Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission on the monitoring and coordination
mechanism for road projects.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
23. The Committee hopes that certain measures taken recently in respect of making loans from
Banks as secured loans; separating forest clearance from the environmental and efforts made to
revise Concession Agreement will certainly go a long way in expediting our highways development
programmes.
(Para 35 of ibid)

5
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
24. Observations have been noted. No action called for.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
25. The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
26. In this regard, a disturbing aspect about Planning Commission’s approach towards highways
construction came to notice of the Committee. To Committee’s utter dismay, the Planning
Commission instead of promoting and facilitating highways construction is alleged to have been
exceeding its brief. The Committee feels that the Commission’s overbearing attitude was causing
unease amongst the line Ministries/Departments. It is the considered opinion of the Committee that
documents/papers prepared by the line Ministries for implementing a project may be seen by the
Commission just as is done by the Department of Law and Department of Expenditure; it should
refrain from commenting upon engineering and technical aspects and should confine itself to
planning and allocation/management of resources only. Moreover, the ultimate accountability for
anything done or not done rests with Ministry and not with the Planning Commission. For example,
in the case of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, the Committee learnt that even
Concessionaire Agreements are being finalized in the Commission on the basis of models being
followed in Western Countries. If it is true, the Committee feels that Planning Commission by doing
so was going beyond its original mandate visualized by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, whose idea was
to have such a body which could facilitate faster growth and development in planned manner. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Concessionaire Agreement devised by the Planning
Commission should be reformulated in concurrence with the Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways to address the local conditions and changing circumstances. The Committee feels the
Western models will not work in our country because we have our own peculiarities and
constraints.
(Para 36 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
27. The working of Planning Commission is beyond the control of this Ministry. A copy of the
recommendations is being sent to Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission for appropriate
action.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
28. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and expects the Ministry to obtain
responses from the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance on the Committee’s
observations/recommendation and forward to the Committee at the earliest.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
29. The Committee has strong reasons to conclude that PPP as a model for the development
of road projects needs to be reviewed seriously in the light of our experience so far in this regard.
That the private capital is mainly for profit is borne out by the fact that the profitable projects are
being bid out fast. A vast country which needs faster connectivity to its length and breadth has
to adopt an alternative model of project development which is development driven and not profit
driven. Since profitable projects are sold out first, the Government is facing problem in getting
bidders for such non-profitable road projects as those in LWE and North-East Areas. India needs

6
faster construction of roads and the Committee, therefore, recommends that all such projects
without bidders should be developed with the budgetary support from the Government and Planning
Commission needs to be more practical and careful about its role and function.
(Para 37 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
30. The Ministry agrees with the recommendation of the Committee. Accordingly, Ministry has
decided to take up more projects on Engineering Procurement Construction (EPC) mode through
budgetary support.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
31. The Committee notes the reply.
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS (NHDP)
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
32. The Committee observes that performance of NHDP from 2006 onwards has not been very
good. For instance out of the 1000 Km. envisaged in NHDP-VI in 2006, the Government could
not award even a single contract till March, 2013. Likewise, out of the 19,800 Km. envisaged in
the NHDP IV , just 187 Km. could be completed till March 2013. Apart from the stated reasons
such as poor market conditions, economic slow down, strict stipulations of RBI for funding
projects, poor response of bidders for projects, the Committee feels that poor performance of
NHDP projects may be due to reasons narrated in previous paragraphs. The Committee, therefore,
feels that the Government should look into such aspects and try to curb such practice to prevent
breakdown of implementation of projects.
(Para 50 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
33. Keeping in view unfavorable market condition for BOT projects, leading to slippage of target
for award of projects under NHDP (projects for only 1,116 km. was awarded as against the target
of 8,100 km.), current financial year 2013-14 onwards Ministry has decided to take up more
projects on Engineering Procurement Construction (EPC) mode through budgetary support.
As far as expressway is concerned it is to mention that in November, 2006 the Government
approved under NHDP Phase-VI, construction of 1,000 km. expressways through PPP on DBFOT
pattern at a total cost of Rs.16,680 crore.
The total land acquisition cost for Delhi-Jaipur and Vadodara-Mumbai Expressway is about
Rs.5,500 crore and Rs.6,000 crore respectively. The overall resource constraint, it would be
difficult to take up these projects till financing arrangements are finalized.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
34. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and hopes that taking up of road
projects under EPC rather than the much hyped PPP model will help the NHAI to complete
NHDP projects within time with permissible cost escalation of projects.

7
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
35. The Committee feels that environment and forest clearance are necessary components of
any development. However, there is no point in delaying the clearance or keeping it in abeyance
for unduly long, affecting the viability of the projects. The Committee recommends that the
Government should fix a specific time frame within which the concerned authorities have to take
a decision on such clearances. There should be an effective coordinating mechanism with different

clearance. The Committee is meeting regularly every month. As such there is no delay on the
part of the MoEF in granting environment clearance once the proposal reaches to them. The
delays occur mainly in conducting Public Hearing by the State Pollution Control Board at district
level. This delay can be curtailed if the SPCB convenes public hearing within one month from
the date of receiving documents. Alternatively, the Public Hearing can be exempted in the projects
involving widening.
38. With regard to forest clearance, the delays occur mainly in processing the proposals at State
level. No time limit has been prescribed for processing the application. At times the proposal takes
more than one year in reaching at the level of MoEF, New Delhi/Regional Office. There is no
prescribed time limit for processing such cases.
39. Considering all the factors the following measures can be taken for cutting down the delays
in clearances.
Environment Clearance:
1. Public Hearing was earlier exempted for widening projects under EIA notification 1994.
Under the new EIA notification 2006 public hearing is made mandatory. The process
of public hearing is time consuming and hence if exempted will considerably reduce
the time period.
2. Keeping in view the normal size of projects, the length of NH should be increased
from 30 km. to 100 and widening upto 60m.
Forest Clearance:
1. The powers for granting forest clearance for diversion of protected forest land may
be delegated to MoEF, Regional Office, irrespective of the area.
2. A time limit of 3 months may be prescribed for processing and recommending the
forest proposals at the State Government level.
3. Powers up to 40 ha. may be granted to Regional Office of MoEF.
Meetings are held regularly with Ministry of Environment and Forests to review the pending
proposals.

of Rajasthan on a pilot basis so as to create an area dedicated to the development of various
commercial activities related to the transport sector.
107. Rs.2.50 crore was released as mobilization advance during 2012-13. The remaining amount
of Rs.22.50 crores is to be released in suitable instalments after progress of work. The work is to
be executed by the Society, set up by the Government of Rajasthan for executing and running the project.
108. Based on experience from this pilot project, the facility is to be replicated throughout the
country.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
109. The Committee may be appraised on the outcome of pilot Transport Hub at
Railmagra, Rajasthan.
STRENGTHENING PUBLIC TRANSPORT SYSTEM
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
110. The Committee feels that strengthening of Public Transport System is the only way to
provide comfortable, smooth and safe transport system for the public. The Committee hopes that

19
though only 70% of the allocated funds could be spent during 2012-13, the Ministry should
improve its performance during the current fiscal so that the public transport gets the much needed
fillip.
(Para 135 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
111. As less fresh proposals were received from States/State Transport Undertakings/
Corporations during 2012-13 seeking financial assistance under the Strengthening Public Transport
Scheme and also request for release of 2 nd/3rd installment were not received from most of the
beneficiary States/STUs/ SRTCs in r/o proposals sanctioned during 2010-11 and 2011-12, the
;funds earmarked could not be fully utilized.
112. For better implementation of the scheme, meetings are now proposed to be organized with
the State Governments/ implementing agencies from time to time to monitor /review the scheme.
Regular follow-up action with concerned agencies which are responsible for implementation of the
scheme will be taken.
113. The suggestions of the Committee for timely execution of the sanctioned projects including
better utilization of funds have been noted for compliance .
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
114. The Committee notes the reply and would like to know reason for lack of fresh
proposals from States for seeking financial assistance under the scheme. It is of the view
that the Ministry should impress the State Governments to utilize the funds allocated under
the head effectively so that public transport system in the country gets a boost.
CREATION OF NATIONAL ROAD SAFETY BOARD
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
115. The Committee expresses its concern over the inordinate delay in further processing the
Legislation by the Government after it had submitted its report on the Bill in 2010. The Committee
would like to see that most of its concern/recommendations are accommodated.
(Para 137 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
116. The Government has examined the recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing
Committee and initiated necessary process to incorporate certain amendments in the bill in line with
the recommendations of the Committee for consideration of the Parliament.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
117. The Committee notes the reply and observes that the delay on the part of the
Ministry in bringing an amended National Road Safety and Traffic Management Board Bill
after incorporating the recommendations of the Committee exposes its seriousness towards
strengthening of road safety mechanism in the country.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
118. The Committee after examining the information and data furnished by the Ministry as well
as NHAI feels that Gross Budgetary Support for road sector, one of the major infrastructure

20
sectors, is dwindling. The Ministry during the deliberations had accepted that, in fact, non-
availability of funds for road projects forced many concessionaires to withdraw from their projects
during the last year. The reduced GBS during the Twelfth Plan Period would in fact make the
matter from bad to worse. The Committee hopes that revised guidelines of RBI on funding of road
projects will bring necessary financial inputs from the private players.
(Para 138 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
119. Ministry agrees with the recommendation and the observation has been noted.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
120. The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
121. The Committee feels concerned about the poor spending of its allocations by the
Ministry. The Ministry has consistently shown very low spending of its allocations for road
transport sector which comprises important schemes like road safety, driving training and
research, procurement of road safety and pollution testing equipments and National
Highways Accident Relief Scheme. The Committee calls upon the Ministry to improve its
performance in spending allocations for road transport sector.
(Para 139 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
122. The sug gestions of the Committee for proper planning and execution of the road transport
project including better utilization of funds have been noted for compliance .
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
123. The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
124. The Committee notes that while on the one side allocations of funds for roads are being
reduced, its targets on various road related projects are being increased despite of non-clearance
of their backlog. The Committee feels that the Ministry should either go for enhancement of funds
at RE stage or revisit its targets fixed and modify them accordingly on the basis of ground realities
faced by them in executing road projects.
(Para 140 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
125. This Ministry will try to ensure utilization of the entire BE allocation funds within first three
quarters and solicit additional allocation during RE stage.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
126. The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the Ministry will try to utilize the
allocated funds towards all the projects to the maximum possible extent.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
4. The Committee appreciates 108% increase in the Twelfth Plan allocation but takes a serious
note of the fact that during the Eleventh Plan period, of the total Gross Budgetary Support of
Rs.3337.58 crore, the Ministry could incur actual expenditure of Rs. 2151.53 crore only. With such
a poor spending during Eleventh Plan, 108% enhancement in the allocations for the Twelfth Plan,
throws a big challenge before the Ministry to optimally utilize the enhanced amount during the
Twelfth Plan. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take necessary steps right from
the beginning itself to ensure that the on-going as well as proposed projects go as per the schedule.
No expenditure should be incurred hurriedly at the fag end of the year and it should be as per the
guidelines in this regard. Moreover, delay should also be avoided as it ultimately results into cost
and time overruns. There should not be any compromise on the quality of works.
(Para No. 6 of 194
th Report)
Reply of the Government
5. Noted for compliance.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7. The Committee notes with concern that the Ministry was not able to utilize its funds mainly
due to ship-building and dredging subsidy schemes. It could have been avoided with proper
assessment and foresight as these schemes are not new. Underutilization, in fact, defeats the
purpose of having a planned budget and allocations itself. The Ministry has claimed that except
IWAI, the Shipping and Port sectors have expended the allocations satisfactorily. Whereas,
compared to the BE, the expenditure incurred in the Port Sector is only 54.77% and 33.56% by
the other organization like DCI, ALHW, SCI, etc., altogether in the Shipping Sector the expenditure
is about 71.77%.
(Para No. 10)
Reply of the Government
8. Prior to formulation of budget estimates, generally Ministry ascertains from Shipyard
Association of India (SAI) as to how many ships are likely to be delivered by different yards during
the year so that adequate outlay is kept for honouring the subsidy claims of the shipyards in
respect of the vessels to be delivered. However, in the last couple of years it has generally been
observed that Shipyards have not adhered to the delivery schedule with the result that a major part
of the outlay are left unutilized with no fault of the Ministry. Although, these outlays have
substantially been reduced at RE stage but still a good part thereof remained unutilized. For the year
2012-13, Shipyard Association of India projected the requirement of Rs. 817 crores but seeing to
the past trend of expenditure, Ministry pegged the Budget Estimates at Rs. 400.00 and same was
reduced to Rs. 220.00 crores at RE stage. As the utilization of funds during the year was closely
monitored on monthly basis therefore, resulting we succeeded in utilization of 100% of the outlay
kept at the RE stage.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
9. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee however is not able to assess and
make any observation in this regard without knowing the reason as to why the Shipyards
are not being able to adhere to the delivery schedule and the efforts made to overcome
them. These reasons may not be strictly under Ministry’s control yet, it cannot remain a
mute spectator in this regard. Ministry should ensure that improved methodology be
adopted in assessing the actual requirement of funds for subsidy schemes as the current
procedure proved to be faulty and shipyards should strictly adhere to the delivery time.

and there are under-utilization as well. Major reductions have taken place in Ports, Ship Building

increased. The Committee once again recommends that, the Ministry should project a realistic
demand, prepare right estimate and also execute its plans properly.
(Para No. 11)
Reply of the Government
11. Noted for compliance.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13. The Committee observes that the GBS of 2012-13 at the BE stage was Rs. 817 crore which
was reduced to Rs.502 crore in the RE. The actual spending was Rs.494.83 crore. The Committee
feels that due to reduction/under-utilization of the allocations, the Planning Commission had to peg
the GBS during 2013-14 to Rs.852 crore even though the projected demand by the Ministry was
Rs.1329.42 crore. It can be seen that about 30% of the projected demand has been cut by the
Planning Commission. The Committee is of the view that such a cut in allocation to the Ministry
of Shipping could have been avoided if the funds were expended optimally during 2012-13 as the
Plan allocations have been decided on the basis of actual expenditure made in the previous year.
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may make it sure that its proposed plan expenditure
during 2013-14 may be kept as per schedule so that the present allocation of Rs.852 crore may
not be reduced at the RE stage as done in the previous years, leading to more cuts in the
succeeding years.
(Para No. 16)
Reply of the Government
14. Planning Commission fixes the Budget Estimate and Revised Estimate based on expenditure
trends as well as overall resource availability. In order to ensure that Plan expenditure keeps pace
with the schedule of expenditure of the projects, periodic review meetings are taken by Ports,
Shipping and IWT wings of the Ministry. Secretary (Shipping), also on a quarterly basis reviews
the Plan expenditure. The Committee’s recommendation to the Ministry that Plan expenditure during
2013-14 be kept as per schedule has been noted for compliance.

15. The Committee notes the efforts made by the Ministry through periodic review

2013-14 is utilized optimally.

28. Chennai Port Trust : The reasons for negative growth in ChPT is due to stoppage of
handling of coal from 11.5.2011 in pursuance of order of High Court of Madras and due to the
ban on export of iron-ore. Though ChPT is trying to compensate the loss with alternate cargo, the

port is striving hard to transform the port from mono-commodity to multi-commodities. During the

new cargo, M/s RITES has been asked to prepare a detailed study and submit a Techno-economic
report on feasibility of development of infrastructure for handling of container, liquid cargo,
LNG etc.
31. Jawahar Lal Nehru Port Trust: The negative growth at JNPT is mainly due to slow down
by PPP partners on account of drastic reduction in tariff by TAMP. So far as JNP owned and
operated terminal is concerned there is an increase in traffic of about 17.53% in terms of TEUs.

35. The major commodities which had declined are POL(Crude), POL(Product), Coking Coal,

Crude pipeline while the shortfall in POL(Product) can be attributed to the fall in coastal imports

throughput of the port.

47. Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) is a composite entity comprising Kolkata Dock System (KDS)
and Haldia Dock Complex (HDC) under one umbrella and common Board of Trustees. Consolidated
Annual Accounts of KoPT are prepared as a corporate entity and sent to the Ministry of Shipping

in KDS and separate Balance Sheets are drawn up for Management Information System (MIS).
Management and control of both the docks of Kolkata Port Trust are administered by a common
Board of Trustees and the Chairman is the executive head of both the docks and also of the
organization as a whole.
48. It is to be appreciated that productivity level of the two dock systems are not comparable

historical and geographical reasons. KDS has to bear the expenses of about 30,000 pensioners and

Committees for examining relationship between Kolkata Port Trust and
Haldia Dock Complex
A. Two-Man Committee
In 1975, Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport constituted a
Committee to examine the Working and Financial Position of the Kolkata Port and other allied
matters which included likely economic effects of Kolkata and Haldia Dock Systems operating
together as one port or separately as two ports. The Committee comprised Shri A.K. Mukherjee,
Dy. Comptroller and Auditor General of India and Shri P.R. Subramaniam, Former General Manager,
Bombay Port Trust. The findings and recommendations of the Committee submitted in June, 1976
on the issue of effect of commissioning of Haldia Dock Complex on Kolkata Dock System were
as follows :–
● Both Kolkata and Haldia Dock Systems are situated on the same river. The RT works
taken up by the Kolkata Port will have to be executed by one authority.
● In the interest of efficiency and economy, entire dredging work in the river should
remain under one authority.
● The river Bhagirathi-Hooghly is an extremely tricky waterway and therefore, hydraulic
study, river survey and river maintenance should remain under one authority to achieve
optimum result.
● With regard to the complex pilotage problem over 126 miles of fairway and shortage
of pilots, it is necessary that one authority should control the pilotage service. This will
ensure coordination of pilotage service to the best advantage of the two systems.
● As one port complex, Kolkata – Haldia will economically share the common workshop,
drydock, etc. Development of parallel facilities at Haldia will be wastage of scarce
financial resources.
● The two dock systems working as separate ports are likely to incur heavier
expenditure by way of overheads.
● As per paper prepared by IIPM, Kolkata Dock System would break even in 1987,
irrespective of operating alone or with Haldia as one unit. Haldia would break even in
1992 if it operates alone. Benefit/cost ratio from 1995 onwards would be higher for
the two dock systems operating together than if they operated as two ports.
● Port users (Chambers of Commerce, Shipping and Trade Interests, Labour Trustees,
State Government) had given memoranda or evidence showing that they were
overwhelmingly in favour of the two dock system being administered by one authority.
● If the two dock systems operated separately, overheads would be heavy, cost and
charges in Kolkata would increase, procedural difficulties would arise for exporters and
importers and competition may develop between Kolkata and Haldia for general cargo
traffic.

40
● Without any central assistance, the deficits of KDS were likely to be much less than
HDC. With dredging subsidy, KDS was likely to show surplus much earlier than Haldia.
There was very little likelihood of Haldia being saddled with the deficits of KDS if the
two systems operated as one port complex. The combined results of the two dock
systems would be better financially than are likely to be if they operate as separate
ports.
● Problem of surplus labour in Kolkata would not affect Haldia. Care should be taken
from the beginning that no restrictive practices among the labour developed at Haldia
as in Kolkata (restriction on inter-sectional movements).
● For day to day operation at Haldia, autonomy can be ensured by giving adequate
powers, both executive and financial to Haldia Management.
● In the matter of administrative arrangement for the ports or the dock systems situated
in the same river or estuary or in close proximity to another, the international trend
is to have one administrative authority. [ Eg. Port of London Authority for London and
Tilbury on Thames; Port of Rotterdam with Euro Port near Sea entrance; Bremen with
Bremerhaven; Port of Hamburg and Copshaven near the sea; Five dock systems on the
Garonne-Gironde River System in France operate under one authority; Port of
Baltimore and its new terminal at Dundalh Bay; Port of Philadelphia with facility at
Delaware Bay for deeper drafted vessels].
● It is the general practice that where the existing port authority on the river creates new
facilities down the river for obtaining deeper draft, the new dock system thus created
operates as a part of the older port. Similarly, when a number of port authorities exist
in close proximity, the tendency is to amalgamate them under one authority. This trend
is rational and allows the separate dock system to operate more economically and
optimally utilize the facilities by avoiding wasteful competition.
● In view of the above, the Committee recommended that the two dock systems should
be placed under the same Trust Body. Haldia should have an organization invested with
adequate power. It should have a General Manager ( subsequently designated as Dy.
Chairman) corresponding in status to the Dy. Chairman of Kolkata Port Trust and he
should be a member of the Board of Trustees and work directly under the Chairman
and the Board. The personnel in HDC will have separate cadre. The accounting of
Haldia and Kolkata should be separate. At the end of the month, a combined account
should be prepared treating the accounts of the two dock systems as subsidiary
accounts. Common services should be apportioned suitably. HDC should operate as
complementary to KDS as one Trust Body.
In June, 1977, Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping & Transport accepted the
recommendations of the Committee in respect of the two dock systems being placed under one
Trust Body. To ensure development of Haldia on healthy lines, Govt. issued further instructions on
the accounting system, personnel matters (separate cadres with separate promotional opportunities),
cost apportionment, major repairs to mechanical plants and machinery at KDS, not developing
restrictive labour practices at Haldia, etc.).
B.  Laxminarayan Committee
After commissioning of HDC in February, 1977, certain difficulties were highlighted in
respect of inter-personnel relationship, establishment powers, operational matters like calling of
ships, providing pilots, transfer of funds from Haldia to Kolkata, lack of workshop facilities,

41

unit.
● Full powers of Chairman, KoPT to Dy. Chairman, HDC including powers of

● Separate cadre for personnel working at Haldia to be set up.
● Pilotage service should be gradually separated and pilots should be based at Haldia.

14.1.2.1 Planning
With a view to study the fuel consumption pattern in the dredgers and fix norms of fuel
consumption, DCI had engaged M/s TERI to evolve a specific fuel consumption norm

the fuel consumption. The production process of the trailer suction hopper dredger is
cyclical and the output is influenced by the cycle comprising of Sailing, Dumping and
Loading. Depending on the time period of these three factors within a cycle, the major
influencing factors for variation in the fueI consumption are the soil characteristics, type
of dredging assignment, type of dredger deployed for a particular assignment.
The fuel consumption norms indicated by the original equipment manufacturers (OEM),
which are valid for normal working conditions, are variable in the actual working
conditions and dependent on the various factors brought out above.
The MOU norms for fuel consumption are fixed basing on specific fuel oil consumption
data given by OEMs as adjusted by the trends in actual consumption. As such the MOU
norms tend to be higher than the norms suggested by OEMs at the time of supply of

14.1.2.2 Procurement
As per the Board approved Purchase Procedure of DCI vide Chapter VI, Exceptions and
Deviations, Sl. No. 6.1, it is stated that tender procedure need not be followed in the
cases where the prices are controlled by Government or Government bodies, such as
POL. As such, view of the Audit that Purchase Procedure is not followed by not inviting
tender for supply of fuel and lubricants is not correct.
Based on the need for supplying fuel at dredging sites located at various ports on both
coasts, and the sourcing from IOC based on the prices controlled by Government, the
system followed by the company for procurement of fuel and lubricants is as follows:
The indent/requisition is raised by dredgers and forwarded to the concerned project
office with copy to Head Office. The indents are made taking into consideration the
available fuel on board and the requirement for the dredging operations. On receipt of
the indent, the project office intimates the bunker requirement, place and time of supply
to IOC and closely coordinates the timely fuel supplies. The payment for the supplies
is made at Head Office basing on the scheduled price lists. The fuel oil consumption is
monitored from Head Office. Since a formal system of indenting/ordering/receiving land
bill payment/monitoring is in existence, the contention of Audit that the Company did not
follow a regular internal control procedure is not correct.
The Company tried to identify suitable alternate source of supply for bunkers from other
companies like HPCL, BPCL etc., which proved unsuccessful due to non response/
insufficient infrastructure by these companies. The companies like HPCL/BPCL expect
assurance from DCI for the off take of minimum assured quantity for developing
infrastructure in ports whereas in case of IOC, the company is well established and
having fully developed facilities in all ports in India.
IOC declined to extend the credit facilities for supply of fuel and lubricants due to their
present financial crunch. All the PSU oil companies are facing similar crunch. Hence to
ensure uninterrupted supplies of fuel the request of IOC to make weekly progressive
payment of Rs. 4 crore to be adjusted against invoices for supply was accepted.
However basing on the adjustments carried out the excess paid amount if any, is being
reduced regularly from the advance payments.

50
14.1.2.3 Issue and consumption of fuel lubricants
The present bunkering system being followed in the Company is stated by the Audit.
However the statement that there is no laid down procedure for recording consumption
of fuel on board the dredgers is not correct. Quantities of bunkers received, consumed
and balances are recorded in the logs maintained on board dredgers. The data from these
logs is furnished to HO in the Daily Utilisation Reports (OUR). The system of reconciliation
of fuel consumption is based on the OUR and Engine Log Book data. The OUR data
received from the dredgers comprise of reserve on board along with fuel consumption
on day to day basis and is being monitored.
Supply of fuel at Sethusamudram Canal Project
Dredgers Sagar Hansa and Pacifique were hired on daily rate basis and there was no
specific clause in the Charter Party (CP) Agreements that the rate payable was subject
to any specific production guarantee. The fuel oil to be provided by charterer as per the
daily consumption given in the CPs was based on the technical specifications of the
dredgers and not related to or subject to specific production. The estimated
production(material dredged as measured in the hopper) arrived and indicated in the CPs
was only for the purpose of regularisation of cost of spares and repairs of soil touching
parts. In any case, the said estimated production cannot be taken as actual production.
Considering this estimated production as guaranteed production and evaluating excess
issue of fuel is technically not appropriate and realistic. Further technically no direct
relation can be established between the fuel consumption and production as there are
other related factors like dredging cycle, dumping distance, soil characteristics, area of
deployment and condition of equipment used - have bearing on both consumption and
production.
The designed theoretical consumption of fuel oil varies from dredger to dredger depending
on factors like design of Main Engine, dredging and other equipment, their capacities,
usage and operating performances, age of the vessel and condition, as also the type of
soil dredged. It also varies depending on the grade of fuel oil used. Variable parameters
like dredging cycle, dumping distance, area of deployment cause a major impact on fuel
consumption. In view of these conditions, direct comparison of fuel oil consumption
between two dredgers is not appropriate even though the installed power/ capacities are
similar.

51
14.1.2.4 Claims for reimbursement of fuel escalation
The claims for fuel escalation are raised at project offices where all claims on the
customer are made. For settling the claims, customer requires copies of bills with pass
orders as proof of payment. The delays in raising fuel escalation claims are partly due
to delay in receiving bills form IOC for adjustment after making the weekly advance.
In some instances the bills were received two to three months after supplies. This matter
is being continuously pursued with lOC. After receipt of the bills from IOC the same
are being verified for the quantity supplied, passed for payment/adjustment against
advance and forwarded to project offices for raising the claims. This process involves
time and sometimes delays are occurring in the process.
The long outstanding escalation claims are related to the long outstanding dredging
claims which are in turn due to disputes. Customers did not make payments of these
escalation claims as the related dredging claims were not accepted by them. However,
all efforts are being made to obtain payment in respect of long outstanding claims
As regards comment of Audit that due to non existence of any contractual provision
relating to levy of interest on delayed payment of fuel escalation claim, the Company
suffered interest loss, the following is submitted.
Except, Kolkata Port, all other Ports award dredging contracts basing on Tenders.
Tender clauses are specified by these Ports, which vary from port to port. The
Company, upon receiving tender documents analyzes the tender conditions and seek
necessary amendments/modifications to the tender conditions keeping in view, the
technical feasibility, commercial viability and Company’s interests. However, the tenders
being open tenders and in case the ports are not willing to modify the tender conditions
to include interest payment for delayed payment of escalation bills. The Company is left
with no option except to go by the tender conditions so that it is not disqualified due
to non-compliance of tender conditions. In fact, the Company has taken deviations and
sought payment of interest on delayed payments over the agreed time schedules in
almost all the tenders which, however, the respective ports have not agreed to.
In respect of contracts awarded on nomination basis, as most of these contracts are
awarded on long term basis, it is not possible to insist on uniform payment conditions
including escalation payments keeping in view the longstanding relationships with these ports.

52
14.1.2.5 Oversight Role
Governance by the Board of Directors.
The fuel consumption norms as reflected in the MOU parameter are fixed not only
basing on the OEM recommended SFOC but also the actual consumption trends
observed with the experience gained over the years. The actual performance against
MOU targets is submitted to Board of Directors on quarterly basis and the performance
is analyzed and discussed in the Board meetings.
The conclusion of the audit that targets of fuel consumption are not fixed scientifically
since MOU norms fixed are above the SFOC of the OEM, is not correct since as stated
above the targets are fixed based on OEM norms as adjusted to the actual dredging
conditions.
Review of performance by the Administrative Ministry
The parameters under various categories in MOU like, Financial, Dynamic and Sector /
Enterprise specific, and their respective weightages are determined by OPE which are
reflected in the MOU Guidelines issued by OPE each year. The tri-partite, MOU
negotiation meeting discusses various parameters selected and their weightages with due
consideration as to the “vitality” of the parameter.
Conclusion
The norms for fuel oil consumption are fixed basing on the designed theoretical
consumption norms indicated by the equipment manufacturers (OEM), as adjusted to the
actual working conditions. The consumption of fuel by a dredger varies from port to
port and from site to site within a port depending on the dredging cycle and the soil
characteristics at the site of dredging. As such arriving at a standard rate of consumption
for a dredger is difficult. However, the norms are fixed most scientifically taking various
operational parameters into account.
The procurement of the fuel oil is as per Board approved purchase procedure for
supplies whose prices are controlled by the Government. The procurement from IOC is

53
due to its existing facilities to supply the requirement of both fuel oil and lubricants to
the dredgers at all the dredging locations in the country and at the time of requirement
by the dredgers for continuous dredging operations.
Fuel consumption by dredgers is continuously monitored through the Dredger Utilisation
Reports sent regularly by the dredgers. Claims for fuel escalation are being made at
earliest possible time after obtaining ‘invoices’ from IOC.
Considering the above factors, the conclusion of Audit that the Company lost opportunities
to save Rs. 164.63 crore over period of four years, is hypothetical.

STATUS NOTE ON SHORE HANDLING OF CARGO/CHARGES LEVIABLE AND THE

On the subject, the following information is furnished.
2. Under the Kolkata Port Trust, various agencies and firms undertake different types of cargo
handling activities at KDS and HDC for which different types of licences and/or permits
are issued by port.
3. The provisions regarding issuance of different types of Licenses/Permits were first laid
down in 1949 in the By-laws of the Commissioners for the Port of Kolkata. The licences
covered under this include the following:
Sl. No. Type of License Section of By-law
(i) Stevedoring License (Sec 4A) for Stevedoring activity Sec 4A
on board ships
(ii) Ship’s servicing License for Chipping, Painting work. Sec 4A (2) (A)
(iii) Ship’s servicing License for supply of Watchmen or Dock Sec 4A (2) (B)
Clerical and Supervisory Workers
(iv) Ship’s servicing License for Ship Chandling, Dubashing, Sec 4A (2) (C)
Victualing, Ship’s maintenance and repairs, Surveying or
any other service not specifically mentioned in the By-law.
(v) Hawker’s License Sec 76
4. Subsequently, as the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 came up, which empowered the Board
of Port Trusts to pass regulations to control various activities concerning the ports. In line
with the same, the Calcutta Port Trust (Licensing of Stevedores) Regulations came in force
in 1987.
5. Although Haldia Dock came into being in the year 1977, the on board handling of cargo
have been undertaken by port through deployment of its own workforce. Shore handling of
cargo at HDC is done by different agents (commonly called as Handling Agents) appointed
by the concerned importers/ exporters. Normally, the agencies who were working at KDS
and are having Stevedoring or Clearing or Shipping Agency License were allowed to
undertake activities as Handling Agent in Haldia. No separate license was thus enforced for
undertaking such activities at HDC since beginning. It may be on the same logic that HDC
being a part and parcel of KoPT, the licenses issued from KDS are also valid as the same
are valid at Budge Budge, Diamond Harbour or Saugor which are far away places from
KDS.
6. With the introduction of private equipments in the Container Operation at KDS, the need for
license to Handling Agents was felt necessary and accordingly based on the rate for
54

55
Handling Agent’s license was first time included in the Scale of Rates on 10.03.88.
Procedure for issuance of Handling Agency License by Traffic Manager at Kolkata was
framed. The present Scale of Rates for KoPT is also having a provision of issuance of
Clearing-Forwarding/Handling Agency license for a period of two years.
7. Relevantly, till 2007, for all bulk and break bulk cargo at Haldia (excluding at mechanised
berths), transfer of cargo on shore to the hook point to stack yard and vice versa  is
arranged by the concerned importer/exporter at HDC for which they engage their service
providers (called as Handling Agents). KoPT started issuing license to them from 1988 as
stated in para 7 above. Prior to that, no license for such shore operation was in vogue;
but based on the declaration of the importer or the exporter concerned, permits were being
issued for bringing in equipments and manpower for such operation.
8. The exclusive provision of shore handling (including transportation) of bulk and break bulk
cargo at the port along with the charges thereof was first created in 2007 under Section
6 of KoPT’s SoR, which was approved by TAMP. However, beside this the said SoR, under
Note (i) of Section 6, also contained a provision as follow:
“Port reserves the right to supply or not supply labour/equipment for shore handling
operation other than tippling of wagon.”
Based on this provision, KoPT for the first time, considered engaging a contractor for
integrated ship-shore cargo handling operation at Berth No. 2 & 8 only through an open
tender floated in 2007 and ABG Haldia Bulk Terminal Ltd. was inducted as the contractor
for providing such services on behalf of KoPT, for which KoPT could levy tariff approved
by TAMP. At other berths, however, the importers/exporters continued to arrange shore
handling of cargo through their appointed agents.
9. However, consequent to the unilateral decision of M/s ABG Haldia Bulk Terminal Ltd. to
withdraw themselves from Haldia Dock, the cargo handling operation vis-à-vis  revenue
earning of KoPT faced a set back resulting in drop in revenue of KoPT. In this context,
various issues including revenue loss of KoPT as well as non-generation on income from
shore activities at other berths was raised by the both print and electronic media.
10. In course of exploring alternative avenues for additional revenue generation, discussions
were held at appropriate levels. Accordingly the issue of levy of royalty on service providers
was discussed with KoPT’s counsel Sri Jayanta Mitra, Bar-at-Law who opined in favour of
levy of royalty on the service providers under Sub-section 3A of Section 42 of the MPT
Act, 1963. The said counsel opined for levy of such royalty by appointing service providers
through open auctioning. Upon placement of proposal, levy of such royalty was approved
by the Board on 12.10.12, which, however, excluded commodities like container & liquid
cargo.
11. In Board’s meeting held on 13.12.12, it was resolved to send the Board’s aforesaid
approved proposal to the Ministry of Shipping for their necessary approval towards levy of
such royalty and auctioning of Handling Agent licenses on the basis of performance
indicators & TAMP approved tariff.
12. Relevantly, so far the Ministry has notified policy and levy only in respect of Stevedoring
Activities, which is different from shore handling operations. As gathered from the other
Indian Major Ports, shore handling operations at these ports are mostly done by the service
providers appointed by the concerned importers/exporters and no levy is imposed there on
such service providers.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture having authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this Two Hundred and Eighth Report on Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendations/observations of the Committee contained in its One Hundred Ninety Fifth Report
on the Demands for Grants (2013-14) of Ministry of Tourism.

Hundred Ninety Fifth Report were received from the Ministry of Tourism on the 6 th August, 2013.

REPORT

the observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and Ninety Fifth Report on
Demands for Grants (2013-14) of the Ministry of Tourism, which was presented to both the
Houses of Parliament on 3
rd May, 2013.
2. The Action Taken Replies received from the Ministry in respect of all the observations/
recommendations contained in the Report have been categorized as follows:–

Para Nos. 10, 11, 12, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 40, 50, 58, 61, 91, 100, 101, 102, 107,

(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Department replies:

(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Department have not
been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos . Nil

livelihood of local inhabitants and attempt to minimize such conflicts.
● The type and scale of eco-tourism development should be compatible with the
environment and socio-cultural characteristics of the local community; and
● It should be planned as a part of the overall area development strategy, guided by an

161. The Committee observes that sky rocketing of airfares and lack of Government control over
it has recently affected the domestic tourist movement in the country. The Committee also observes
that higher user fee and ATF surcharges have eventually made the air traffic journey un-affordable
to many. The DGCA has taken some steps in this regard. The Committee however, recommends
that a more regular and strict watch on predatory airfares being resorted by the airlines needs to
done to prevent unreasonable airfares especially during the peak seasons.
(Para No. 132 ibid)

25
Reply of the Government
162. The recommendation of the Committee has been noted for compliance. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
163. The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
164. The Committee also observes that the rail travellers are facing problems due to shabby
coaches which are usually unclean with rodents roaming freely. The toilets are very dirty and are
seldom cleansed during the journey. Beggar menace and under quality food served are other areas
to be immediately attended. All these problems have made the train journey a nightmare for most
of the travellers and the tourists in particular. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism
may take up the matter with Railway Board so that the train journey may be made attractive and
comfortable to the tourists.
(Para No. 133 ibid)
Reply of the Government
165. Prime Minister’s  Office has constituted an Inter Ministerial Coordination Committee for
Tourism Sector (IMCCTS) under the Chairmanship of the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister
to facilitate the resolution of inter-ministerial issues involved in the development of tourism in the
country, as well as issues raised by Industry Associations in the tourism sector. The Ministry of
Tourism takes up all such issues through this Committee with the Ministry of Railways.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
166. The Committee desires to know the follow up action in this regard.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
167. The Committee observes that we are not utilizing the full potential of tourism in India. We
always feel very sad about the fact that, probably, there is no country like ours that has snow,
hills to seas and beaches, adventure tourism, wildlife tourism, medical tourism, etc., within the
country. India has such a wide variety and destination. In spite of that, the confidence does not
seem to come that we are able to actually reach anyway close to using our potential.
(Para No. 134 ibid)
Reply of the Government
168. The Ministry of Tourism has a target to increase India’s share of International Tourist
arrivals to at least 1% by the end of Twelfth Plan and provide adequate facilities for domestic
tourism to sustain the growth of 12.16% during Twelfth Plan period.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
169. The Committee hopes that the decline in rupee value may bring more international
tourists to the country as a trip to India is cheaper than before.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this Two Hundred and Ninth Report on “Action Taken Replies by the Ministry of Civil
Aviation on the observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and Ninety First
Report on Demands for Grants (2013-14) of the Ministry of Civil Aviation”.

Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented on the 3
rd May, 2013 to the
Parliament.

Hundred and Ninety First Report was received from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 1 st October, 2013.

17th December, 2013.

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation
on the observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and Ninety First Report on
Demands for Grants (2013-14) of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, which was presented to both the
Houses of Parliament on 3
rd May, 2013.
2. The Action Taken Replies received from the Ministry in respect of all the observations/
recommendations contained in the Report have been categorized as follows:–
(i) Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Department:
Para Nos. 7, 10, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 47, 61, 62, 63, 73, 76, 82, 88, 91, 93,
101 and 103
(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view
of the Department replies:
Nil. 69, 80, 94 and 102
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Department have not
been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos. 87, 99 and 100
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry are still
awaited:
Para Nos. 10, 37, 38, 88, 89, 90 and 92
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of these recommendations/
observations, which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be
furnished to it at the earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee
contained in the One Hundred and Ninety First Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry and
recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the
succeeding paragraphs
ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
5. The Committee finds that the spending pattern of Plan funds has been poor during
2012-13 which needs a lot of improvement. The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Civil
