MOU to protect the interest of Indian carriers/airport operators. The enhancement in traffic
entitlements has been done in a phased manner with sector specific capping, limiting the
operational flexibility of the foreign carrier and providing adequate time to Indian carriers to
plan and consolidate their position to keep pace with growing Indian aviation market. Further,
stakeholder consultation is invariably done prior to bilateral negotiations and views of all the
stakeholders including the national carrier is taken into account by inter-ministerial group
comprising of representatives from various ministries/departments to decide the negotiating
strategy and mandate for the negotiating team. The recent negotiations in respect of India-Abu
Dhabi air services matters was done as per the mandate given by a Group of Ministers. The
bilateral traffic rights to Indian carriers are allocated as per laid down guidelines. However,
primacy of the national carrier has been retained as traffic rights are allocated to other carriers
only after considering the operational requirements of Air India.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
73. The Committee notes the reply and feels that the issue of bilaterals with UAE leaves
several questions unanswered. The Ministry’s reply suggests that this decision was taken
more on subjective consideration than objective/concrete ones. The real impact of this will
be against the interest of domestic carriers.

13
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
74. The Committee finds that already, India is struggling to create a world class hub at Delhi,
faced with competition from airports like Dubai and Doha in the Gulf and Bangkok, Hong Kong
and Singapore in South East Asia and despite leading airports like Delhi and Mumbai having been
privatized. While Delhi and other private airports along with the Government of India have made
huge investments in upgrading infrastructure and building new world class terminals, they are
hampered by the competition posed by these well-established hubs and their aggressive mega
carriers. Allowing Abu Dhabi to come up as another hub which is only about three hours flight
away from the major Indian metros might have adverse impact on our efforts to establish a world
class hub in India.
(Para 87 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
75. At present, 6 state of the art airports have been developed at metro cities namely Delhi,
Mumbai, Bangalore, Hyderabad,, Chennai and Kolkata. In addition, Airports Authority of India (AAI)
has also modernized and upgraded 35 airports and several Greenfield airports are also coming up
in important cities. It has been identified that airports at metro cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata
and Chennai can emerge as strong hub airports while Hyderabad and Bangalore also have fair
potential for development of hub airports. The Government of India has already constituted a
standing Inter-Ministerial Group(IMG) comprising of Secretary (Civil Aviation) as Chairman with
representatives from Planning Commission, Department of Revenue, Department of Economic
Affairs, Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Ministry of External Affairs
and Ministry of Home Affairs to remove the bottlenecks and to provide the right coordination
mechanism for the development of aviation hubs in India.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
76. The Committee finds the reply abjectly evasive; it has not responded to the issue/
apprehension underlined by the Committee in the above recommendation. The Ministry in
future should be precise and to the point in its replies.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
77. The Committee feels that creating hubs needs time and also a home carrier with a critical
size to be able to sustain the hub. Air India has just started to create a hub in Delhi as its chosen
hub, which needs to be encouraged/supported in its endeavour. The development of events will,
no doubt, have adverse impact on Air India’s efforts in this regard.
(Para 88 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
78. Air India established a hub at Delhi Airport in the year 2010-11 with a time table in order
to take advantage of the infrastructure facilities available at T3. The integrated terminal at Delhi
serves at a gateway point to the East and West. Delhi serves as an effective Hub. Flights from
various domestic destinations connect to the flighs from Delhi to USA, UK, South East Asia, Middle
East and Gulf. The additional bilateral entitlements to Abu Dhabi would not affect the carriage of
traffic by AI as Air India would be operating direct services to destinations in Europe and North
America.

14
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
79. The Committee notes the reply and would like to know the grounds/basis based on
which it has said that said bilaterals with UAE would not affect Air India traffic.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
80. The Committee finds that Air India is already struggling to make a turn around as Indian
passengers prefer to travel via the foreign hubs. Rs.30,000 crores of taxpayer’s money is being
pumped into it by the Government to keep it afloat and signs of certain turnaround is already
visible.
(Para 89 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
81. The recommendations of the Committee noted for compliance.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
82. The Committee notes the reply as interim reply only.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
83. The Committee is of the opinion that in this way, Air India will be denied the ability to
establish direct services to long haul destinations with the B787 Dreamliner that they have ordered
for this very purpose. If the Ministry supports the development of more and more hubs outside
India, thousands of crores of taxpayer’s money will go waste, not to mention the investment of
thousands of crores made by private enterprise along with the Government in developing world
class airports in Delhi and other major metros.
(Para 90 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
84. The recommendations of the Committee noted for compliance.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
85. The Committee notes the reply as interim reply and further action on the
observations of the Committee may be appraised duly.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
86. The Committee notes that no sound Civil Aviation Policy exists in India which is the need
of the hour. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should come out with
a clear Civil Aviation Policy with an aim to provide growth to the national carrier and national
airports.
(Para 92 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
87. In view of the significant growth of the sector and the current problems being faced, the
need for a National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP) is being felt again. The Minister of Civil Aviation

15
had also desired that a Civil Aviation Policy be formulated to address the long term issues of the
Civil Aviation sector. Accordingly, a Committee has been constituted under the Chairmanship of
Secretary.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
88. The Committee would like to know terms of reference, date of constitution,
composition of the Committee alongwith the period within which it is supposed to submit
its report.
SALE OF BILATERAL BY JET AIRWAYS
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
89. The Committee was informed that Jet Airways sold three of its slots in London to the
Ethihad Airlines and the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation has confirmed that the Ministry is
aware of the development. The Committee feels that carriers have no right to sell the bilateral
allotted to them to other airlines that too foreign airline. The Committee recommends that the
Government should take away the slots from Jet Airways and the airlines should be penalized for
selling the national property – bilateral.
(Para 94 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
90. The slots are permissions to use runway and airport infrastructure and are allocated by the
airports to the airlines as per their procedure. The airlines at Heathrow (London) are free to swap/
trade the slots with any other airline through lease or buy it from other airlines. This operates on
the principle of willing buyers and willing sellers. As demand exceeds supply at Heathrow, slot
trading is now the principle means of entry. This is purely the function of Airport coordination Ltd.
of Heathrow airport and the airlines. The Government of India has no role in allocation of slots
at any foreign airport including Heathrow Airport. Jet Airways has informed that they were
allocated 1 pair of slots in November, 2005 and subsequently bought 3 pairs of slots in 2005 and
2006 and out of which 1 pair of slots has been sold by them to Omen Air. Jet Airways have
further informed that they have also sold the remaining 3 pairs of slots to Etihad airways and have
subsequently leased them back after due compliance with relevant statues, rules and regulations and
are using these slots for their operations.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
91. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
SETTING UP OF ARANMULA AIRPORT IN KERALA
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
92. The Committee finds that the proposed Greenfield airport in Aranmula (Kerala) is 120 km
from Trivandrum and 90 km from Cochin, both are international airports and it is violative of the
Government policy of not allowing an airport within 150 km. Moreover, the Kochin International
Airport and Thiruvananthapuram Airport are brand new airports and there is no scope for saturation
of capacity in these airports in near future. The Committee notes that the proposed Aranmula
Airport is violating the principles of 150 kms distance rule and the saturation of the nearby existing

16
airports. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the proposal for construction of Aranmula
Airport may be reconsidered by the Government.
(Para 99 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
93. Clause 8.1 of Policy for Airport Infrastructure envisages that (a) No Greenfield airport
would be allowed within an aerial distance of 150 kms of an existing civilian airport and (b) In
case a Greenfield airport is proposed to be set up within 150 kms of an existing civilian airport,
the impact on the existing airport would be examined. Such cases would be decided by the
Government on a case to case basis.
94. Ministry of Civil Aviation had granted necessary site clearance for the project and necessary
comments from Ministry of Defence, Directorate General of Civil Aviation, Planning Commission,
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Home Affairs and Airports Authority of India.
95. In its 13
th meeting of the Steering Committee on Greenfield airports held on 17 th August,
2012, the Committee noted that the nearest civilian airports are Cochin and Thiruvanathapuram. The
project falls within an aerial distance of about 150 kms from the existing airports at Cochin and
Thiruvanathapuram. In the meeting, the State Government which is the promoter of Cochin airport
and AAI which owns and operates Thiruvanathpuram airport supported the proposal. After detailed
discussion, the Committee recommended to the Central Government for grant of ‘in principle’
approval for setting up of the airport. The Central Government accepted the recommended of the
Steering Committee and granted ‘in principle’ approval to the project.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
96. The Committee is aghast to note that the Ministry of Civil Aviation had granted site
clearance etc. and ‘in principle’ approval has been accorded to the Project.
(Para 99)
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
97. The Committee in its 131
st Report on the Closure of Bangalore and Hyderabad Airports
expressed its apprehensions over the closure of existing Government owned airports to facilitate the
private Greenfield airports there. The Government took shelter behind the Concession Agreement
signed with the two private airport operators to justify the closure of government owned airports
in Bangalore and Hyderabad. In this backdrop, the Committee fails to understand the logic behind
granting ‘in principle’ approval by the Central Government for Aranmula Greenfield Airport project.
The Committee feels that the Government should come out with a clear policy decision on new
airports within 150 km radius of existing one.
(Para 100 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
98. The Government of India, keeping in view the enormous growth in air passengers and to
encourage infusion of greater investment in airport sector, pronounced a policy for Greenfield
Airport in April, 2008. Clause 8.1 of the Policy for Greenfield Airports envisages that (a) No
Greenfield airport would be allowed within an aerial distance of 150 km of an existing civilian
airport and (b) In case a Greenfield airport is proposed to be set up within 150 km of an existing
civilian airport, the impact on the existing airport would be examined. Such cases would be decided

17
by the Government on a case to case basis. Hence the Government is having a clear policy in the
matter.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
99. The Committee feels that Government’s policy for “Greenfield Airports” as
implemented is not in favour of airports operated by “Airports Authority of India”.
General Observations
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
100. The Committee finds that except equity boost for Air India, the Union Budget 2013 has
nothing special to offer for the Indian aviation sector. The industry’s most vociferous demand of
reduction of sales tax on ATF which varies from 4-25 from states to states and ‘declared goods’
status for ATF could not be addressed by the Government in this year’s budget also. ATF price
in the country remains among the highest and this is the main cause for higher cost operations
of air service providers.
(Para 101 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
101. The matter of placing V AT on ATF under declared Goods category (which attracts a lower
and uniform rate of 5% ) under the provisions of Central Sales Tax Act was taken up with Ministry
of Finance. However, this has not been agreed to by Ministry of Finance. Separately, Ministry of
Civil Aviation had taken up the matter of reducing V AT on ATF with several State Government. The
State Governments of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand have reduced V AT on ATF to 4%.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
102. The Committee recommends that efforts may be made to rationalize taxes and
observes that uniform sales tax on ATF throughout the country will stabilize the cost of
operation of air service providers.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
103. The Committee feels that the much hyped creation of Civil Aviation Authority to take care
of all the regulatory and investigative needs of the aviation sector with more powers is still pending
with the Ministry. The Ministry had been informing the Committee for couple of years now that
they are contemplating the Civil Aviation Authority to bifurcate and delineate the functions of policy
maker, regulator and investigator in civil aviation sector. The Committee hopes that the draft Bill
for the purpose would be taken on priority to give the authority required shape.
(Para 102 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
104. A Cabinet Note and a Bill for setting up of a Civil Aviation Authority have been submitted
to the Cabinet.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
105. The Civil Aviation Authority of India Bill, 2013 is under the consideration of

18
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.
A Report containing the recommendations/observations of the Committee on the Bill will be
submitted separately.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
106. The Committee hopes that allocation of additional funds for Air India and Airports Authority
of India at RE level will help these organizations to carry on their programmes/projects for the
betterment of aviation industry in the country.
(Para 103 of ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
107. Ministry is pursuing with Department of Expenditure for grant of additional budget at RE
stage.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
108. The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the continuous efforts taken by the
Ministry for allocation of additional funds at RE stage for Air India and Airports Authority
of India with Ministry of Finance will yield some positive results.

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
observations/recommendations as contained in its One-Hundred and Eighty-Eighth Report on
“Functioning of Commission of Railways Safety” which was presented to both the Houses of
Parliament on 27
th February, 2013.
2. The Ministry of Civil Aviation submitted the interim Action Taken Replies on 7 th October,
2013 and the final Action Taken Replies on 22 nd January, 2014 containing the views of Ministry
of Railways also. The Committee heard the views of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Railway
Board on the Action Taken Replies in its meeting held on 27
th January, 2014. The observations/
recommendations contained in the Report have been categorized as follows:—
(i) Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry:
Para Nos. 23, 56, 57, 84, 85, 86, 96 and 97
(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Ministry replies:
Para Nos. 57, 58, 73, 85, 87 and 97
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not
been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos. 16, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 55, 56, 59, 71, 72, 84 and 98
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry are
still awaited:
Para Nos. 8, 17, 18, 42, 48, 49, 50, 76, 77 and 94
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which
have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the
earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the concerned Ministries. The recommendations of
the Committee contained in the One Hundred and Eighty Eighth Report, action taken/views thereon
by the Ministries of Civil Aviation and Railways and further recommendations/observations of the
Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
5. However, after the first round of discussions with the both the Ministries separately and
also with the CCRS, the Committee found that the two Ministries had quite different, sometimes
opposite views on certain crucial issues relating to effectiveness, autonomy and need to empower
and restructure the CRS. The Ministry of Railways maintained that the CRS was fulfilling its
mandate effectively and had enjoyed complete autonomy and that its views are taken quite seriously
and most of its recommendations are implemented and that there was no need to disturb the
existing arrangement to further restructure/empower CRS. The Ministry of Civil Aviation which is
also Central Government for the CRS had expressed contrary views on many such issues.
(Para No. 8 of 188
th Report)

2
REPLY FROM M/O RAILWAYS
6. Noted. It is reiterated that the existing institution of the Commission of Railway Safety
under the Ministry of Civil Aviation is working satisfactorily. There is no interference from the
Ministry of Railways in the functioning of the Commission.
STAND OF MINISTRY OF CIVIL A VIATION
7. Effectiveness of Commission of Railway Safety is much below the required level as present
set up is such that Commissioners have to rely on facilities extended by Railways. Chief
Commissioner of Railway Safety is of the opinion that Commission of Railway Safety needs to be
restructured, with a view to strengthen the organization, so as to improve its efficiency and
effectiveness, with least reliance on Railways for technical and logistic support.
ACTION TAKEN
8. A proposal to appoint consultant to examine the present functioning of the CRS with a view
to suggest reforms for augmentation, strengthening and restructuring the organization so as to
improve its efficiency and effectiveness is under active consideration with Ministry of Civil
Aviation. Subsequent action shall be initiated after submission of the report by the consultant.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
9. The Committee observes that the replies submitted by both the Ministries of Civil
Aviation and Railways are divergent and diagonally opposite. The Committee strongly feels
that it is high time that both the Ministries sorted out their differences on crucial issues
related to CRS. The Committee is pleased to note that a proposal to appoint consultant to
examine the present functioning of CRS is under active consideration of the Ministry of
Civil Aviation. The Committee desires that urgent steps should be taken to finalize the
proposal and implement the same.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
DUALITY OF COMMAND
10. Thus, CRS functions under Rules framed by both the Ministries under the Railways Act.
While accident investigation related rules are issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, accidents
inquiry related rules were issued by the Ministry of Railways. Though the CRS is under the
administrative control of Ministry of Civil Aviation, it takes its origin and discharges its duties as
per the Rules and Regulations framed under the Railways Act. The Committee feels that
involvement of two Ministries - Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Civil Aviation, leads to
avoidable confusion and also makes it difficult to apportion the responsibilities due to duality of
control and command in the functioning of CRS. It also leaves scope for conflict of interest for
Ministry of Railways.
(Para No: 16 ibid)
REPLY FROM M/O RAILWAYS
11. As far as the Ministry of Railways is concerned, there is no confusion in functioning of
the Commission of Railway Safety under the Ministry of Civil Aviation even when it takes its origin
and discharges its duties under the Railways Act 1989 as the duties and powers of both Ministry
of Railways and the CRS are well defined. Whenever any dispute arises in respect of any aspect
of the functioning of the Commissioner of Railway Safety (CRS), it is resolved by both the

3
Ministries mutually within the framework of the Act. Ministry of Railways and the Commission of
Railway Safety under the Ministry of Civil Aviation are Government bodies functioning in the public
interest and carrying out their respective duties as defined in the Act. There is no interference or
exercising of influence on the part of the Ministry of Railways in the working of the Commission.
Commissioners of Railway Safety are completely independent and exercise their independent and
free judgment while discharging their duties under the Act.
STAND OF MINISTRY OF CIVIL A VIATION
12. Commissioners of Railway Safety are concerned with the safety control aspects of the
operations of the railways, whereas Ministry of Railways plays the role of operator and regulator
both. There have been instances when Railway Board has not kept balance between its role as
operator vis-a-vis role of regulator.
13. Unilaterally changing of rules, schedule of dimensions and manuals etc. by the Ministry of
Railways without the concurrence of MoCA (administrative ministry in r/o CRS) has been a cause
of concern for the CRS. Such actions lead to lowering/compromising with the desired safety
standards. Further such action on the part of Railways leads to confusion/differences between the
two organizations. The issue is to be addressed on priority basis.
ACTION TAKEN
14. Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation vide its DO letter dated 08.08.2013 to Railway Board,
has proposed to formalize the process of fixing minimum requirements/standards ( e.g. Schedule of
Dimensions, Standards for fixed Structures and rolling Stocks and Rules governing Train
operations) which regulate railway Safety.
15. In response to Secretary MOCA letter, Ministry of Railways have withstood with their
earlier reply and opined that for changing the rules and Standards it is not obligatory to consult
the Commission of Railway Safety as per statute.
16. No conclusive decision reached due to stand of the Ministry of Railways as conveyed
above.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17. The Committee feels that stand taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation as well as
the Railways do not address the concerns of the Committee on the duality of command in
discharging the functions of CRS. The Committee is of the considered view that having a
separate legislation for CRS, which could prove to be an effective solution to such avoidable
confusion, needs serious thought and deliberation.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
18. Besides, under the Railways Act the term Central Government means the Ministry of
Railways. There being some overlapping in safety related issues between the Railway Board and
CRS as it is, this confusion gets further confounded. Although Ministry of Railways denied the
existence of such confusion, instances of unilateral action by the Railway Board for deciding
standards and codes and informing the Commission of Railway Safety without any involvement/
consultation with the latter were brought to the notice of the Committee. The Committee is
constrained to conclude that such an arrangement is suitable to Ministry of Railways which is why
it does not want to disturb the existing arrangement.
(Para No: 17 ibid)

4
REPLY FROM M/O RAILWAYS
19. As per Section 60 of Indian Railways Act, the power to make rules for regulating the
traveling upon, and the use, working and management of Railways lies with Central Government
i.e. Ministry of Railways. The Commission of Railway Safety has to discharge its duties within the
framework of rules formulated by Ministry of Railways.
20. As per statute it is not obligatory to consult the Commission before any amendment/
revision/deletion/addition to General Rules and other Rules, standards, codes and manuals.
STAND OF MINISTRY OF CIVIL A VIATION
21. As per the transaction of Business Rules – when the subject of a case concerns more than
one department, no decision can be taken or order issued until all such departments have
concurred, or, failing such concurrence, a decision thereon has been taken by or under the
authority of the Cabinet.
The stand of the Railways that the Commission of Railway Safety has to discharge its
duties within the framework of rules formulated by the Ministry of Railways is legally incorrect.
Commissioners of Railway Safety have been bestowed responsibility and powers by the Act of
Parliament, to inspect/inquire/investigate and then to report on safety related issues to Government.
Section 60 of the Indian Railways Act, 1989 as referred to by the Ministry of Railways mentions
about the carriage of passengers rules only and not on operation. Operational rules are actually the
subject matter under Section 29(2)(c) of the Railways Act.
22. Section 29 is reproduced below:
Power to make rules in respect of matters in this Chapter ( Ch V-Opening of Railways)–
(1) The Central Government, by notification, make rules to carry out the purposes of this
Chapter.
(2) In particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules
may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:-
(a) The duties of the railway administration and the Commissioner in regard to the
opening of a railway for the public carriage of passengers;
(b) The arrangements to be made for and the formalities to be complied with before
opening a railway line for the public carriage of passengers;
(c) for regulating the mode in which, and the speed at which rolling stock used on
railways is to be moved or propelled; and
(d) the cases in which and the extent to which the procedure provided in the Chapter
may be dispensed with.
23. Concurrence of MoCA (CRS) is essential before making any amendment/ revision/ deletion/
addition to operational rules.
ACTION TAKEN
24. Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation vide its DO letter dated 08.08.2013 to Railway Board,
has proposed to formalize the process of fixing minimum requirements/standards ( e.g. Schedule of
Dimensions, Standards for fixed Structures and rolling Stocks and Rules governing Train
operations) which regulate railway Safety. In response to Secretary MOCA letter, Ministry of

5
Railways have withstood with their earlier reply and opined that for changing the rules and
Standards it is not obligatory to consult the Commission of Railway Safety as per statute.
25. No conclusive decision reached due to stand of the Ministry of Railways as conveyed
above.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
26. The Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules clearly delineate the functions of
various Ministries/Departments of Government of India. The Committee recommends that the term
Central Government occurring in the Railway Act should adequately be defined to demarcate the
functions of Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Civil Aviation to avoid any confusion in respect
of powers, mandate and autonomous working of CRS between the two Ministries.
(Para No: 18 ibid)
REPLY FROM M/O RAILWAYS
27. The Indian Railway Act, 1989 deals with functioning of Railways and as such it is implied
that “Central Government” means Ministry of Railways. Wherever Commission of Railway Safety
(CRS) is specifically mentioned, it is automatically refers to Ministry of Civil Aviation as under the
Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, Commission of Railway Safety has been
clearly stated under the Ministry of Civil Aviation. Roles, powers, duties of CRS are quite clearly
defined in the Act and there is no confusion in this regard.
STAND OF MINISTRY OF CIVIL A VIATION
28. In this connection attention is drawn towards the Transaction of Business rules whereby
when the subject of a case concerns more than one department, no decision can be taken or order
issued until all such departments have concurred, or, failing such concurrence, a decision thereon
has been taken by or under the authority of the Cabinet.
29. It is therefore imperative that in all matters which pertain to safety of public, Railways
independently should not amend/revised/delete/add to General Rules and other Rules, standards,
codes and manuals rules without consulting and concurrence of the Commission of Railway Safety.
Term Central Government is not required to be defined. Once transaction of business rules are
followed considering that Railway Safety is also business of MoCA, things would be in order.
ACTION TAKEN
30. Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation vide its DO letter dated 08.08.2013 to Railway Board,
has proposed to formalize the process of fixing minimum requirements/standards ( e.g. Schedule of
Dimensions, Standards for fixed Structures and rolling Stocks and Rules governing Train
operations) which regulate railway Safety.
31. In response to Secretary MOCA letter, Ministry of Railways have withstood with their
earlier reply and opined that for changing the rules and Standards it is not obligatory to consult
the Commission of Railway Safety as per statute. No conclusive decision reached due to stand of
the Ministry of Railways as conveyed above.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
32. As regards consulting CRS in fixing standards/specifications for the purpose of
inspection/investigation etc., the Committee finds that the response of the Railways too
technical in saying that under the statute they are not required to do so. The Committee

6
feels that the idea of consultation with the CRS in this respect, no doubt has definite merit
as standard/specification are very closely linked with the inspection and investigation by
CRS effectively. The Committee hastens to add that the CRS could not have a free hand
in this regard as it might affect Railways working adversely as over all safety is mainly
their responsibility under the Railways Act. The Committee emphasizes the need to have
regular consultation in this regard between the CRS and Ministry of Railways.
33. The Committee notes that there are grey areas between both the Ministries on the
issues of rules making and fixing of minimum requirements/standards. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the matter may be placed before the Cabinet Secretary to arrive
at a decision on the points on which there are serious differences between both the Ministries.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
34. The Committee raised the issue of adequacy of existing rules, legislations relating to Railway
Safety and a need, if any, to amend these to meet the present day requirements, the Ministry of
Railways informed that the existing rules, legislations relating to Railway Safety were adequate and
that there was no need to amend them. However, review of safety standards is a continuous
process and amendments in the manuals, codes, general rules, etc. are made as and when required.
(Para No: 19 ibid)
REPLY FROM M/O RAILWAYS
35. Noted.
STAND OF MINISTRY OF CIVIL A VIATION
36. It is again reiterated that concurrence of MoCA (CRS) is necessary, in all matters which
pertain to safety of railway passengers and also before making any amendment/ revision/ deletion/
addition to General Rules and other Rules, standards, codes and manuals is given effect to by
Ministry of Railways.
ACTION TAKEN
37. Ministry of Railways has in its reply has confirmed in affirmation regarding compliance of
the recommendation made by the Committee. However, it remained silent/non-committal in seeking
concurrence of Ministry of Civil Aviation before making any amendment/revision/deletion/addition to
General Rules and other Rules, standards, codes and manuals etc., and other matter pertains to
safety of railway passengers.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
38. The Committee is not satisfied with reply furnished by Ministry of Railways as they
have not spelt out any details of review of the safety standards. It seems that the Ministry
has not taken the recommendation of the Committee due with required seriousness.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
39. It was brought before the Committee that whenever the Ministry of Railways propose to
change any rules relating to railway safety, the same is referred to CRS, but modifications or
changes in standards or codes pertaining to railway safety were not referred. Thus the changes/
modifications in safety codes are implemented without consultation with CRS. As per the
Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules when the subject of a case concerns more

7
than one Department, no decision can be taken or order issued until all such departments have
concurred, or failing such concurrence, a decision thereon has been taken by or under the authority
of the Cabinet. As such any modification/change of rules or standards by the Ministry of Railways
needs the concurrence of Ministry of Civil Aviation also.
(Para No: 20 ibid)
40. The Annual Report of CRS for 2010-11, gives specific examples of amendment/modification
of rules/policy in respect of safety train operations without the information/involvement of the
office of CRS. One such examples was revised Policy Circular dated the 12th July, 2010 on the
‘sanction of speed of nominated trains on specific routes’ and the increase of speed of trains
without the approval of Commissioner of Railway Safety of the concerned Zone, resulting in
danger to travelling public.
(Para No: 21 ibid)
41. The Committee is of the view that any decision taken by the Ministry of Railways in
respect of matters relating to railway safety should have the concurrence (not merely consultation)
of the Ministry of Civil Aviation as per the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules.
(Para No: 22 ibid)
REPLY FROM M/O RAILWAYS
42. Responsibility for safety in the working and operation of Railway rests solely with the
Ministry of Railways.
43. As per Section 60 of Indian Railways Act, the power to make rules for regulating the
traveling upon, and the use, working and management of the Railways lies with Central
Government i.e. Ministry of Railways. The Commission of Railway Safety has to discharge its
duties within the framework of rules formulated by Ministry of Railways. As per statute it is not

Conclusion
182. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism
and Culture presented its One-Hundred and Eighty-Eighth Report on “Functioning of
Commission of Railways Safety” to both the Houses of Parliament on 27
th February, 2013.
The Report inter-alia contained the observations/recommendations of the Committee on the
following issues:—
(i) Duality of command on Commission of Railway Safety (CRS)
(ii) Fixing of safety standards
(iii) Inspection by CRS
(iv) Investigation of railway accidents
(v) Implementation of recommendations of CRS
(vi) Separation of roles of operator, regulator and investigator
(vii) Human resources in CRS; and
(viii) Recommendations of high level safety review committee on safety architecture
on Indian railways (Dr. Anil Kakodkar Committee)
183. The Ministry of Civil Aviation submitted the final Action Taken Replies on 22
nd
January, 2014 which contained the views of Ministry of Railways on each of the
recommendations of the Committee.
184. The Committee after examining the Action Taken Replies found that most of the
replies submitted by both the Ministries of Civil Aviation and Railways are divergent and
diagonally opposite. The Ministry of Railways had submitted that the existing system of the
CRS under Ministry of Civil Aviation is working satisfactorily and that there was no need
to empower/restructure the CRS; it is working very well; and the Committee’s observations
and apprehensions are unfounded. The Committee also found that the Ministry of Railways
was not willing to consult the CRS in fixing the minimum requirements/standards which

29
regulate railway safety. The Ministry of Railways informed the Committee that a stand-
alone Legislation for the CRS as recommended by this Committee in 2005 is still under
their consideration. The Ministry is still having reservations on allowing the CRS to carry
out the ‘annual periodical inspection’. On other major observations of the Committee the
Ministry of Railways submitted non-committal replies only.
185. The Ministry of Civil Aviation, on the majority of observations of the Committee,
replied that a proposal to appoint a consultant to examine the issues raised by the
Committee is under active consideration of the Ministry. The replies of the Ministry in
respect of expansion of the CRS in terms of HR and creation of extra Zones, investigation
of rail accidents and addressing the shortcomings faced by CRS in carrying out its day-
to-day function are very casual and evasive. Actions on these issues, the Committee feels
are to be taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation without involvement of Ministry of
Railways.
186. The Committee after analyzing the replies and also hearing the representatives of
Ministry of Civil Aviation and Railways feels that stand taken by the Ministry of Civil
Aviation as well as Railways do not address the concerns of the Committee for the effective
and efficient working of CRS. The Committee is of the considered view that having a
separate legislation for creating an empowered/autonomous body as CRS, which could prove
to be an effective solution to prevailing short comings and confusion, needs serious
consideration and implementation. But the Ministry of Railways for reasons better known
to them does not appear to be in favor of a separate legislation, although the Ministry of
Civil Aviation did not express any reservation about this.
187. The Committee also emphasized upon the need to draw up clear demarcation of
functions of Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Civil Aviation in the working of CRS. The
Committee notes that both the Ministries are not able to arrive at a consensus on the
issues of rules making and fixing of minimum requirements/standards. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the matter may be placed before the Cabinet Secretary to take
a view in the light of observations/recommendations of the Committee in consultation with
both the Ministries. The Committee still feels that any change in specifications/standards by
the Ministry of Railways in respect of matters relating to railway safety should not be one-
sided; involvement of CRS has to be there. We have to evolve a system in which CRS is
also involved in fixing/changing specifications/standards without, of course, resulting in any
hurdles for the Ministry of Railways in its day-to-day working. Ministry of Railways also
should be careful in dealing with CRS so that its efficiency is not jeopardized.
188. The Committee has desired that the difficulties faced by CRS in conducting accident
investigation should be adequately addressed by both the Ministries of Civil Aviation and
Railways. The Committee also recommends that the proposal to increase the number of
circles of CRS should be expedited.
189. The Committee invited the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Chairman,
Railway Board to appear before the Committee to examine all the issues afflicting the CRS.
However, the Chairman, Railway Board could not appear before the Committee. The
Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation while deposing before the Committee informed that
issues highlighted in the Report of the Committee will be discussed with the Chairman,
Railway Board and suitable remedial action will be taken as per the discussions within four
weeks timeframe. The Committee hopes that some positive result will come out in the
coming days to strengthen the functioning of CRS.

30
30
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which
have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the
earliest. (Para 3)
The Committee observes that the replies submitted by both the Ministries of Civil
Aviation and Railways are divergent and diagonally opposite. The Committee strongly feels
that it is high time that both the Ministries sorted out their differences on crucial issues
related to CRS. The Committee is pleased to note that a proposal to appoint consultant to
examine the present functioning of CRS is under active consideration of the Ministry of
Civil Aviation. The Committee desires that urgent steps should be taken to finalize the
proposal and implement the same. (Para 9)
The Committee feels that stand taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation as well as
the Railways do not address the concerns of the Committee on the duality of command in
discharging the functions of CRS. The Committee is of the considered view that having a
separate legislation for CRS, which could prove to be an effective solution to such avoidable
confusion, needs serious thought and deliberation. (Para 17)
As regards consulting CRS in fixing standards/specifications for the purpose of
inspection/investigation etc., the Committee finds that the response of the Railways too
technical in saying that under the statute they are not required to do so. The Committee
feels that the idea of consultation with the CRS in this respect, no doubt has definite merit
as standard/specification are very closely linked with the inspection and investigation by
CRS effectively. The Committee hastens to add that the CRS could not have a free hand
in this regard as it might affect Railways working adversely as over all safety is mainly
their responsibility under the Railways Act. The Committee emphasizes the need to have
regular consultation in this regard between the CRS and Ministry of Railways. (Para 32)
The Committee notes that there are grey areas between both the Ministries on the
issues of rules making and fixing of minimum requirements/standards. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the matter may be placed before the Cabinet Secretary to
arrive at a decision on the points on which there are serious differences between both the
Ministries. (Para 33)
The Committee is not satisfied with reply furnished by Ministry of Railways as they
have not spelt out any details of review of the safety standards. It seems that the Ministry
has not taken the recommendation of the Committee due with required seriousness.
(Para 38)
The safety of the traveling public is the concern of the Government as a whole.
Therefore, all the Ministries involved should play a role in formulating the safety
regulations/rules, etc. More consultation means more practicable policies. The Committee is
not satisfied with the reply and it reiterates its recommendation on the decisions taken by
the Ministry of Railways in respect of matters relating to railway safety. (Para 48)
The Committee is yet have arguments, convincing or unconvincing, against a stand-
alone legislation for CRS as recommended by it in its 83
rd Report, and reiterated in

31
188th Report in 2013. It is disappointed to see that it is still under consideration. The
Committee takes serious note of such an evasive reply and directs the Ministry of Railways
to submit a note on this further for its consideration. The Committee feels that this reflects
the non-committal attitude of the Ministry of Railways for providing much needed autonomy
to CRS in real terms. (Para 56)
The Kakodkar Committee report which remains under consideration for last more
than two years may be debated at the earliest in consultation with all the stakeholders. The
Committee would like to have inputs in this regard from both Ministries within two months
for its consideration. (Para 57)
The Committee notes the reply and feels that the role of CRS, at present, is
restricted to accident investigation only and not for periodic safety audit of railways. The
stand taken by the Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Civil Aviation on the codification
of minimum standard of railway tracks and rolling stock should come to a logical
conclusion. (Para 65)
The Committee does not agree with the stand taken by Ministry of Railways in this
regard and feels that legal opinion on this ought to have been taken in 1953 itself. It
desires that the opinion of Ministry of Law and Justice on the Executive Order issued by
the Ministry of Railways in the year 1953 relieving CsRS of their duty of annual periodical
inspection may be got expedited. The Committee may be appraised on the opinion tendered
by the Ministry of Law and Justice. The Law provides for periodic inspection of railways by
CRS. It is not clear why CRS is not exercising this function. The Committee may be
apprised why the CRS is not undertaking suo-motto inspections. (Para 73)
The Committee notes the reply and desires that the difficulties faced by CRS in
conducting accident investigation should be adequately addressed by both the Ministries of
Civil Aviation and Railways. The Committee finds that the proposal to increase the number
of circles of CRS falls under the domain of Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of
Railways has no objection to it. The Committee recommends that it should be expedited.
(Para 87)
The Committee is also not in a position to comprehend why Ministry of Civil Aviation
was not increasing the staff strength of CRS to cope-up with the increase of the Railway
network. The Committee also feels that the Ministry of Civil Aviation is equally to be
blamed for the present situation of the CRS. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Ministry of Civil Aviation should take immediate steps to increase the number of
Circles of CRS as well as to augment the staff position of CRS. (Para 88)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 93)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 100)
The Committee is unhappy to note that such a deadlock between the Ministries
undermine such serious issues as railways safety. The Committee would like to impress
upon both the Ministries that a conclusive decision should be reached on the issue of
forwarding of the reports of investigation into accidents of Section 120 as enquired by the
Railway Administration. The Committee desires that all the accident investigation reports
may be available with the CRS to enable a better safety environment for the traveling
public. (Para 108)
The Committee finds that the replies submitted by Ministries of Civil Aviation and
Railways are of routine nature. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that a proper

32
system should be put in place to ensure the compliance of accepted recommendations
and other follow-up actions taken by the Ministry of Railways, in a periodical manner.
(Para 117)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 123)
The Committee recommends that the Kakodkar Committee recommendation that are
under consideration for a long time should be expedited to arrive at a conclusion
particularly those relating to Railway Safety Authority as proposed. Safety of the public
should be the utmost criteria while deciding on the recommendation rather than the powers
and jurisdictions of particular Ministries or governmental agencies. (Para 129)
The Committee fails to understand the reply of the Ministry of Civil Aviation
regarding not filling-up the vacancies in CRS so far. The Committee feels that follow up
action on the report by the consultant who is yet to be engaged to examine the present
functioning of CRS would take considerable time and that the filling up of vacancies in CRS
cannot be postponed for such a long duration. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Ministry of Civil Aviation should take immediate action to augment the staff strength
and restructure the CRS. (Para 136)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 141)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 146)
The Committee happy to note the reply. (Para 151)
The Committee notes the reply and it may be appraised on the status of
implementation of the recommendations of HLSR Committee, particularly on the
strengthening of CRS. The Committee recommends that an early decision may be taken on
the recommendations of HLSR Committee. (Para 156)
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation will
pursue the creation of two posts of CsMRS vigorously with the concerned departments.
(Para 161)
The Committee notes the reply and finds that restructuring of CRS is the need of
the hour which should be taken up on priority by both the Ministries. (Para 169)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 174)
The Committee notes the reply and feels that the replies furnished by both the
Ministries are evasive and non-committal. The Committee finds that both the Ministries are
responsible for the present poor state of affairs of CRS. The Committee hopes that
restructuring of CRS on priority and greater co-ordination between the two Ministries will
address the shortcomings of the existing system. (Para 180)
The Committee also finds that Ministry of Civil Aviation, directly and indirectly, puts
blame for all the ills in CRS on Ministry of Railways. But feels that restructuring and
expansion of CRS is their responsibility. However, the Ministry in its Action Taken Replies
has repeatedly said that a consultant will be appointed to address all the issues raised in
respect of CRS by the Committee. As for having a study done by a consultant is fraught
with many ifs and buts causing undue delays. Who will appoint the consultants and what
will its mandate etc.? What if Ministry of Railways has any objection or reservations about
these aspects? Therefore, the Committee is very apprehensive about consultant route, which
cannot provide solution to all the ills being faced in this regard. (Para 181)

33
Conclusion
The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism
and Culture presented its One-Hundred and Eighty-Eighth Report on “Functioning of
Commission of Railways Safety” to both the Houses of Parliament on 27
th February, 2013.
The Report inter-alia contained the observations/recommendations of the Committee on the
following issues:—
(i) Duality of command on Commission of Railway Safety (CRS)
(ii) Fixing of safety standards
(iii) Inspection by CRS
(iv) Investigation of railway accidents
(v) Implementation of recommendations of CRS
(vi) Separation of roles of operator, regulator and investigator
(vii) Human resources in CRS; and
(viii) Recommendations of high level safety review committee on safety  architecture
on Indian railways (Dr. Anil Kakodkar Committee)
(Para 182)
The Ministry of Civil Aviation submitted the final Action Taken Replies on
22
nd January, 2014 which contained the views of Ministry of Railways on each of the
recommendations of the Committee. (Para 183)
The Committee after examining the Action Taken Replies found that most of the
replies submitted by both the Ministries of Civil Aviation and Railways are divergent and
diagonally opposite. The Ministry of Railways had submitted that the existing system of the
CRS under Ministry of Civil Aviation is working satisfactorily and that there was no need
to empower/restructure the CRS; it is working very well; and the Committee’s observations
and apprehensions are unfounded. The Committee also found that the Ministry of Railways
was not willing to consult the CRS in fixing the minimum requirements/standards which
regulate railway safety. The Ministry of Railways informed the Committee that a stand-
alone Legislation for the CRS as recommended by this Committee in 2005 is still under
their consideration. The Ministry is still having reservations on allowing the CRS to carry
out the ‘annual periodical inspection’. On other major observations of the Committee the
Ministry of Railways submitted non-committal replies only. (Para 184)
The Ministry of Civil Aviation, on the majority of observations of the Committee,
replied that a proposal to appoint a consultant to examine the issues raised by the
Committee is under active consideration of the Ministry. The replies of the Ministry in
respect of expansion of the CRS in terms of HR and creation of extra Zones, investigation
of rail accidents and addressing the shortcomings faced by CRS in carrying out its day-to-
day function are very casual and evasive. Actions on these issues, the Committee feels are
to be taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation without involvement of Ministry of Railways.
(Para 185)
The Committee after analyzing the replies and also hearing the representatives of
Ministry of Civil Aviation and Railways feels that stand taken by the Ministry of Civil
Aviation as well as Railways do not address the concerns of the Committee for the effective
and efficient working of CRS. The Committee is of the considered view that having a

34
separate legislation for creating an empowered/autonomous body as CRS, which could prove
to be an effective solution to prevailing short comings and confusion, needs serious
consideration and implementation. But the Ministry of Railways for reasons better known
to them does not appear to be in favor of a separate legislation, although the Ministry of
Civil Aviation did not express any reservation about this. (Para 186)
The Committee also emphasized upon the need to draw up clear demarcation of
functions of Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Civil Aviation in the working of CRS. The
Committee notes that both the Ministries are not able to arrive at a consensus on the issues
of rules making and fixing of minimum requirements/standards. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the matter may be placed before the Cabinet Secretary to take a view in
the light of observations/recommendations of the Committee in consultation with both the
Ministries. The Committee still feels that any change in specifications/standards by the
Ministry of Railways in respect of matters relating to railway safety should not be one-sided;
involvement of CRS has to be there. We have to evolve a system in which CRS is also
involved in fixing/changing specifications/standards without, of course, resulting in any hurdles
for the Ministry of Railways in its day-to-day working. Ministry of Railways also should be
careful in dealing with CRS so that its efficiency is not jeopardized. (Para 187)
The Committee has desired that the difficulties faced by CRS in conducting accident
investigation should be adequately addressed by both the Ministries of Civil Aviation and
Railways. The Committee also recommends that the proposal to increase the number of
circles of CRS should be expedited. (Para 188)
The Committee invited the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Chairman,
Railway Board to appear before the Committee to examine all the issues afflicting the CRS.
However, the Chairman, Railway Board could not appear before the Committee. The
Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation while deposing before the Committee informed that
issues highlighted in the Report of the Committee will be discussed with the Chairman,
Railway Board and suitable remedial action will be taken as per the discussions within four
weeks timeframe. The Committee hopes that some positive result will come out in the
coming days to strengthen the functioning of CRS. (Para 189)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this Two Hundred and Eelventh Report on “Upkeep of various Monuments in Delhi,
National Museum and other important issues pertaining to the Ministry of Culture”.
2. The Committee in the first chapter of this Report has dealt with upkeep of various
important monuments in Delhi. Most of the issues raised here were under examination of the
Committee for a long time and recently the Committee heard the views of the Ministry of Tourism,
Ministry of Culture, Aga Khan Trust for Culture, Archaeological Survey of India and INTACH on
27
th January, 2014 on the subject. Similarly, the portion pertaining to the National Museum is also
based on the replies received from the Ministry of Culture on the 167 th and the 179 th Reports of
the Committee. Given the crucial importance of the subject, the Committee has made further
observations/recommendations in this Report for follow up action.
3. The Committee has also dealt with several outstanding issues on which recommendations
were given in various Reports earlier but, those have not been implemented fully. The Committee
understands that if implemented, it will go a long way in protecting the cultural heritage of the
country and the interface of culture with tourism will certainly be better.
4. The Committee is thankful to the Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Tourism for their
written and oral replies/submissions on different occasions. The Committee is also thankful to Aga
Khan Trust and INTACH for their participation in the meeting.
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 18
th February, 2014.
