Reply of the Government of Kerala
13. Kerala Tourism earnestly supports the suggestion. The Government of India can make the
cruise terminal in Cochin one of the elements in the Incredible India campaign. Kerala Tourism
strongly supports the idea of training/workshop and will take a proactive role in organizing them.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
14. The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee is of the opinion that the
steps taken by the Ministry of Tourism need to be monitored regularly to achieve the
targets. The Committee recommends that water sports and water taxis proposed in Chennai
also can be included in the other viable ports. The Committee expresses its concern over
the past accidents involving cruise boats/houseboats etc. where many tourists lost their lives
and to remind that the luxury boats need to be procured without any compromise to the
safety norms prescribed for it. The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism is silent
about giving publicity to the cruise tourism potential of Kochi Port in their Incredible India
Campaign. The Committee reiterates its recommendations that cruise terminal in Kochi
may be included as one of the elements in Incredible India Campaign.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
15. The Committee notes that Alappuzha and the adjoining regions have great potential in
backwater cruise tourism. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism, Government
of India should give all out efforts to provide adequate infrastructure for backwater tourism and
provide the necessary finances for the purpose.
(Para 16)
Reply of the Government
16. Information sought from the State Government of Kerala, which is yet to be received.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17. The Committee finds the reply evasive. The delay in securing the reply in time must
have been dealt with seriously. The Committee further recommends that Ministry of
Tourism should make all out efforts to provide adequate infrastructure for backwater
tourism in Alappuzha and provide the necessary finances for the purpose.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
18. The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Central/State Government for
providing wellness tourism and accreditation of wellness centres. The responsibility of the
Government and stakeholders adhering to the conditionalities speaks volumes about the importance
being accorded to tourists’ safety and clean business ethics by the tourism fraternity in Kerala.
Further, the drive undertaken for providing financial assistance under the Market Development
Assistance Scheme (MDA) and giving exposure to Wellness Tourism Service Providers shows the
pro-local people and pro-entrepreneurial approach. The Committee would like the State/Central
Government and all concerned to come up with such solution providing ideas so that the wellness
tourism in Kerala is developed as brand of its own to attract tourists from world over.
(Para 20)

4
Reply of the Government
19. The Ministry of Tourism accepts the recommendation of the Committee. Under the MDA
scheme, the following Wellness Tourism Service Providers from Kerala have availed support:
● Amala Ayurvedic Hospital and Research Centre, Thrissur has participated in FITUR,
International Tourism Trade Fair, Madrid held from 30 th January – 3 rd February, 2013.
● Rajah Beach Ayurveda Hospital, Thrissur has participated in PATA India Chapter Road
Show-2012 at Auckland, Sydney and Melbourne held from October 1-5, 2012.
20. The Ministry of Tourism organized a sensitization workshop in August, 2011 in Cochin to
encourage wellness centres to adopt the accreditation of wellness centres developed by National
Board for Accreditation of Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH) in consultation with the
Department of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH). The
Government of Kerala also has a system of approving wellness centres.
21. Wellness tourism has also been specifically promoted at various international platforms such
as World Travel Mart, London, ITB Berlin, ITB Asia and Arabian Travel Mart, Dubai. Wellness
Tourism is also promoted by the Ministry through its centralised print, electronic, internet and
outdoor campaigns and also Road Shows and Know India seminars.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
22. The Committee notes the reply. These were the information available with the
Committee at the time of preparation of the Report in July, 2013. It seems that Ministry
has not taken any further action on the recommendation of the Committee. The Committee
recommends that the Government may take further necessary steps to promote wellness-
tourism.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
23. One of the emerging tourism products in the State of Kerala is Medical Tourism. But large
scale support from the Union Government is required to develop this potential. There have to be
efforts from the Ministry of Tourism to promote Medical Tourism including Ayurveda, Siddha,
Unani etc., in association with Kerala Tourism. The issues relating to issuing Medical Visa also need
to be addressed.
(Para 22)
Reply of the Government
24. The Ministry of Tourism provides Market Development Assistance (MDA) to Medical Tourism
Service Providers i.e., Representatives of Hospitals accredited by Joint Commission for International
Accredited Hospitals (JCI) and National Accreditation Board of Hospitals (NABH) and Medical
Tourism facilitators (Travel Agents/Tour Operators) approved by the Ministry of Tourism,
Government of India and engaged in Medical Tourism; for participation in approved Medical/Tourism
Fairs/Medical Conferences/Wellness conferences/Wellness Fairs and its allied Road Shows (PMT).
Hospitals and Wellness Centres from the State of Kerala have availed MDA scheme over the years.
25. The Ministry of Tourism organized a sensitization workshop in August, 2011 in Cochin to
encourage wellness centres to adopt the accreditation of wellness centres developed by National
Board for Accreditation of Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH) in consultation with the
Department of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH). The
Government of Kerala also has a system of approving wellness centres.

26. The steps taken by the Government to promote Medical/Health Tourism include promotion
in overseas markets through Road Shows, Know India seminars, participation in Travel Marts, and

27. The Ministry of Tourism has raised issues relating to grant of Medical Visa/Medical
Attendant Visa to foreign nationals, in the Inter-Ministerial meetings held with the Ministry of Home
Affairs, Ministry of External Affairs and other concerned Ministries.
28. Kerala Tourism welcomes the suggestion of the Committee. Government of India may
extend suitable financial assistance under MDA scheme (Market Development Assistance Scheme)
to promote “Wellness Tourism” as significant sub brand the world over. Department of Tourism,
Government of Kerala has already launched a global campaign called “Kerala the Home of
Ayurveda” and we seek suitable assistance from Government of India for such focused campaigns
in wellness tourism sector.
29. The Government of India may launch a scheme for the promotion of medical tourism.
Kerala Tourism will support and co-operate in this initiative by charting clear plans and specific
budgetary outlays in consultation with the private players.
30. Ministry of Tourism may also take action to have medical visas issued on an expeditious
basis, which will remove the pain element in the process.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
31. The Committee may be apprised of the outcome of the meetings held with the
concerned agencies in the matter of granting medical visa to tourists. The Committee
recommends that the Government of India and Government of Kerala should coordinate
with each other in promoting wellness tourism at global level and effort be made for
expeditious issuance of medical visa/medical attendance visa.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
32. The cardinal principles for development of eco-tourism are really laudable. The Committee
appreciates the efforts of Kerala Government in maintenance of environmental integrity and
development of tourism in an ecologically sustainable manner. During its visit to Eravikulam
National Park, Munnar, Periyar Wild Life Sanctuary and Gavi National Park, Thekkady, the
Committee got a first-hand experience of the functioning module as to how the pristine beauty of
the locations were maintained and development of eco-tourism’s way was paved.
(Para 27)
Reply of the Government of Kerala
33. Eco-tourism is an agenda that needs to be brought on to the national centre-stage and
proposes that the Government of India should commit special financial packages for developing
eco-tourism centres like Gavi, Eravikulam, Munnar belt of destinations and other major destinations
in the State into world class destinations.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
34. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India may
take necessary steps to provide special financial packages for developing eco-tourism
centres like Gavi, Eravikulam, Munnar and other major destinations.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
35. On the basis of interaction with various stakeholders and its first-hand experience, the
Committee feels that various satellite towns adjoining Thekkady have immense tourism potential. In
view of the fact that Thekkady and the adjoining Kumily towns are already saturated, the
Committee emphasises the need to develop the satellite towns/villages as tourist destinations. The
Committee further recommends that the Union Ministry of Tourism and Government of Kerala
should cooperate with each other to ensure that satellite villages of Thekkady are provided with
adequate infrastructure to develop as tourist destinations.
(Para 40)
Reply of the Government of Kerala
36. As recommended by the Committee, Kerala Tourism is committed to promote satellite
villages of Thekkady and other similar destinations with the assistance of Government of India. A
master plan in this regard is already under preparation.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
37. The Committee desires that details of the master plan may be communicated to it. The
Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism, Government of India may support the
initiative to promote satellite villages of Thekkady as tourist destinations.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
38. The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to establish a full-fledged museum in Thekkady
to have first hand experience to the tourists about the social, cultural, traditional and historical aspects
of the region. This will give authentic information on the people and culture of the area. The Committee
also recommends that museums should be established at all the tourist destinations.
(Para 41)
39. The Committee was told that there is a State-owned vegetable farm near Kumily. The
Committee recommends that a Botanical Garden may be established in Kumily, if need be, the State
owned farm may be converted into a Botanical Garden.
(Para 42)
40. The Committee further recommends that vehicular traffic may be restricted inside Periyar
Wild Life sanctuary. The present parking area which is inside the forest area may be shifted out
of the sanctuary. Only the battery operated vehicles may be permitted from the parking lot to the
sanctuary/boat landing area. At Eravikulam National Park, Munnar, the Committee observed that
battery operated vehicles are used for transporting tourists to the National Park. The same model
can be adopted in Periyar Sanctuary also.
(Para 43)
Reply of the Government of Kerala
41. Department of Tourism, Government of Kerala agree with the recommendations and will
take all possible measures to bring them to fruition. We will also approach the Government of India
with specific proposals for financial support in this regard.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
42. The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee notes with dismay that even
after a year since the recommendation of the Committee submitted to Parliament, the

Committee does not know the reasons for this. The Committee reiterates its
recommendations and expects to have a response in this regard of the steps taken.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
66. Muziris (the present day Kodungalloor and the adjoining areas) is reputed to be the ancient
world’s greatest trading centre in the East. As the focal point of commerce for over 2500 years,
this bustling sea port traded in everything from spices to precious stones with the Greeks, Romans
and the rest of the world. It was also the doorway to India for varied cultures and races:
Buddhists, Arabs, Chinese, Jews, Romans, Portuguese, Dutch and even the British.
(Para 57)
67. The representatives of Kerala Tourism informed the Committee that the Muziris Heritage
project is in the active stage of implementation and they are planning to link it with the spice route
project. The Committee is fully in agreement with the Kerala Tourism initiative to club it with the
Muziris Heritage project, one of the biggest conservation projects in India showcasing a culture of
3000 years or more, which is already partnered by various departments of State Government of
Kerala, Central Government and the UNESCO. This would make Kochi, Muziris and Malabar the
Heritage Circuit of Kerala. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism, Government of
India should give all the support required for promoting spice route and Muziris Heritage Project.
(Para 58)
Reply of the Government
68. Ministry of Tourism has sanctioned an amount of Rs.4052.83 lakh towards the project

Chapter–I : Tourism in Kerala
The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee is of the opinion that the
steps taken by the Ministry of Tourism need to be monitored regularly to achieve the
targets. The Committee recommends that water sports and water taxis proposed in Chennai
also can be included in the other viable ports. The Committee expresses its concern over
the past accidents involving cruise boats/houseboats etc. where many tourists lost their lives
and to remind that the luxury boats need to be procured without any compromise to the
safety norms prescribed for it. The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism is silent
about giving publicity to the cruise tourism potential of Kochi Port in their Incredible India
Campaign. The Committee reiterates its recommendations that cruise terminal in Kochi
may be included as one of the elements in Incredible India Campaign. (Para 14)
The Committee finds the reply evasive. The delay in securing the reply in time must
have been dealt with seriously. The Committee further recommends that Ministry of
Tourism should make all out efforts to provide adequate infrastructure for backwater
tourism in Alappuzha and provide the necessary finances for the purpose. (Para 17)
The Committee notes the reply. These were the information available with the
Committee at the time of preparation of the Report in July, 2013. It seems that Ministry
has not taken any further action on the recommendation of the Committee. The Committee
recommends that the Government may take further necessary steps to promote wellness
tourism. (Para 22)
The Committee may be apprised of the outcome of the meetings held with the
concerned agencies in the matter of granting medical visa to tourists. The Committee
recommends that the Government of India and Government of Kerala should coordinate
with each other in promoting wellness tourism at global level and effort be made for
expeditious issuance of medical visa/medical attendance visa. (Para 31)
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India may
take necessary steps to provide special financial packages for developing eco-tourism
centres like Gavi, Eravikulam, Munnar and other major destinations. (Para 34)
The Committee desires that details of the masterplan may be communicated to it.
The Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism, Government of India may support
the initiative to promote satellite villages of Thekkady as tourist destinations. (Para 37)
The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee notes with dismay that even
after a year since the recommendation of the Committee submitted to Parliament, the
Governments of India and Kerala State have not taken any steps to implement it. The
Committee does not know the reasons for this. The Committee reiterates its
recommendations and expects to have a response in this regard of the steps taken.
(Para 42)
Regarding waste management at Periyar Tiger Reserve and exorbitant charges of
boat tickets, no concrete and specific step has been taken to resolve it. The Committee
reiterates its recommendations. The Committee desires that the Ministry of Tourism

33
may furnish a proper response to it after obtaining feedback from the Government of
Kerala. (Para 49)
The Committee feels that the reply given by the Ministry of Tourism is too general
in nature and the recommendations of the Committee could not get the desired attention.
The Committee desired to know the follow up action in this regard. The Committee
reiterates its recommendation. The Ministry of Tourism Government of India may please
supply the Committee the specific initiatives taken to implement the recommendation of
the Committee. (Para 54)
The Committee is not satisfied with the reply. The Committee notes that Ministry of
Tourism, Government of Kerala being the principal stakeholders had the major role to take
initiatives to implement the recommendation of the Committee. However, no such
information has been furnished to the Committee. The Committee reiterates its
recommendation above and instructs the Ministry of Tourism Government of India to
further take up the matter with the Government of Kerala. (Para 60)
The Committee is happy that Government of Kerala is in agreement with
Committee’s recommendation. The Committee however, feels that there is a need to have
a closer and regular coordination between Ministry of Tourism, Government of India and
Ministry of Tourism, Government of Kerala to augment and promote tourism and its allied
activities. The Committee would like to know the steps taken by the Government of Kerala
on the recommendation of the Committee. (Para 65)
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should take up the matter
with the Ministry of External Affairs and Ministry of Culture to ensure the success of spice
route project and Muziris Heritage Project. It needs to be taken up with utmost priority and
seriousness. (Para 70)
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee feels that the Government of Kerala
needs to place concrete proposals and clearances required before the Ministry of Tourism,
Government of India. It expects the latter to pursue the matter on urgent basis. (Para 74)
The Committee notes that considerable time has elapsed since the constitution of the
Empowered Group of State Transport Minister for the rationalization of Motor Vehicle Taxes.
The Committee, therefore, desires to know the recommendations of the Empowered Group
on the terms and references prescribed for the purpose. The Committee further
recommends that the matter may be pursued with the Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways and other concerned State Government authorities. (Para 79)
The Committee appreciates the new imitative of running ‘South Splendor Tourism
Train’ on the pattern of ‘The Palace on Wheels”. The Committee hopes that the increased
inflow of tourists due to this train will have cascading effects on tourism and allied
activities specially hotels, guest houses, restaurants, gift Shoppe etc. (Para 83)
The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee recommends that the
taxation need to be reviewed to help tourism industry grow further. The Ministry of Tourism
may pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance. (Para 87)
The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee would like to know the
action taken by the Government of Kerala in this regard. The Ministry of Tourism,
Government of India may facilitate the matter with the Government of Kerala. (Para 91)
The Committee notes the reply and is of the opinion that if an owner can run a star
hotel without serving liquor there, what is the harm in it? However, serving of liquor
without a license should be dealt with seriously. (Para 95)

34
The Committee takes note of the reply. (Para l0l)
The Committee takes note of the reply. (Para 107)
The Committee takes note of the reply. (Para 112)
The Committee notes the reply which has come from the ASI through the  Ministry
of Tourism. The Committee feels that the issue has not been addressed by the Ministry of
Tourism with the seriousness it deserved. It appears that its contents have not been gone
through seriously except copy-pasting the reply given by ASI otherwise the information
could have been furnished correctly. The current reply does not contain the action taken by
the Ministry of Tourism on the issues pointed out by the ASI. The Committee desires to
know the opinion of Ministry on it. (Para 120)
The Committee would like to know the steps taken by the Government of  Kerala
in this regard. (Para 124)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 127)
Chapter–II : National Highways in Kerala
The Committee acknowledges the problems faced in the land acquisition. The
Committee recommends that the Government agencies should chalk out a via media to sort
out the problems. (Para 130)
The Committee appreciated the steps taken by the Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways solving the bottlenecks on the land acquisition related issues in Kerala. The
Committee, in view of the reply of Government of Kerala on the issue of land Acquisition
for National Highways, recommends that the complaints with respect to alignment of various
stretches in view of the local sentiments should be taken care of by the NHAI. However,
the Committee also suggests that the State Government of Kerala may take up the
challenge of land acquisition appropriately in view of the importance of the National
Highways for the economic development of the State. (Para 134)
The Committee hopes that a closer and regular coordination with the State
Government will help improve the condition of roads in Kerala. (Para 139)
The Committee notes the reply and feels that the MORTH has not properly addressed
the issue of rehabilitation and resettlement as per the reply furnished by the Government of
Kerala. The Committee notes that the MORTH is not ready to  address the Kerala specific
conditions on the plea that this might invite demands for similar packages from other States.
The Committee feels that the MORTH should factor in the peculiarities of Kerala in views
of its outstanding record in promotion of tourism; such States need to be rewarded for good
work. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that a special package may
be given to Kerala as far as land acquisition is concerned. (Para 143)
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee recommends that the concerns of
the Government of Kerala in the matter should be addressed properly by the NHAI.
(Para 149)
The Committee feels that instead of blaming a whole State of not paying the Toll,
the NHAI should look into the real issues and reasons for such a situation, if the people
are reluctant to pay Toll. The Committee also feels that people’s protest to tolls is not
specific to Kerala only, but also in other parts of the country. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that Government may revisit their Toll Policy throughout the country
especially in Kerala and formulate an acceptable solution to the real issue. (Para 154)

35
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 158)
The Committee notes the reply and feels that the Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways will take up the issue with the State Government of Kerala to resolve all the
issues concerning land acquisitions. (Para 162)
The Committee desires to know the details of the Grade Separators at a cost of
Rs.1450 crore. As regards 4 laning of the 5-9 km. road connecting Cochin Port, the reply
of the NHAI is evasive. The Committee recommends that feasibility study may be conducted
at the earliest. (Para 168)
Chapter–III : National Waterways in Kerala
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee observes that the NW-3 is fully
operational, even though the works started many years back. The Committee hopes that the
entire stretch of the NW-3 with the dredging of the remaining 12 km. between Thakazhy
to Kollam will be completed without further delay. The interruptions by local people may be
addressed at State level. (Para 173)
The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee desires that the feasibility
report of the NATPAC may be furnished to the Committee. (Para 176)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 179)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 182)
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee, however, would like to know the
normal procedure followed by IWAI in other waterways while disposing the dredged soil.
(Para 185)
The Committee recommends that in disposing of the dredged soil, the local body of
the area may be involved if the interference of locals are hampering the work. The
Committee further recommends that bank protection is to be ensured by the IWAI not only
to protect the land along the shores, but it may reduce the siltation in the channels. So the
initial spending on bund can be recovered later on in the form of saving the maintenance
dredging costs. (Para 186)
The Committee appreciates the efforts made to form a co-ordination committee to
resolve the issues. (Para 187)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 191)
Chapter–IV : Cochin Shipyard Limited
The Committee is not satisfied with the reply given to para nos. 163, 166, 167 and
172 by the Ministry of Shipping. It expects the Ministry to be serious towards its
responsibility of addressing the real issues. The Committee reiterates its recommendation
and desires the Ministry of Shipping to take up the issues contained in the
recommendations with the concerned Ministries/Government agencies under intimation to
the Committee. (Para 197)
The Committee takes note of the reply. (Para 200)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this Two Hundred Fourteenth Report on “Action taken by the Government on the
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee contained in its Two Hundred First Report on
Functioning of National Akademis and other Cultural Institutions – Issues and Challenges”.
2. The Two Hundred First Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented on the 17
th October, 2013 to the Parliament.
3. The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Two
Hundred First Report were received from the Ministry of Culture on the 22 nd September, 2014.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 10 th December, 2014.

The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Culture on
the observations/recommendations as contained in its Two Hundred and First Report on
“Functioning of National Akademis and other Cultural Institutions– Issues and Challenges”, which
was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 17
th October, 2013.
2. The Action Taken Replies have been received from the Ministry of Culture vide their O.M.
dated the 22 nd September, 2014 in respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the
Report.
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of all the further
recommendations/observations, which have been made in this Report should be furnished to
the Committee at the earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee
contained in the Two Hundred and First Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry and
recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the
succeeding paragraphs.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
5. The fact that three high-powered Committees had to be constituted for reviewing the
functioning of these institutions at regular interval is a clear indication that these institutions were
not working on the expected lines almost from the beginning and that need was being felt for
making them more effective, relevant and visible. Secondly, the fact of missing files relating to
these high-powered Committees reflected the lack of required concern in the Ministry of Culture
about working/performance of these bodies or it was helpless in doing anything in this regard due
to reasons beyond its control, perhaps because of autonomy enjoyed by them. The Committee,
therefore, decided to look into these issues and while examining the matter, it found that its
apprehensions were not unfounded and the problems were deeper than expected.
(Recommendation at Para 5 of 201st Report)
6. The Committee notes that though the Haksar Committee had also recommended for review
of the constitutions in 1990s, nothing could be done by the Government till now. The Committee
was informed that the Committees have been constituted for Lalit Kala Akademi and NSD to review
their constitutions and this Committee is not aware of their outcome. The Committee would like
to be apprised about this. (Para 22 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
7. There is no record available of the implementation of various recommendations of these
Committees in the Ministry. However, these recommendations are also being taken into consideration
by the High Power Committee constituted recently as per recommendations contained in this report.
8. Updated Status : Copies of report of Bhabha Committee, Khosla Committee and Haksar
Committee were made available to the HPC.
9. The HPC submitted its Report in May, 2014 and the same is under examination in
consultation with concerned organizations.

2

Committee should include officials from the Akademies and at least two external experts. It has
suggested that for each Institution concerned in HPC’s Report a small group be set up to study

11. HPC’s Report was circulated to all concerned and also uploaded on this Ministry’s website.
At present the views/comments of various Akademies on HPC’s report are being obtained and

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
12. The Committee notes the fact of missing records regarding implementation of
recommendations of Bhabha Committee, Khosla Committee and Haksar Committee. Aside
from much resources, public money, time and efforts gone waste, it reflects the attitude of
those who were responsible to examine/implement them. The Committee hopes that the
findings of the present High Powered Committee set up by the Ministry would not meet the
same fate.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
13. The Committee agrees that having autonomous cultural institutions with a link to
government remains a valuable notion in principle. The fundamental problem, however, is that these
were set up at a different time altogether, and they are alleged to have not been able to connect
with the actual arts constituencies of the day in the desired manner. The Committee feels that this
problem expresses itself in the linked areas of mandate; structure; accountability; inclusiveness;
networks; and imaginative outreach of programmes. Culture in general and the arts in particular can
never work with an unchanging or unresponsive or bureaucratic template. If the basic driver of
the akademis is to be autonomous and imaginative support for dynamic, ever-changing and
heterogeneous arts practices and practitioners, the institutions need to be reenergized from time to
time. We have unfortunately failed on that account. Emphasizing the urgent need for doing so, the
Committee recommends that the Government should come out with a road map in this regard in
the light of our experience so far. The Committee would like to be informed about steps to be
taken for this purpose. (Para 26 of ibid)
14. The Committee feels that the entire field of art and culture did not get the required attention
for decades, despite the foresight and commitment of the Founding- Fathers who knew the
significance of ‘culture and arts’ in our efforts for the nation-building. They set up these
institutions because they knew that this power is superior to other forms of power. But
unfortunately, these institutions, over the time, are alleged to have developed the vested interests -
monopolized by a few persons or group who have earned titles of ‘Culture Vultures’ or ‘Culture
Czars/Czarinas’, etc. Their products are described as being uninspiring, not showcasing the
composite culture of India. India is not known even to Indians precisely because these agencies
have not been able to live upto the expectations. These have still remained merely as subordinate
offices instead of becoming institutions of national glory. Be that as it may, the Committee feels
a deeper review of their organisation, composition, functioning and vision is called for urgently.
Professionalism of the highest order alone can salvage these institutions from the patronage of
unscrupulous people. The persons entering the portals of our premier cultural bodies, apart from
being from the field of art and culture also should be an evolved human being. In view of this,
the Committee recommends a comprehensive review of the Constitution as well as working of
these autonomous bodies – Sahitya Akademi, Lalit Kala Akademi, Sangeet Natak Akademi, National
School of Drama, Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts and National Gallery of Modern Arts to

3
attune them to the present day realities and requirements. The aim should be to get rid of the
vested interests that may have led to ‘cronyism’ and ‘self-perpetuating administration’. Only artists
should get opportunity to manage these bodies to make them truly professional, more responsive
and accessible. Their autonomy should be preserved at all costs, but we should ensure that it does
not lead to autocracy of a few. Autonomy and accountability are two sides of the same coin, one
cannot exist without the other. (Para 27 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
15. As desired by the Parliamentary Committee, a High Power Committee has recently been
constituted under the Chairmanship of Shri Abhijit Sengupta, Secretary, Culture (Retd.),
Government of India to address the various concerns expressed by the Parliamentary Committee
in regard to various Akademis under the Ministry of Culture.
16. Updated Status : The High Powered Committee has submitted its report. HPC has
recommended that a working group should be set up, chaired by a senior officer of the MOC, with
the three Secretaries of the Akademis, experts in the arts and at least one legal expert to draw up
the new Constitutions of the Akademis. Thereafter the Government will have to use its overarching
powers to direct the Akademis to adopt these changes. Recommendations of the HPC are under
consideration in the Ministry.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17. The Committee notes the reply and hopes that Ministry this time will try to live upto
expectations and come out with the most practicable and effective mechanism that may take
care of the problems faced today in these bodies as expeditiously as possible. This
Committee shall try to monitor any major step required to be taken in this regard. It also
calls upon the Akademis and other institutions to utilize this opportunity in making them
more responsive, effective and accountable. The Committee reiterates its observation made
earlier that “culture in general and arts in particular, can never work with an unchanging
or unresponsive or bureaucratic template”.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
18. The Committee feels that art and culture are inextricably linked with our traditions which
should be viewed as an evolving and organic thing. At the same time, these are not merely a thing
of the past, they have close correlation with the present as well as the future. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that efforts have to be made to create a composite, holistic understanding
of culture that can happen only if our premier cultural organizations such as the various Akademis
have a proper synergy amongst themselves. (Para 28 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
19. The various Akademis under the Ministry of Culture have synergy among themselves or
with other educational and cultural institutions. For example, the Indira Gandhi National Centre for
Arts (IGNCA) has over the years established a network with like-minded organizations in various
fields both Government and non-Government as also educational institutions. To name some: Prasar
Bharti, Sangeet Natak Akademi, National School of Drama, Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav
Sanghrahalay, Zonal Cultural Centres, several organizations in the North-East, including the North
East Hill University, Delhi, University, Jawaharlal Nehru University, Indraprastha University, Calicut
University, Benaras Hindu University, Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, NCERT, and
British Library.

4
20. IGNCA believes in the synergy of institutions and interdisciplinary studies. For instance on
8th March (International Women’s Day), 2013, the IGNCA in collaboration with the ZCCs and a
NGO working in the area of women’s health started a year-long campaign on ‘Cultural barriers in
women’s health.’ Through its Bal Jagat programme, the IGNCA has contacted over a hundred
schools, with emphasis on government schools and those run for underprivileged children, and
conducted workshops, film screenings and storytelling sessions, relating to Indian arts, culture and
heritage.
21. Sahitya Akademi encourages proper synergy among similar institutions like State Akademies,
educational and cultural institutions like Sangeet Natak Akademi and National Book Trust etc.
through which programmes are organized in collaboration.
22. The CCRT in its endeavour to enlarge its scope of working with other sister organizations
and to share its expertise with them, has developed certain collaborative inter-art as well as
educative programmes which are being organized in collaboration with ZCCs on various themes for
the benefit of student community.
23. Keeping in view the expertise available at CCRT, the CBSE had taken the help of CCRT to
prepare modules in the form of printed material as well as audio visual programmes on Indian
Culture for the courses. The NCERT in collaboration with CCRT has designed the syllabus on Art
Education for secondary level students and also produced educational material using the resources
of CCRT.
24. Further, synergy amongst various cultural organizations is also established through Central
Advisory Board on Culture and the Sub-Commission on Culture. However, the High Power
Committee is also examining these aspects.
25. Updated Status : The High Powered Committee has submitted its report. HPC has observed
that at the programmatic level, synergy must be in academic collaboration. The three Akademis
could jointly support inter-disciplinary studies. They should hold joint workshops and discussions
in areas of common theoretical importance. Recommendations of the HPC are under consideration
in the Ministry.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
26. The Committee notes the reply regarding synergy amongst the Akademis, cultural
and educational institutions but feels that it leaves much to be desired. Its level needs to
be enhanced and expanded.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
27. The Committee feels that there is hardly any contradiction between what the Committee
found and the argument given by the Ministry of Culture about overlapping of their mandates/
activities. The Committee also agrees that strict compartmentalization in this regard may neither be
possible nor desirable. But the Committee is convinced and Haksar Committee also talked about
this, that there is a scope for avoiding duplication of activities which causes wastage of resources
and efforts. This may be streamlined to reduce such duplications to a great extent. Thus, the
activities of the institutions need to be synergised for promotion and protection of our art and
culture in more efficient and effective way. (Para 30 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
28. The various Akademis under the Ministry function as per their respective mandate. In this,
although they collaborate with similar institutions, they try to avoid duplication of activities because

5
each organization has its own mandate. As mentioned above, the High Power Committee is
examining these aspects also.
29. Updated Status : The High Powered Committee has submitted its report and its
recommendations are under consideration in the Ministry in consultation with all concerned
organisations.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
30. The Committee hopes that the duplication if any, as mentioned above would be
cautiously eliminated to a great extent after new report is implemented.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
31. Our cultural akademis do not seem to interact nor do they have any sustained or
meaningful dialogue with schools, colleges and universities – even in the metros, leave alone the
vast remainder of the country. As a result, the akademis, for the most part, work like museums
in the wilderness. In the existing scenario, the Committee feels that our schools need to integrate
cultural education as part of their curriculum. This has to become mandatory for it to be
effective. (Para 32 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
32. Integrating cultural education in school curriculum is within the jurisdiction of the Ministry
of HRD. As far as the Akademis under the Ministry of Culture are concerned, some of them
already impart training on cultural matters to youth of the country directly or indirectly.
33. The CCRT was set up precisely for distinct functions relating to “Propagation of Culture
among Students”, which was not being addressed by any institution in the educational set up. It
was solely for this reason that a conscious decision to set up CCRT in 1979 was taken in order
to discharge its responsibilities towards its people for propagation of cultural values through
teachers and students.
34. CCRT has trained more than 1.2 lakh teachers in the field of cultural education and has
created a niche for itself in providing cultural education in schools. The CCRT has trained these
teachers covering 450 plus districts of the country. It is heartening to mention that most of the
schools are from rural backgrounds. The CCRT has worked with every State Education
Department in the length and breadth of the country. The teachers are trained in the methodologies
of linking education with culture.
35. Sahitya Akademi is involving more and more young writers for their programmes in 24
different languages recognized by the Akademi and also gives Yuva Puraskar to writers of the age
of 35 and below in these languages. Akademi has also involved school children in the programmes
organized under Children’s Literature. These programmes are not only held in the main cities but
also in remote places of the country.
36. Recently instructions have been issued that all those organisations/NGOs that are given
grants by this Ministry, would also give performance in at least two schools of their choice in the
place of their operation.
37. Committee’s observation that schools need to integrate cultural education as part of their
curriculum, the same has been conveyed to Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department
of School Education and Literacy who are concerned in the matter.

6
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
38. The Committee appreciates the work initiated by CCRT in training teachers by
liaising with State Education Departments in the country. The Committee advises the
Ministry to guard against mine or thine attitude. It has passed the onus of integrating
cultural education with curriculum as suggested by it, on to the Ministry of Human
Resource Development (HRD). It would have been appropriate had the Ministry of Culture
tried to put its head with Ministry of Human Resource Development to work together in
this regard.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
39. Education and culture are inseparable and will remain incomplete without one another. The
Committee, therefore, feels that the mandate of the akademis needs to be re-articulated to
emphasise links among the akademis as well as with a range of educational institutions. They
should interact with the Indian universities and educational institutions with a view to propagate,
preserve, and enrich our heterogeneous culture. Such a link would also promote arts education,
essential if we are to build a new generation of culture and arts “managers” with a vision.
(Para 33 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
40. A High Power Committee has been constituted to look into these issues. It is however,
mentioned that some of the Akademis are already involving educational Institutions in their
activities. For example, Sahitya Akademi regularly organizes literary activities with various
educational institutes/universities and colleges. The Akademi also collaborates with these educational
and literary institutions to organize its programme which are quite in number. Sahitya Akademi also
gives financial assistance under its Grants-in-Aid scheme to the educational institutes, literary
associations, universities and colleges from time to time and from the past experience, the Akademi
is having very healthy relationship with the educational institutions.
41. CCRT is working in the field of Cultural Education by way of providing education to the
in-service teachers, teacher educators and administrators, producing supplementary reading
materials on cultural education in the form of printed and audio-video teaching aids; sensitizing
students to the rich cultural heritage of India. It conducts programmes under the schemes
“Propagation of Culture among college and school students”, interlinking of education with culture
and Cultural Talent Search Scholarship Scheme. During the training programme the participating
teachers are required to interact with local school students thus facilitating the participating
teachers to translate the open handed learning in their respective institutions.
42. Further, the CCRT, working closely with NCERT and CBSE, was successful in introducing
heritage crafts and other forms of arts in the curriculum. The CCRT worked with NCERT in
preparation of position papers of the National Focus Group of National Curriculum Framework
2005 and made various recommendations. The CCRT is also in the final stages of starting Distance
Learning Training Programme with the help of Central Institute of Educational Technology (CIET)
of NCERT. These programmes will enhance the reach of CCRT to new heights quantitatively
without compromising on its quality and bring new resources into contact.
43. The NSD as a premier theatre teaching and training institute does not confine itself to the
academics happening within its classrooms and studios. It also interacts with students and teachers
across the country having drama departments in various universities through various ways of
teaching, conducting workshops, participating in seminars, evaluating research documents and also
participating in selection committees for various appointments.

7
44. Under its Outreach Programme or in other words, NSD’s Extension Programme, the
institution’s effort is to reach out to all young theatre enthusiasts and practitioners across the
country to train and provide them various theatrical inputs through theatre workshops of short/
long term durations. The participants of these workshops are not merely uneducated and
unemployed youths but come from educational institutions and in-service NGOs or Government
offices. Over the years beyond two decades, a large number of school/college going youths have
been immensely benefitted by these workshops.
45. The Theatre-in-Education Wing of the NSD engaged in imparting education through the
medium of theatre has been of immense use for children in the age group of 8–16 years. Through
this wing’s training programme, a great sense of confidence and personality building in the children
has been developed. Currently, the activities of TIE Company are largely located in and around
Delhi. It is so because of constraints of manpower and finance resource.
46. The Theatre-in-Education Company has also taken up the task of educating in-service
teachers of the country through the medium of theatre which subsequently helps the teachers in
educating their students. This programme has been successfully running in Agartala at Tripura for
the last two years and has won high appreciation.
47. As far as IGNCA is concerned, it is working with many academic institutions, universities
like Delhi University, JNU, BHU, and Pondicherry University etc. and with academicians from all
over the country. It also collaborates with organizations such as NCERT, CCRT, to promote art
education in schools and colleges through academic and outreach programmes. It also concentrates
on research and publication of fundamental texts and volumes of fundamental terms in the arts,
humanities and cultural heritage of India and the project for multi volume encyclopaedia of Indian
arts. Apart from dissemination through Bal Jagat programme and collaborative research, IGNCA
plays a major role in academic content generation.
48. The Sangeet Natak Akademi serves as a member of the General Council of Central Board
of Secondary Education, New Delhi and from time to time imparts desired information on the basic
concepts in the syllabus at academic level; also provide expertise in framing the syllabus on the
element of performing arts for the NCERT.
49. Ministry of Culture has been considering ways and means by which the urgent need for
arts management in India is addressed. To ensure that the process of arriving at an institutional
structure has wider participation and transparency, a Conclave attended by people of eminence was
held in March, 2014 at IIM, Bangalore.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
50. The Committee notes the reply but feels that all these activities were confined
mainly to Metro cities and colleges/universities located there. It needs to be expanded to
rural areas with the help of State Governments and renowned NGOs working in the area.
It would also help in locating and nourishing talents scattered all over the country.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
51. The Committee is of the opinion that a cultural Akademi would be meaningless if it does
not have programmes to reach out to the people at large, especially the youth. In addition to
interventions in educational spaces, this also calls for more planned involvement with the
community in general and the youth in particular by organizing workshops, short term appreciation
courses, residencies in colleges and schools. Besides, equally important is to have a closer interface
with the Media - print, electronic and social media through Internet. All the artists and art forms
may be provided with adequate platforms. Akashvani and Doordarshan may be roped in to provide

8
more opportunities to the artists and art forms. They should be used as a platform to disseminate
art and culture and various art forms. In other words, their mandate needs to be re-articulated to
balance the existing emphasis on showcasing with a more inclusive approach that takes the
akademis to people. (Para 35 of ibid)
52. The Committee notes that the efforts in India are largely targeted at getting children to learn
art forms – namely dance and music. Many drop out very soon and few see this as a real career
option. Incentives are far and few to get them engaged and interested. The Committee feels that
to avoid this disinterest, another level of intervention is required, to make them aware of what these
traditions are; at least to a point where they can identify some very basic ideas of the performing
and visual arts. While the Ministry of Culture set up the CCRT with somewhat a similar idea of
reaching out and creating opportunities for young children, especially from smaller cities, and all
regions including the North-East, the program needs to be seriously reviewed and updated. Further
it should be linked with other ongoing efforts of the Ministry. (Para 36 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
53. The present status of the various Akademis in these matters is as follows:
CCRT organizes training programmes which aim at creating awareness of the fundamental
principles underlying the development of culture. CCRT has been involving youth in her
programmes by providing national scholarships to young talented children. More than
10,500 scholarships were given to young students who have now created a niche for
themselves. As far as the dissemination of art, culture, various art forms and various
schemes are concerned; CCRT has been propagating the senior scholarship programmes
through trained teachers and also through young scholarship holders.
The CCRT has recently been transferred the Cultural Heritage Youth Leadership Programme
(CHYLP). This scheme will benefit school students of backward classes and rural areas.
It is estimated that hundreds of students will get benefited by exposure to arts and this
number will multiply in the subsequent years. The CCRT has been training the teacher
educators of the District Institute of Education and Training (DIETs) which was set up in
each District for training Primary or Upper-primary school teachers. The CCRT has trained
the teacher educators of more than 400 DIETs out of 542 DIETs functioning in the various
States. CCRT intends to cover all the DIETs in the next 3 to 4 years by not only providing
training but also enriching the educational resources in these DIETs. These educational
resources are provided free of cost to the teacher educators. At the philosophical core of
the CCRT lies a commitment to holistic education, encompassing the cognitive, emotional
and spiritual development of children. The CCRT emphasizes education grounded in cultural
knowledge and understanding as conducive to clarity, creativity and independence of
thought, tolerance, and compassion. In sensitizing students, teachers and others to the arts
and cultures of India, the CCRT aims to encourage local communities to take the lead in
the preservation of their cultural and natural heritage, and to promote respect for diversity.
Considering the impact of the electronic media on the viewers and realizing the
responsibility rests with the cultural institutions working under Ministry of Culture, CCRT
has produced quality productions towards fulfilling the objectives of linking education with
culture. This educational material is the outcome of the continued interaction with the
scholars, experts and educators, and is based on careful study and research. This material
is given to schools which have sent teachers to the CCRT to train, and teacher trainees are
initiated into using these in a variety of teaching and learning situations in the schools, for
curriculum teaching and extension work. In addition, the material is available for sale at the
CCRT headquarters and at its regional centres for general access also. The CCRT is signing

9
a MOU with Doordarshan (Bharati) to telecast these productions for wider circulation and
reach.
In order to build up a pervasive consciousness of the rich natural and cultural heritage of
North-East region, including Sikkim through the utilization of students in the conservation
of our heritage, the CCRT organized workshops in different North-Eastern States. The
primary, middle, secondary and senior secondary school teachers from all parts of the
country were introduced to innovative methods in classroom teaching using specific art
forms and traditional crafts of this region.
Sahitya Akademi, does a lot of programmes for youth which involve poetry readings, short
story readings, inviting them for national and regional seminars and also translation
workshops as and when organized apart from the Annual Yuva Puraskar given to young
writers.
NSD, through its outreach programme, has been educating and training young people having
interest in theatre arts across the country. Later on, these young people have either pursued
the theatre arts for their higher education and thereafter, joining some professional career
or practicing the same for its promotion in their region. This has helped in preserving the
dying performing art forms in different parts of the country.
To support the performing artists of the younger generation, the Sangeet Natak Akademi has
introduced Ustad Bismillah Khan Yuva Puraskar in 2006, to give recognition to the young
artistes. These artistes are featured in the festival of music dance and drama held after the
Award Ceremony. The Akademi provides financial support and training to young artists by
providing training under its various schemes, to sustain the rare and dying art forms such
as Kuttiyattam, Chhau, instrument making and mask making etc. set up in different regions
of the country. In addition, seven ZCCs are also actively concerned with preservation of
art and culture including folk and tribal art and culture in the country.
54. The High Power Committee set up by the Government recently will also look into these
recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee.
55. Updated Status : The High Powered Committee has submitted its report and its
recommendations are under consideration in the Ministry in consultation with all concerned
organisations.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
56. The Committee notes the reply and further recommends that the Akademis and
CCRT must collaborate with Universities like IGNOU for spreading cultural programmes in
India. IGNOU is a National University dedicated for distance learning and is presently
running an education channel “Gyandarshan”, which is highly popular and accessible to
everyone. In Gyandarshan direct interaction of teacher and students gets telecast. These
Akademis and CCRT can telecast its programmes on Gyandarshan for wider dissemination
of art and culture.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
57. The Committee found that the Secretariat of these cultural institutions were manned by the
people who have little idea/knowledge about how to manage Arts and Culture. Many of them lack
professionalism required for the field. The Committee feels that a cultural cadre distinct from the
regular administrative cadre needs to be created to man the functioning of the Akademis, Museums
and other cultural institutions. This should consist of individuals who may be ‘generalists in the

10
arts’. Courses would have to be introduced for educating them in the arts to make them conversant
with different forms of theatre, dance, music, poetry and literature, painting, sculpture and
architecture. Courses in ‘art administration’ could be part of the regular educational stream or even
special courses created under the Ministries of HRD and Culture to produce right kind of persons
to administer our cultural institutions in a better way. The Committee further recommends that
the Ministry should seriously consider the creation of cultural cadre on the above lines.
(Para 37 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
58. It is not possible to have a culture cadre common to all Akademies as their requirements
are quite different. The Akademies already have specialists in different fields with which the
respective Akademies are concerned and in view of the uniqueness of their respective expertise, it
may not be possible to utilize the same in any other Akademi.
59. CCRT has assured that being a training institution; they can organize 2 or 3 programmes
for the personnel of the Ministry of Culture and Ministry of HRD. These programmes can be of
one week duration. The CCRT would like to organize two such programmes in CCRT Hqrs, Delhi
and one programme in Regional Centre, Hyderabad the modalities of logistics of which can be
worked out.
60. CCRT organized a training programme for the Directors of ZCCs. This course was followed
by another training programme for the 2nd tier officials of the ZCCs. The Centre organized very
recently another programme for the Librarians and Library professionals in CCRT in the month of
March, 2014 which was attended by 42 librarians from different States/UTs.
61. Training policy for all organisations is being formulated. With a view to create awareness
about Arts Management in the country, an Arts Management Conclave was recently organised at
IIM, Bangalore wherein top experts in such fields participated. The conclusions drawn therein are
being processed. National Museum Institute, a deemed University, organises regular courses in
History of Art, Conservation and Museology. ASI also has a training Institute namely Institute of
Archaeology where training in archaeology is imparted to students and the officers of ASI.
62. Updated Status : HPC has also made certain recommendations in this regard. It has
suggested that a cultural administration pool be created appointment to which would be on contract
basis. Some of these positions can be in the Ministry while others can be placed in various
Institutions under the Ministry. The recommendations of HPC are under examination in consultation
with organizations concerned.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
63. The Committee agrees with the Ministry of Culture that these Akademis are not
alike and their requirements are quite different. But apart from this Committee, the HPC
also has proposed to create a common/separate cultural administration pool. The Committee
feels that the Ministry has to either strengthen any of its present cadre/service or create
a new service/cadre from the persons belonging to the field of Art and Culture.
64. Akademis and other apex cultural organizations were expected to be the custodians
of our rich cultural heritage. But unfortunately, most of them had been understaffed most
of the time, mainly due to large number of vacancies for very long time. Moreover, higher
positions are being manned by the persons on deputation from sundry background. These
institutions, no doubt, have done some good work but a long term vision to promote art and
culture is yet to develop in the country. In this regard, the Committee would like to
emphasize that the proposal for the creation of a cultural cadre should be carefully
considered on the lines suggested by it.

Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
65. Regarding Lalit Kala Akademi, there were serious allegations of malpractices and counter
allegations by its Chairman and Secretary. The Garhi studios were occupied by vested interested
and the guidelines for allotment of studios could not be implemented properly. There were

Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
72. The Committee reiterates all its observations made about the functioning of our premier

Sangeet Natak Akademi and National School of Drama” and 167
th Report on the “Functioning of
National Museum” submitted earlier to Parliament. In fact, the report in hand is a result of the
callousness and apathy noticed on the part of Akademis as well as the Government to any attempt
to reform these institutions. Fate of a number of important reports such as Bhabha Committee
(1964), Khosla Committee (1972), Haksar Committee (1989) including Parliament’s Reports is a
testimony to this as no actions have been taken on recommendations of these Committees. These
Akademis are always mired in one controversy or the other. Our Founding-Fathers gave them
autonomy to keep the politics away from culture but today politics seems to have crept into them
from the back door. The Founding-Fathers of these institutions had strong faith in the integrity of
the community of writers and artists but could not foresee the problems plaguing these institutions
today. (Para 49 of ibid)
73. The result is a lack of transparency in process and accountability in terms of outcomes.
In fact, their autonomy without transparency and accountability has become a double-edged
weapon to be used as per one’s convenience. In administrative parlance, accountability is not about
control but about responsibility for which autonomy has to be exercised. In other words,
accountability is not an administrative tool but a moral obligation on those who have the
responsibility to give an account of their work and performance. Besides, legitimacy and credibility
of these institutions can only be established if they observe adequate transparency in their
functioning. Unfortunately, these elements are currently conspicuous by their absence. As a result,
these institutions have failed to live upto the expectations and are being misused by those in power
selectively by marginalizing/ignoring deserving others. This crisis situation has been further
compounded by the role of the Ministry of Culture characterized by apathy, lack of concern and
sometimes helplessness. There is hardly any mechanism to ensure accountability and transparency
in their working by the Ministry. Once or twice, the Ministry did try to become pro-active in this
regard, it was met with stiff resistance and the matter went up to highest level in the executive
ladder. As such, normally the Ministry has little option but to keep off. It interferes only when it
feels that it should. (Para 50 of ibid)

representations given by Secretaries of all the Akademis emphasizing the need for their
restructuring. (Para 51 of ibid)

Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
79. As per their constitution/MOA, Secretaries are the executive head of the Akademis. In fact,
their constitutions are vague about the limits of Presidential authority and therefore, sometimes the
Chairmen try to exercise powers which they do not have and intervene directly in day-to-day
administration. Many of the decisions taken by them are not put to ratification by General Council
or Executive Council. Responsibility for any lapse/violation done by the Secretaries while
implementing the direction of the Chairman, ratified or not, would obviously lie with the Secretaries
and not the Chairmen. It has resulted, more often than not, in a running feud between the two.
In such a situation, main work of the Akademis gets a back seat as most of the time, energy and
scarce funds are wasted on unproductive/unwarranted things as cases go to the Court quite too
often. It has been found that during this running feud between the Chairmen and the Secretary,
Ministry either remains a mute spectator or it intervenes only when it feels to do so. The
Committee emphasizes the need for delineation of power between the Chairmen and Secretaries on
the one hand and Government of India on the other to avoid any possibility of violation of rules
and regulations in the course of exercise of administrative powers by the Chairmen/Secretaries of
these Akademis. (Para 55 of ibid)
80. Such a situation, the Committee strongly feels, cannot be allowed to linger on and feels it
is high time something has to be done for setting these Akademis in order. The Committee feels
that these bodies get funds from the Consolidated Fund of India and their Demands for Grants are
approved every fiscal by the Parliament on the recommendations of this Parliamentary Committee.
As such, this Committee with all sense of responsibility says that the funds allocated to these
institutions need closer and regular monitoring by conducting their performance audit every year.
There should be a regular review of the functioning of our cultural institutions. These reviews
should be conducted by external persons/committees which should be included in their Annual
Reports that are placed before Parliament. (Para 56 of ibid)

in States also leave much to be desired; strengthening/equipping State Akademis is equally important
otherwise it will be difficult to take activities down to the local level. The Committee would like
to reiterate the Haksar Committee recommendations in this regard for streamlining and
strengthening State Akademi’s and other regional organisations by involving/associating them in the
activities undertaken by the National Akademis. Support should also be extended to research and
documentation aspects in all forms of arts and revival and support of regional and local traditional
art forms. (Para 74 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
129. The various Akademies already function in close coordination with other Akademies and
literary Institutions. Sahitya Akademi makes all efforts to collaborate with the State Akademies and
also the literary associations to organize programmes and also makes it possible to help these
organizations whenever there is a demand from them. The Akademi has the practice to invite
recommendations from the State Akademies for the reconstitution of its General Council.
130. The NSD is always committed to provide all kinds of advisory support relating to academic,
artistic and technical aspects to the State Akademis as and when required. However, as NSD’s
financial resources are limited and not adequate to carry out its own targeted activities, it is not
able to provide any financial support to the State Akademis in furtherance of their cost.
131. The IGNCA works in close coordination with state Akademies and other recognized
organizations and academic institutions as part of its regular research and documentation projects.
For example, in the North-East region, the IGNCA collaborates with all the universities and state
Akademis. It also attempts to work with ZCCs and universities all over the country as part of
outreach also. As regards CCRT, in view of the specialization acquired by it over the years, it is
also playing an important role not only in providing its expertise to other organizations at national
and international level but also get help and co-operation from other Cultural institutions to fulfill
the aims and objectives of its mandate.
131.1 CCRT and Asia/Pacific Culture Centre for UNESCO (ACCU), Tokyo
The CCRT has been providing expertise and resources for Regional Co-operation in Cultural
Activities in the Asian Region to the Asian Culture Centre for UNESCO, Tokyo. The CCRT is the
national co-agency for the ACCU, Tokyo for implementing its programmes. Many other
organizations in the country are also availing the expertise of CCRT and has been associating with
CCRT in their field of work.
131.2 CCRT and Central Board of Secondary Education(CBSE) and NCERT
The CBSE has felt the need of sensitizing the children of non-resident Indians and has
decided to launch accredition courses on Indian Culture for them. Keeping in view the expertise
available at CCRT, the CBSE had taken the help of CCRT to prepare modules in the form of printed
material as well as audio visual programmes on Indian Culture for the courses. The NCERT in
collaboration with CCRT has designed the syllabus on Art Education for secondary level students
and also produced educational material using the resources of CCRT.

22
131.3. CCRT and Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS)
The Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS), which is running vast number of schools in the
country is providing quality education to the students, has been collaborating with CCRT to
organize a number of Workshops on Lifeskills Education for Adolescence (one of the
recommendations in the National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2000).
131.4 CCRT and Zonal Cultural Centres (ZCCs)
The CCRT in its endeavour to enlarge its scope of working with sister organizations and
to share its expertise with them, has developed certain collaborative inter-art as well as educational
programmes which are being organized in collaboration with ZCCs on various themes for the
benefit of student community.
131.5 CCRT and Multi-Cultural Education
The CCRT has been training teachers and teacher educators from UK and USA who visit
India to get trained in multi-cultural education. The CCRT has been organizing academic
programmes for them. These exchanges of the teaching community have largely been responsible
for removing the stereotype images that one has of different cultures and provide true information
and understanding through first-hand experiences. A number of organizations like British Council,
USIEF, Japan Foundation, etc. have been availing CCRT’s expertise in this regard.
131.6. CCRT and Cultural Resources
One of the recommendations of the National Policy of Education 1986 that the CCRT will
be required to develop effective cultural software and also develop modules for cultural technology
like audio-visual projects, set of posters, display album, etc. The CCRT has been producing a
variety of publications and audio-visual materials aimed at providing an appreciation and
understanding of various aspects of Indian art and culture. The educational material developed by
CCRT on Indian art and culture has a great acceptance in most of the Universities, Indian
Embassies in foreign countries, Governmental and non-Governmental organizations in India and
abroad.
131.7 CCRT and Department of Education, Ministry of HRD
132. The CCRT is perhaps one of the unique institutions in the country which is working in the
area of providing aesthetic and cultural values in the educational system. There is a Scheme which
is being implemented by the Department of Education namely ‘Scheme for Assistance in
Strengthening Culture and Values in Education’. Keeping in view the expertise available in the
CCRT, the Department of Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of
India has appointed CCRT as one of its Nodal organizations to implement the scheme.
133. The recently transferred modified scheme of Cultural Heritage Leadership Programme also
has the provision of documentation of local tradition art forms. This scheme will be operationalized
soon by CCRT.
134. Updated Status : The Ministry of Culture also administers a scheme namely, safeguarding
the Intangible Cultural Heritage and Diverse Cultural Traditions of India the object of which is to
preserve and propagate our rich intangible cultural heritage.

over the Zone. Drama, Music and Art may all integrate to make a total concept of every aspect
of our culture through Zonal Cultural Centres. ZCCs are endeavoring to develop in such a direction,

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this Two Hundred Fifteenth Report on “Action taken by the Government on the
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee contained in its Two Hundred Third Report on
Privatization of Services at Airports”.
2. The Two Hundred Third Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented on the 17
th October, 2013 to the
Parliament.
3. The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Two
Hundred Third Report were received from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the 20 th March, 2014.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 10 th December, 2014.
DR. KANWAR DEEP SINGH
