REPORT
The civil aviation sector in the country is the world's ninth largest civil aviation market and
ranks fourth in domestic passenger volume. It is one of the growing sectors of the Indian economy.
India's scheduled airlines carried 67.73 million passengers in 2014 compared to 61.42 million
passengers in 2013. Air traffic in India grew between 20 and 40 per cent for six years starting from
2003, when the Low Cost Carrier module was launched. The civil aviation market in India is all set
to become the world's third largest by 2020. During the next five years, aircraft movements,
passengers and freight at all Indian airports are expected to grow at a rate of 4.2%, 5.3% and 5%
respectively.
2. The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for the formulation and implementation of national
policies and programmes in the civil aviation sector. The Ministry oversees the development and
regulation of civil aviation in the country including establishment of new aerodromes, maintenance
and upgradation of existing aerodromes, regulation of carriage of traffic by air and ensuring civil
aviation safety and security.
3. The civil aviation sector is monitored and regulated by two separate organizations under the
Ministry of Civil Aviation i.e., Directorate General of Civil Aviation and Bureau of Civil Aviation
Security. The Commission of Railway Safety, which deals with matters pertaining to safety in rail
travel and operations and performs certain statutory functions specified in the Indian Railway Act and
the Rules framed thereunder, is also under the Administrative control of Ministry of Civil Aviation.
Ministry of Civil Aviation has the following Public Sector Undertakings/Companies/Autonomous
Bodies under its administrative control:
(i) Air India Limited and its subsidiaries viz. Hotel Corporation of India Limited, Air India
Charters Limited, Air India Air Transport Services Limited, Air India Engineering
Services Limited and Airline Allied Services Limited
(ii) Airports Authority of India
(iii) Pawan Hans Limited
(iv) Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi
(v) Airports Economic Regulatory Authority of India
4. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture
considered the details of budget allocations of the Ministry of Civil Aviation for the financial year
2015-16 at its meeting held on the 30th March, 2015. During the meeting, the Committee heard the
views of the Secretary and other senior officers of the Ministry of Civil Aviation as well as the heads
of organizations under its purview on budgetary aspects.

10. When it was asked about the main areas where the Ministry could not go ahead in the manner/

4
(a) Equity Infusion in Air India - Due to reduction of equity infusion in Air India as per the
Turn Around Plan (TAP), Air India is to arrange funds by way of borrowing which costs
additional amount of interest to be paid by the Government.
(b) Grants-in-Aid for creation of capital to Airport Authority of India - Due to reduction in
budgetary provision, the projects undertaken by Airport Authority of India will be
affected.
11. The Committee notes that the Ministry was able to spend 98.4% of the funds allocated
for Plan schemes and 86.48% under Non-Plan at RE stage in 2014-15. The reasons submitted
by the Ministry for under-utilization of funds which were increased at RE stage except in the
case of equity infusion into Air India, are of routine nature. The Committee observes that
under-utilization of funds in case of National Aviation University and Bureau of Civil Aviation
Security under Plan head was due to slow construction and delay in finalization of schemes/
projects respectively. The Committee notes with concern the under-utilization of funds by
Hotel Corporation of India. The Committee feels that the Ministry should impress upon
organizations under its purview to utilize the allocated funds to the maximum extent possible.
12. The Committee would like to know the reasons for not providing the grants-in-aid to
IGRUA for 2015-16 and how the Institute would manage its expenses henceforth.
13. The Committee also notes that Rs. 3 lakh was utilized for Innovations in Governance
during the year 2014-15. The Committee may be appraised on the achievements made under
this programme.

AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA (AAI)
36. Airports Authority of India (AAI) is developing airport infrastructure along the length and
breadth of the country including remote and far flung areas. AAI came into existence on 01.04.1995
with the merger of National Airports Authority and International Airports Authority of India. The
merger brought into existence a single organization entrusted with the responsibility of creating,
upgrading, maintaining and managing civil aviation infrastructure both on the ground and air space
in the country; with a view to accelerate the integrated development, expansion and modernization
of the air traffic services, passenger terminals, operational areas and cargo facilities at the airports
in the country. It manages 125 airports consisting of 68 operational airports (11 International airports,
8 Customs and 49 Domestic airports), 26 Civil Enclaves (3 International, 4 Customs and 19
Domestic) and 31 Non-Operational Domestic Airports. In addition, AAI provides Air Navigation
Services (ANS) at all civil airports including 9 other airports that are not managed by AAI. AAI also
provides Air Traffic Management Services (ATMS) over entire Indian Air Space and adjoining oceanic
areas with ground installations at all airports and 25 other locations to ensure safety of aircraft
operations. AAI is a Mini Ratna Category-1 Public Sector Enterprise.

PAWAN HANS LIMITED (PHL)
60. Pawan Hans Limited has a paid-up capital of Rs. 245.616 crores. Out of this, 51%
(Rs. 125.266 crores) is contributed by the Government and 49% (Rs. 120.35 crores) by the Oil and
Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC). PHL runs helicopter services for offshore operations,
connecting remote and hilly areas and tourist services.
61. The company is also operating a Training Institute approved by Directorate General of Civil
Aviation, Government of India, for imparting training in the field of Aircraft Maintenance Engineering.
National Institute of Aviation Safety and Services (NIASS) was set up by Pawan Hans with the
primary objective for implementing a world class Safety Management System in its operations.
62. The Committee noted that Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited was allocated Rs.46 crore in B.E.
2014-15 through Internal and Extra Budgetary Reserves (IEBR) which was reduced to Rs. 25.51
crore at R.E. stage. Now, an amount of Rs. 110.95 crore has been allocated through IEBR without
any budgetary support in B.E. 2015-16. When it was asked for the reason for such variation and the
justification for not providing budgetary support to Pawan Hans Helicopter Limited, it was informed
that the IEBR of Rs. 110.95 crores for the year 2015-16 has been projected based on the Budget
Estimate for revenue projection for the year 2015-16. The outcome budget for Rs. 48.95 crores for
the F.Y. 2015-16 will be entirely met out of the available IEBR mentioned above.
63. The main reason for increase in IEBR includes low capital expenditure incurred during
2014-15 and increase in retained earnings for the 2014-15 along with higher generation of projected
operating profit during 2015-16. PHL has not sought for any budgetary support for 2015-16.
64. The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation during the course of examination of Demands for
Grants, further clarified that Pawan Hans has some retained earnings and they have not actually
requested for any budgetary support for 2015-16. He further stated that Pawan Hans is shifting from
acquisition of helicopters to leasing of helicopters, which being more economical, has reduced the
expenditure.
65. The Committee was further informed that Pawan Hans has emerged as one of Asia's largest

81. When it was asked about the reasons for withdrawal of routes by Air India during the last year,
it was informed that Air India continually monitors the carriage/load factors/financial performance of
services on its network and makes efforts to improve their performance. Whenever any services
recurrently give rise to cash losses, AI analyses the reasons for the losses and based on the strategic
importance of such services to its network, arrives at a decision whether to continue or withdraw
such services. While determining the desirability or otherwise of discontinuing operations of loss-
making services, Air India takes into account the revenue contributions made by the subject services
to its other services by way of feeder traffic. As such non-profitability of any one flight is not taken
in isolation as the sole barometer of its financial performance.
82. It was further informed that Air India makes changes to its network to rationalize capacity
offered on various routes to maximize the benefits to the airline. Consequently, periodic adjustments
are done to the schedule to add or reduce capacity from specific routes, introduce new routes, and
restructure existing routes based on the market dynamics and anticipated financial outcome.

'Airline Management Solution Provider on the rationalization and optimization of network by Air India,
the Committee was informed that M/s. SH&E were appointed to undertake the clean sheet exercise
after the merger of erstwhile Air India and Indian Airlines - to provide an integrated network of the
international and domestic operations of the two erstwhile airlines to gain network synergies.
M/s. SH&E completed this task and submitted their report in May, 2010 and effective winter 2010,
the following recommendations of M/s SH&E were implemented:
(i) Developed the hub in the newly offered integrated terminal T3 at Delhi Airport. The
schedule was developed to provide distinct international and domestic banks of arrivals
and departures to facilitate connectivity between domestic-international and domestic-
domestic operations. As of date, with the hub at Delhi, Air India is able to offer 3
international and 5 domestic banks of arrival and departure flights.
(ii) Consequent to the implementation of the hub in Delhi, Air India closed its hub at
Frankfurt airport, which was used for scissor operations to USA/Canada. This closure
helped Air India save significant costs.
(iii) Based on M/s. SH&E recommendations, Air India replaced the B777-200LRs with the
B777-300ER aircraft on its prime India-USA routes for non-stop flights from Delhi to
JFK, Toronto and Chicago. These non-stop operations were implemented with changes
in the operations rules including redespatch of aircraft. This has helped Air India increase
its revenue per flight by using the high density B777-300ERs on the non-stop US routes.
(iv) Phase out the high cost B777-200LRs - based on M/s SH&E's advise, AI commenced
the process of lease out/sale of the 8 B777-200LRs in the fleet. As of date, 5 out of the
8 aircraft have been sold and for the balance M/s SH&E had recommended that the
proportion of the narrow body aircraft be increased in the Air India fleet. So also the
fleet of Air India Express be increased and co-existence of both the brands to be retained
as per market requirements. Each of these recommendations are in various stages of
implementation.
(v) As recommended by SH&E, the wide body fleet size of Air India has been retained at
the level of the firm aircraft acquisitions and no additional growth has been envisaged
in the wide body fleet. Fleet growth is envisaged in the A320 family fleet to enable
increase the proportion of the narrow body capacity.
(vi) Operations from Mumbai to be strengthened when the integrated terminal is offered at
Mumbai airport. Air India is planning to implement this with Mumbai airport being
offered as an integrated terminal by mid 2015.
(vii) Reduce loss making routes. Air India has continuously been reviewing the loss making
routes in the international and domestic markets and improving the schedule by
removing/reducing loss making routes based on market requirements.

like Parasailing, Hot Air Ballooning, Skydiving, Glider flying, Aeromodelling etc. through its 23
associate members using equipment provided by ACI.
117. Aero Club of India is being provided grants-in-aid by Government for development of
aerosports in the country and also to provide trainer aircraft both single engine and multi engine and
simulators to its member flying clubs for imparting quality ab-initio flying training. However, the Club
has not been provided any grants-in-aid for 2015-16.
118. The Committee finds that Rs. 10 lakhs was provided as a Grants-in-aid to Aero Club of
India for flying training and aero sports development during 2014-15 but the Club was able
to spend Rs. 3 lakhs only out of the allocation without any valid reason. The Committee also
feels that the Aero Club of India which is also working with the Ministry of Sports and Youth
Affairs and State Governments to give training to people with gliders and other equipment,
may be provided with necessary budgetary allocation at RE stage.
CIVIL AVIATION POLICY
119. The Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the Committee that a Draft Civil Aviation Policy was
unveiled on 10th November, 2014 to address various issues such as Development of airports,
Rationalizing the cost of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF), Development of the Cargo sector, Institutional
reforms, Enhancing Regional Connectivity, Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) facilities,
Modernization of Air Navigation Services (ANS), Development of Helicopter Aviation, DGCA and e-
Governance. Besides, the draft civil aviation policy also envisages to create four international hubs
and six metro hubs in the country. The places of these hubs will be finalized on the basis of
population and the passenger traffic. The Ministry had invited comments/suggestions of the public/
stakeholders/State Governments on the draft policy. Finalization of Civil Aviation Policy is being
carried out on the basis of comments/suggestions received on the draft policy.
120. The Committee has been consistently emphasizing the need to have a civil aviation
policy for such a growing sector for which India has humongous potential. Now, it is happy that
the formulation of Civil Aviation Policy is already in advance stage. The Committee feels that
the views, comments and suggestions given by the stakeholders from the aviation industry be
given due consideration in finalizing the National Civil Aviation Policy.
121. As regards creating international hubs, Kochi International Airport which is handling a
large number of domestic and international passengers and has already become a hub for
international operations especially to Gulf countries, the Committee feels, may be included.
This airport has substantial international traffic and has immense growth potential.
REGULATION OF AIRFARES
122. The Committee finds that currently there is no transparent mechanism to regulate the
airfare in the country. As a result, airlines are free to charge as much as they can and the
travellers also are caught unawares about it. The Committee does not agree with the
argument of the Ministry that some Rules/Regulations under Aircraft Act, 1934 regulate
airfare in the country.
123. The Committee in view of the hardship faced by common travellers and the air travel
becoming a necessity, cannot agree with this lame excuse, which is purely technical. The said
Act and the Rules framed is more than 80 years old and the civil aviation sector during this

28
period has undergone a sea change. The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that this Act/
Rule also needs to be overhauled now. Secondly, the idea of providing a competition between
airlines in this sector has not worked. Therefore, we are facing the problem of predatory
airfare today. It may also be due to some kind of cartelization amongst the airlines. Even the
benefit of reduction in the price of ATF is also not passed on to the passengers as reduction
in air fares. Therefore, the Committee strongly feels that it is high time now that the
Ministry must step in by putting a regulatory mechanism in place to see that airfares remain
within a reasonable range. The existing system has not worked.
GENERAL OBSERV ATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS
124. The Committee, on scrutinizing of budget papers of Ministry of Civil Aviation finds that
the overall performance of the Ministry during the last year has been satisfactory, but
utilization of funds needs further improvement. The Committee also finds that the Union
Budget 2015-16 shows a huge gap between projected demand and actual allocation. For
example, civil aviation sector was able to get merely 71% of the projected annual plan and
49% of the previous year's allocation at RE stage. The Committee hopes that allocation of
additional funds for Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Bureau of Civil Aviation
Security (BCAS), Air India and Airports Authority of India will help these Organizations to
complete various ongoing aviation projects under their jurisdiction. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation may take-up the requirement of budgetary
support with the Ministry of Finance at RE stage vigorously.
125. The Committee desires the creation of Civil Aviation Authority; absence of such an
agency in India was pointed out by the Federal Aviation Agency during its last audit. The
Committee also had recommended about this. Subsequently, a Bill was brought before
Parliament which was examined and reported by the Committee. The Committee hopes that
the Bill including the recommendations of this Committee in its 203rd Report (on the Civil
Aviation Authority of India Bill, 2013) presented to the Parliament in February, 2014 will be
introduced in the Parliament at the earliest.
126. The Committee also hopes that the Government will finalize the Civil Aviation Policy
on priority so that all the issues concerning aviation sector in the country are duly addressed
and the ever growing aviation sector gets much needed impetus from the Government.

under-utilization of funds in case of National Aviation University and Bureau of Civil Aviation
Security under Plan head was due to slow construction and delay in finalization of schemes/
projects respectively. The Committee notes with concern the under-utilization of funds by

organizations under its purview to utilize the allocated funds to the maximum extent possible.

Civil Aviation during the current fiscal against the allocation of Rs. 6711.74 crores at R.E.
stage in 2014-15. The Ministry was able to get only 49% of the previous year's allocation,
which is too meager to undertake development of airport infrastructure and other related
projects. The Committee feels that the Ministry should pursue for restoration of budgetary
support for its major organizations and important activities, ongoing or new, at RE stage
vigorously. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would be in a position to expend the
allocation under various heads judiciously and optimally during 2015-16. (Para 23)

in allocation will hamper the efforts being made to upgrade their facilities and activities. The
Committee hopes that the DGCA will also improve its performance in utilization of funds. The
DGCA was able to utilize Rs. 32.24 crore out of Rs. 44 crore allocated at RE stage and the
reason attributed for this is the delay in construction of new building for DGCA.
The Committee is surprised to note that the proposed new building for DGCA has been
stuck for several years. The Committee hopes that the land related issues are settled
with the concerned Ministry at the earliest and the project is completed without further
delay. (Para 33)

30

be completed as per a stipulated time-frame so that the functioning of country's aviation
regulatory authority is not compromised. (Para 34)

to have succeeded in getting its 'A' category in aviation safety restored by the Federal
Aviation Administration, U.S.A. It reflects the vision, commitment and hard work done by

Rs. 1973.48 crore allocated at RE stage in 2014-15, which stands at only 56% of spending
allocated funds. The Committee finds that funds allocated under Information Technology,
GSS-Equipment and Technology and Airport System were spent poorly. The Committee would
like to know the reasons for under-utilization of reduced allocation by AAI. The Committee
feels that spending merely 56% of Plan allocation does not augur well for the development
of required airport infrastructure in the country. (Para 52)
The Committee finds that the AAI was allocated a budgetary support of Rs. 80 crore
under Plan Head against the projected allocation of Rs. 117 crore for the year 2015-16. The
Committee was informed that Airports Authority of India has more than 15 airports under
construction or under upgradation, which needs substantial Plan support. The Committee
hopes that necessary funds will be allocated to AAI at RE stage, so that airport projects at
various stages are not affected due to paucity of funds. (Para 53)
The Committee hopes that filling up of vacant posts in Airports Authority of India would
be completed as per the fixed time-frame for a better and safer air travel in the country. The
Committee is of the opinion that the Government should lend a helping hand to AAI in
recovering its outstanding dues from various agencies for the services rendered to them, so
that it can maintain its cash flow at the desired level. (Para 54)
The Committee is not convinced with the reasons submitted for privatization of services
at Chennai and Kolkata Airports which were recently modernized using the tax-payers'
money. The Committee feels that functional autonomy should be given to Airports Authority
of India to exploit more commercial and non-traffic revenues from airports. The Committee,
while appreciating the commitment of AAI in developing airport infrastructure facilities in the
country, still feels that the potential and expertise available with State-run airport operator
is not being fully utilized by the Government. The Committee feels that with the available
expertise and manpower, the AAI can give tough competition to the private airport developers
subject to financial and other operational freedoms available to them. (Para 55)
It was brought to the notice of the Committee that certain airports such as Adampur,
Jabalpur and Calicut are in dire need of various developmental activities. The Committee may
be apprised on the status of declaration of Chandigarh airport as an international one. The
Committee desires that all out efforts be made so that the pending development works at all
these Airports are completed without further delay. The Committee would also like to know
the status of construction of new Greenfield airport in Kushinagar which falls under Buddhist
Circuit. If proposals for PPP are not forthcoming, Airports Authority of India should start the

31
work without delay as there is no doubt about this airport being unviable in view of huge
tourist potential of the place. (Para 56)
The Committee would like to know the reasons for allowing Mumbai International
Airport Limited to increase Floor Space Index (FSI) in the vicinity of Mumbai International
Airport for construction of more hotels. (Para 57)
The Committee finds that major works at the airports being/to be developed by Airports
Authority of India are pending for a long time for expediting, which Airports Authority of
India have to be proactive in getting the procedures fast-tracked with concerned agencies/
Ministries and the State Governments. For example, airports at Kushinagar and Jabalpur and
others are pending, for which approval have been given long back. In Jabalpur, land for
Terminal building and apron have already been given by the State Government, but the

privatization of our airports. (Para 58)

PAWAN HANS LIMITED (PHL)
The Committee observes that Pawan Hans Helicopter Limited has performed well in the
last year. The revenue hours has increased from 30625 in 2013 to 30920 in 2014 and the
average fleet monthly deployment has also increased to 34 in 2014-15 corresponding to 32 in
the previous year. The net profit has increased from Rs. 38.57 crore in 2013-14 to Rs. 43.54
crore in 2014-15. The Committee feels that though Pawan Hans Limited is showing good
performance, but ground realities tell a different story. Its services leave much to be desired.

areas such as health tourism, security, disaster  management, etc. Therefor e, an action plan

The Committee notes the reply. (Para 83)

REPORT
The Ministry of Culture is responsible for the preservation and conservation of the country's
rich cultural heritage and promotion of art and culture. The Ministry functions through two attached
offices, six subordinate offices and thirty five autonomous organisations. There are seven Zonal
Cultural Centres for promoting folk and traditional arts of different regions of the country. There are
also four National Missions viz., National Mission for Manuscripts, National Mission for Monuments
and Antiquities, National Mission on Libraries and Gandhi Heritage Sites Mission.
2. The vision of the Ministry has been to protect the cultural diversity of the country and its
heritage. The mission of the Ministry is to implement sustainable solution through which India's
diverse tangible and intangible culture and ancient heritage will remain universally acceptable.
3. The mandate of the Ministry is to preserve, promote & disseminate all forms of Art & Culture
through (i) Maintenance & Conservation of Heritage, Historical Sites & Ancient Monuments; (ii)
Promotion of Literary, Visual and Performing Arts through various organizations; (iii) Promotion of
Institutional & Individual Non-official Initiatives in Art & Culture; (iv) Administration of Museums to
ensure Preservation, Conservation and to facilitate Public Access to Heritage; (v) Administration of
Public Libraries; (vi) Maintenance of Manuscript Records and their digitization; (vii) Promotion of
Institutions & Organisations of Buddhist & Tibetan Studies; (viii) Preservation of Gandhian Heritage
Promotion of Research and Awareness in field of Art & Culture; (ix) Promotion of Research in
Anthropology & Ethnology; (x) Ensuring Equitable Access to Cultural Goods & Services for benefit
of all Members of the Community; (xi) Promotion of Cultural Industries including Traditional Artisanal
Enterprises; (xii) Catalysing Partnerships at every level to ensure Sustainable Development &
Management of Cultural Resources; (xiii) Promotion of International Cultural Relations; and (xiv)
Observation of Centenaries and Anniversaries of Important National Personalities & Events.
4. The Ministry is the custodian of all the major libraries in the country. It extends grant-in-aid
for library development and is also responsible for all policy matters regarding library development.
Through National Archives of India, the Ministry is responsible for maintenance of all archival records
of the country. The Ministry is involved in protection and promotion of Buddhist and Tibetan Culture
through various institutions located at Sarnath, Varanasi and Leh.
5. The Ministry has a capacity-building programme for all those who wish to excel in the field
of art and culture. Institutions like the School of Archaeology, School of Archives, National Museum
Institute, the Asiatic Society, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Institute of Asian Studies are mentionable in
this regard. Various courses offered by National School of Drama and Kalakshetra Foundation are also
some of the examples of capacity building programmes of the Ministry.
6. The Ministry marks its international presence by way of organising Festivals of India abroad
and is also responsible for implementation of various UNESCO Conventions in the field of culture and
for inscribing world heritage sites.
7. The Budget allocations of the Ministry of Culture for the financial year 2015-16, contained
in Demand No. 20 was taken up for consideration by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture in its meeting held on the 31st March, 2015. The
Secretary and other officials of the Ministry of Culture and its subordinate Organisations made a

examined Budget (2015-16) documents of the Ministry and the replies furnished by the Ministry to
the questionnaires.

12. The Secretary, Ministry of Culture while making a presentation before the Committee, stated
that economy circulars have been put in place by the Government and that the Ministry has rigidly
adhered to the economy circulars in place by a reduction of 10% in Non-plan expenditure, reduction
in travel, seminars, conferences and workshops.
13. The Committee notes that the present Budget Estimates shows an increase of just
Rs.10 crores in comparison to the Revised Estimate last year  i.e.,  2014-15. The Committee is
also surprised to note that the Ministry had to face a sharp budgetary cut at RE stage in the
last financial year. The Committee failed to get a convincing reason for this cut. Given the
importance of the mandate of this Ministry  i.e,  to preserve, protect and promote our vast
cultural heritage, both tangible and intangible, spread across the length and breadth of the
country, the Committee is at a loss to see that Plan allocation to this Ministry has come down

of 2015-16. Such allocation are highly insufficient and the Committee recommends that Plan

against Rs. 864.00 crore approved by the Planning Commission, the Ministry had incurred an

included Rs. 102.00 crore (Rs. 100.00 crore for INTACH as corpus fund and Rs. 2.00 crore for

allocated a sum of Rs. 1455.00 crore for developmental activities of the Ministry of Culture for
Annual Plan 2015-16, thereby resulting in a substantial reduction vis-a-vis the projections(Rs. 762.56
crore) on account of resource constraints. The Plan allocation for 2015-16 pegged at Rs. 1455.00
crore is about 65.61% of the outlay proposed by the Ministry of Culture for the year 2015-16.
Ministry of Finance has not intimated any reason for this reduction in Annual Plan allocation for the
year 2015-16.

organizations/schemes of the Ministry including Archaeological Survey of India, Museums, Libraries,
Scheme of Art & Culture and Centenary Celebrations, etc. Ministry of Culture has, accordingly,
earmarked Plan funds among various cultural organizations/schemes keeping in view their minimum
requirements and overall Plan funds allocated by Ministry of Finance.
30. The financial year 2014-15, Ministry of Culture had achieved more than 50% of the total Plan
allocation. The Ministry has stated that the expenditure level was slowed down to 64% during the
period October - December, 2014 due to the proposed reduction in the allocation at the Revised
Estimates stage. As against RE 2014-15 of Rs. 1500.00 crore, Ministry of Culture has incurred Plan
expenditure of Rs. 1292.37 crore (as on 15/03/2015) during the year 2014-15 which is about 86.16
% of RE 2014-15.
31. The Committee is at a loss to note that allocations had been reduced in almost all
sectors, which has adversely impacted Archaeology, Museums, Libraries and other important
Organizations under the Ministry. Culture imparts important identity to a nation. In the
development paradigm, culture plays a crucial role in the life of a nation. Therefore,
preserving, protecting and promoting our rich cultural heritage assume greater significance,
for which the Ministry must get adequate allocation. The Committee is of the firm view that
with the existing scale of allocation, even the existing schemes and activities of the Ministry
will be difficult to run. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry
should actively pursue the matter of increasing the allocation at the RE stage in the current
financial year, with the Ministry of Finance.

Archaeological Survey of India
58. The major activities of the Archaeological Survey of India are:
1. Survey of archaeological remains and excavations;
2. Maintenance and conservation of centrally protected monuments, sites and remains;
3. Chemical preservation of monuments and antiquarian remains;
4. Architectural survey of temples and secular buildings;
5. Establishment, Maintenance and running of Archaeological museums;
6. Development of epigraphical research and numismatic studies;
7. Expeditions abroad;
8. Training in Archaeology; and
9. Publication of technical reports and research work.
59. The Committee notes that the Archaeological Survey of India created three new Circles in
2013- 14 at Nagpur, Jodhpur and Sarnath by splitting Aurangabad, Jaipur, Patna and Lucknow
Circles.

3685 protected monuments and archaeological sites of national importance in the country which
includes 21 cultural sites inscribed in the World Heritage List by UNESCO.

Governments.

13
Governments for conservation work of the monuments is provided by the Archaeological Survey of
India. In some cases where the request is received for conservation work of State protected
monuments on Deposit Work basis, the ASI takes up necessary execution of the work on deposit of
the funds by the State Governments.
74. The Committee emphasizes the need for greater co-ordination between ASI, State
Governments and the local authorities in the matter of prevention and removal of
encroachments at our monuments. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to
aggressively pursue the matter of setting up the State level Co-ordination Committees, with
the remaining State Governments.
75. The Committee also urges that the field offices of ASI should pursue such cases of
encroachment persistently with the District Authorities on urgent basis and chalk a way out
in such cases. The Committee also underlines the need for adequate follow up of the cases
filed in Court of law against the encroachers.
76. As a preventive measure, the Committee likes the Ministry to consider the idea of
having a Central Force specially for protecting/ guarding our cultural heritage sites/
monuments on the lines of CISF and BSF etc. It can be' utilized both for Central and State
sites.
77. The Committee is unhappy to note that even though ASI issued 1950 demolition orders during
the last 4 years, only 32 such orders were executed. The Ministry's reply states that the
implementation of the demolition orders issued under Section 38(1) and 38 (2) of the Ancient
Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act by the Director General of ASI is a
responsibility of the District Administration.
78. The Committee understands the difficulties faced by ASI in this regard. The Committee is also
aware that there are a number of Court cases against the demolition orders issued by ASI.
79. In this regard, the Committee is of the view that ASI can fulfill its mandate only when
it has an adequate statutory backing to tackle encroachments. The Committee notes that at
present, ASI does not have inherent powers to execute the demolition orders issued by it.
Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that adequate powers should be granted to
ASI under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 which
would equip ASI to execute its demolition orders. The Committee is also of the considered
view that the Act should stipulate the action that can be taken against the District Authorities
in case of laxity or non-co-operation on their part in executing the demolition orders.
80. The Committee also recommends that a Task Force may be constituted in the States
wherein encroachment of monuments situated in communally sensitive areas are to be
removed. The specialized Task Force can co-ordinate with the District Authorities and the ASI
to remove the encroachers.
81. The Committee feels that keeping in view the humanitarian aspect of encroachments,
creation of a separate fund for removing of illegal encroachment & for rehabilitation would
ensure that the monument is protected and also that the encroachers are suitably
rehabilitated, without adversely affecting their lives. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
earlier recommendation that a separate fund is needed for removing of illegal encroachments
and for rehabilitation.

OBSERV ATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
Assessment of the Demands for Grants (2015-16) of the Ministry
The Committee notes that the present Budget Estimates shows an increase of just Rs.10
crores in comparison to the Revised Estimate last year i.e., 2014-15. The Committee is also
surprised to note that the Ministry had to face a sharp budgetary cut at RE stage in the last
financial year. The Committee failed to get a convincing reason for this cut. Given the
importance of the mandate of this Ministry i.e., to preserve, protect and promote our vast
cultural heritage, both tangible and intangible, spread across the length and breadth of the
country, the Committee is at a loss to see that Plan allocation to this Ministry has come down
from Rs.1835 crore in BE 2014-15 to Rs.1500 crore in RE 2014-15 and to Rs.1455 crore in BE
of 2015-16. Such allocation are highly insufficient and the Committee recommends that Plan
allocation for the Department be increased adequately at RE stage. (Para 13)
Twelfth Five Year Plan
The Committee notes that against the proposed outlay of Rs.18608.94 crore, only
Rs.7275.00 crore were earmarked for the Twelfth Five Year Plan. Due to this severe
downsizing, many important Schemes mentioned above, could not be taken up by the Ministry.
Since three years of the plan period have been over, the Committee recommends that for the
remaining two years, the Plan allocation for the Ministry of Culture should be hiked so that
important schemes/projects should not suffer. The Committee also would like to know the
rationale for abandoning the three schemes in the Museum Sector by the Ministry along with
an impact-assessment Report. (Para 16)
Spending pattern during the Twelfth Plan
The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry was able to spend more than 90%
of its allocation during the first three years of the Twelfth Plan. At the same time, the
Committee observes that better planning and supervision could have definitely improved the
pace of utilization. (Para 20)
2015-16
The Committee notes that the group- wise allocation will help the Ministry to reallocate
funds among the Schemes subsumed within the group, when the need arises. The Committee
hopes that this financial arrangement would impart more flexibility to the Ministry in terms
of allocation, leading to optimum utilization of funds. Nevertheless, the Committee desires
that due care and caution should be exercised to ensure that the new scheme of allocation
does not affect the progress of existing schemes/ programmes of the Ministry and also the
functioning of vital Organisations under the Ministry. The Committee would like to emphasize
that the interse fund allocation of the grouped heads should be brought to the notice of the
Committee at appropriate time. (Para 27)
23

24
Ministry's Projected Demand vis-a-vis Budgetary allocation
The Committee is at a loss to note that allocations had been reduced in almost all
sectors, which has adversely impacted Archaeology, Museums, Libraries and other important
Organizations under the Ministry. Culture imparts important identity to a nation. In the
development paradigm, culture plays a crucial role in the life of a nation. Therefore,
preserving, protecting and promoting our rich cultural heritage assume greater significance,
for which the Ministry must get adequate allocation. The Committee is of the firm view that
with the existing scale of allocation, even the existing schemes and activities of the Ministry
will be difficult to run. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry
should actively pursue the matter of increasing the allocation at the RE stage in the current
financial year, with the Ministry of Finance. (Para 31)
Non-Plan
Even the Non- Plan allocation of the Ministry, the Committee believes, does not inspire
confidence as the success of Plan activities largely depends upon the Non- Plan activities.
Existence of large number of vacancies and lack of adequate manpower at various levels
particularly in ASI, will certainly adversely affect the regular upkeep, maintenance,
protection and preservation of our cultural heritage. Pace of expenditure in this section,
Committee hopes would be maintained in future also. (Para 34)
Issues Taken up/pending with Ministry of Finance
The Committee notes that the sums demanded by the Ministry of Culture are required
for not only existing schemes, but also for new ones declared mid way by the Prime Minister
as well as Finance Minister. The Committee, therefore, strongly endorses the request put
forth by the Ministry to the Ministry of Finance. The Committee is of the firm view that
reduced allocation for vital Schemes of the Ministry would adversely affect the core activities
of the Ministry, thereby, undermining the mandate of the Ministry. (Para 36)

2013-14 was due to varied reasons such as non-filling up of vacant posts, delay in completion
of works, postponement of some programmes etc. (Para 38)

to ensure that under-utilization of funds does not occur. The Committee is of the view that
periodic monitoring by the Ministry, of the progress of schemes/programmes would help in
identifying the reasons for under-utilization at an early stage and in taking remedial action.
Further, the Committee stresses upon the need for strict monitoring and supervision of the
utilization of the grants given to the Organisations under the Ministry. (Para 39)
Filling vacant posts should also be expedited or outsourcing some activities may also be
considered. (Para 40)
The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for the failure in properly assessing the

The Committee emphasizes the need for greater co-ordination between ASI, State
Governments and the local authorities in the matter of prevention and removal of
encroachments at our monuments. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to
aggressively pursue the matter of setting up the State level Co-ordination Committees, with

The Committee also urges that the field offices of ASI should pursue such cases of
encroachment persistently with the District Authorities on urgent basis and chalk a way out
in such cases. The Committee also underlines the need for adequate follow up of the cases
filed in court of law against the encroachers. (Para 75)

having a Central Force specially for protecting/ guarding our cultural heritage sites/
monuments on the lines of CISF and BSF etc. It can be utilized both for Central and State
sites. (Para 76)
In this regard, the Committee is of the view that ASI can fulfill its mandate only
when it has an adequate statutory backing to tackle encroachments. The Committee
notes that at present, ASI does not have inherent powers to execute the demolition orders
issued by it. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that adequate powers should be
granted to ASI under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958
which would equip ASI to execute its demolition orders. The Committee is also of the
considered view that the Act should stipulate the action that can be taken against the District

2. Since the Chairman of the Committee was not able to attend the meeting, the Members
unanimously requested Yogi Adityanath, Member of the Committee, to chair the meeting. The Chair
welcomed the Members of the Committee and informed that the representatives of Ministry of Culture
and its subordinate organizations have been called to brief the Committee about the Demands for
Grants (2015-16) of Ministry of Culture. The Chair welcomed the Secretary and other officials to
the meeting. The Chair asked the Secretary to make a presentation on the Budget allocations made
to the Ministry, expenditure and achievements made during the last year, the adequacy of budgetary
provisions made to each head etc. The Committee wanted to know about the areas where the Ministry
failed to fully utilize the funds, the details of fund allocations to the Museums, Libraries,
Archaeological Survey of India, Zonal Cultural Centres etc.
3. While making a presentation before the Committee, the Secretary, stated that economy
circulars have been put in place by the Government and that the Ministry has rigidly adhered to the
economy circulars in place by a reduction of 10% in Non-plan expenditure, reduction in travel,
seminars, conferences and workshops. On the issue of encroachment of monuments, the Secretary
apprised the Committee that he had written to the Chief Secretaries of all State Governments/ Union
Territories requesting formation of State level Co-ordination Committees in this regard and that
positive response has been received from four State Governments. He also stated that Jammu &
Kashmir Government recently constituted the State level Co-ordination Committee.
4. The Secretary informed the Committee that the ASI had made an assessment of a requirement
of ` 200 crores approximately for construction/repairs of nearly 250 kms. of perimeter of masonry/
grill fencing of the protected monuments. However, a proposal of ` 100 crores for construction of
perimeter walls was not acceded to by the Ministry of Finance. The Secretary also apprised the
Committee that a conservation policy and an excavation policy had been notified and that the
guidelines on notification and de-notification of monuments have been drafted and uploaded on the
website. He also stated that ASI had identified 25 monuments which would be upgraded in first phase
as Adarsh Smarak.
5. The Members raised the need for the proper upkeep and maintenance of the monuments and
heritage sites at Sanghol, Punjab; Ram Tirath, Amritsar; Bhaini Sahib, Ludhiana; Birth Place of Bhagat
Singh; Hampi, Karnataka; Bijapur Adila Shahi's property; Gol Gumbaz, Karnataka; Bijapur Pattadakal
Aihole; Pureshwar Temple, Kutch; Dholavira village, Kutch; and Raniganj, Pratapgarh, U.P. One of
the Members of the Committee suggested that the ancient Sanskrit texts and handwritten books in
the Sadhu Ashram, Hoshiarpur and Bhirgu Sanhita which is an astrological classic may be considered
to be included under the National Mission for Manuscripts.
6. Members of the Committee also raised various queries which were replied to by the Secretary.
The Chair directed that written replies to the points not answered, may be sent within a week.
7. The meeting adjourned at 1:00 
P.M. for tea/refreshment to meet again after a short duration.

Airpor ts Authority of India (A .A.l .) for civil aviation purposes . These enclaves, co nsist of 
terminal buildings, aprons, taxiways and have been established in such a way that they do 
not interfere with the operational and security requirements of the defence airfields within 
which they are located .. Such enclaves were created at these 28 airfields, as no separate civil 
airport/ infrastructure was considered feasible at that statio n because of the land intensive 
and cost intensive nature of deve lopment, aodl also because these did not lend themselves to 
regulatory requirements of air space, given the existence of the defe nce airfields. The No 
Ojection Certificate from defence authorities could not be obtained under such compulsions .

2. Not all lbe 28 airfields were originally oonstructed for defence purposes. Six of these 
viz., Bbuj, Bagdogn, Vi.ba!cbapatnam, Silcbar, Port Blair and Gwalior were initially civil 
airports, but were Jatu oouverted into defence airfields.

3. The Department of Civil Aviation in their note submitted to the Committee bas 
stated that the civil enclaves operate under a number of constraints which may be 
summarised tts under:-
(a) Owing to sbonage of space at almost all defence airpons where civil enclaves are 
operating , a lim.ited area has been given for creating civil infrastructure . 
Expansion I modification of already created terminal buildings poses considerable 
problems, since there is no additional space available for modular expansion. 
(b) Because of space constraints, AAJ is unable to create cargo/ commercial 
infrastructure. 
(c) Air Traffic control is managed by the defence authorities on these airfields. 
Therefore, the entire watch-hour is dependent upon the requirements of defence 
force. 
(d) Time slots for the civil aviation is dictat ed by the defence requirements and civil 
aviation has to accept this constraint. In most cases, defence has been very 
cooperative in their endeavour to care to civil requirements. 
(e) The radio navigational aids, lighting system, etc. provided at defence airfields are 
commensurate with the defence requirements and their operational standards. 
However, these mostly fall below ICAO norms. AAJ bas therefore to provide 
these facilities at their expense. 
(f) Given defence requirements , often, expansion of watch hours becomes a great 
problem. 
(g) The radio navigational aids provided by the AA1 have to be serviced and 
maintained. While doing so, technical personnel have to face some problems on 
account of security constraints. 
(h) Despite heavy investments by the AAI in the defence airfields, returns to them are 
negligible, as air traflic control is handled by defence authorities and the tanding 
fee is collected by the de'fence authorities and deposited in the Consolidated Fund 
of India. 
(i) Power supply at defence airfields, at times, is not sufficient to cater to the needs of 
the civil enclave. Wherever possible, AAI has created independent power sources 
to cater to its own needs. 
(j) Administration and Coordination : The command and control of the defence 
airports are under their respective commanders. Control over civil enclave,s is 
exercised by the Airport Directors nominated by AAl. The latter have been 
advised, and maintain very close administrative coordination with the defence 
commanders in all matters. Usually all help is provided by the defence 
commanders. 
(k) Legal problems : Any dispute over land or legal requiremenu are referred to AAl 
Headquarters who in turn take it up with Defence Headquarters for their 
indulgenc~ and help. Most of the difficulties are sorted out through coordination 
meetings at appropriate levels with mutual cooperation. 
4. The Conimittee at its meeting held on the 20th February. 1996 heard the views of the 
Secretary, Department of Civil Aviation, and also the Defence Secretary in the matter . 
. )YJ!jler.deposing before the Gornrnittee, Secretary. Department of Civil Aviation has stated 
miiJ tJi.e problep~s at these c!,yil enclaves have incrl}a.SC#, during> ~e, last fiv~ years a~ th~re has 
been rapid growth in air traffic. The COI\~trairlts have been . felt more at such places C!.S

Bangalore, Goa, Pune and Cochin. When aslced about the long term plans/scientific studies 
for these civil enclaves, the Secretary informed the Committee that there were no such long 
term plans for the development of these enclaves. However, Department of Civil Aviation 
has identified plans for new airports keeping in view growing traffic requirements. Airports 
at Cochin, Bangalore and Goa have been given top priority. Separate airports at Cochin and 
Bangalore are being set up. An alternative site for new airport at Goa is yet to be identified. 
There are seven airports viz., Jodhpur, Pune, Agra, Allahabad, Chandigarh, Bagdogra and 
Gwalior which would acquire importance within the next five years or so and problems in 
these airports are proposed tO be tackled in a similar manner. 
5. As regards the investment made by the Airport Authority of India, the Committee 
has been informed by the Secretary that so far an investment of Rs. 251 crores has been 
made in these civil enclaves. This includes expenditure on (i) aerodrom works such as 
pavements, terminal and ancillary buildings, (ii) navigational aids and (iii) ground safety 
services. The revenue from these enclaves was however not commensurate with the 
investment made therein . Sources of revenue earning from these enclaves include Radio 
Navigational Facility Charges (RNFC) and non-traffic revenue. The major chunk of revenue 
i.e. landing charges collected ther efrom goes. to the Consolidated Fund of India and is then 
allocated to defence in the following year. The revenue so collected does not come back to 
the Airport Authority for investment in the development of aviation infrastructure. The AAl 
also does not get budgetary support from the Government. 
6. The Committe e has been informed by the Secretary that these enclave s also face 
severe constraints on account of shor tages of space which does not allow them to create 
additional cargo I commercial infrastructure and instal navigational aids such as DVOR ILS 
ere. Consequently, these enclaves do not meet lCAO specifications for civil operations. The 
maintenance staff at times is also not allowed to maintain the facilities. 
7. The Committee was .informed that Air Traffic Control (ATC) watch hours of defence 
airfields are controlled by the Defence For\OCS according to their own requirements. The civil 
flights are by and large restricted between 10.00 a.m. to 8.00 p.m. and not adjusted in case 
of delay due to bad weather or technical reasons. 
8. The Committee also heard the Defence Secretary on the matter. The Defence 
Secretary informed the Committee that there had been maximum possible cooperation from 
their side to accommodating civi.l aviation operation at these civil enclaves . On being asked 
whether Ministry of Defence have ever given a thought about separating civil enclaves from 
defence airfields or shifting of some of their airfields which are located in the cities, the 
Defence Secretary informed the Committee that keeping in view the high use of these 
airports, separate airfields at Goa (international) & Agra are under consideration. A 
Committee has been set up to examine the issue and the report is expected very shortly. As 
regards the shifting of defence airfields fro m its existing location, the Secretary stated that 
location of an airfield is important from the point of view of the operational plans of the 
armed forces.

9. The Committee noted the const raints being faced by the Department .of Civil 
Aviation at the Civil enclaves in the defence airfields. These constraints have adversely 
affected the operation of civil flights during the last 4-5 years due to the considerable 
increase in air traffic. Th~ 'problem has been more acute particularly at the places such as 
Bangalore, Cochin, Goa and. Agra wherc; .,~xpansion of infrastructural facilities is needed, 
given the tourist as well as commercial traffic. These places are now attracting more 
international Oighl$. The Committee has noted that there has been full cooperation from the

REPORT
Roads play an important role in the infrastructure development of the country. India has a
vast road network of 48.65 km. of which the National Highways and the State Highways together
account for 2,41,178 kms. The length of National Highways network is only 96,260 kms. (at present)
constituting about 1.9% of the total road network in the country and carrying about 40 per cent of
the total traffic across the length and breadth of the country. The Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways has been entrusted primarily with the functions of construction and maintenance of
National Highways (NHs), administration of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 Central Motor Vehicles Rules
1981, National Highways Act, 1956, National Highways Fee (Determination of Rates and Collection)
Rules, 2008, formulation of broad policies relating to road transport, environmental issues, automotive
norms etc. besides making arrangements for movements of vehicular traffic with neighbouring
countries.
2. The Road Transport Wing of the Ministry is concerned with the formulation of broad policies
related to road transport besides making provisions for the movement of vehicular traffic with the
neighbouring countries. The development and maintenance of National Highways are being done on
agency basis. The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), State Public Works Departments
(PWDs) and the Border Roads Organization are the main agencies. Out of the total length of
96,260 km. of National Highways, 55,904 km. is with the State Public Works Departments (State
PWDs), 32,279 km. with the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), 3,866 km. with the
Border Road Organization and 1,117 km. with National Highways Infrastructure Development and
Construction Limited, balance length of 3,094 km. is yet to be entrusted to the executing agencies.
3. Demand No. 83 containing the details of budget allocations of the Ministry of Road Transport
and Highways for the financial year 2015-16 was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture at its meeting held on the 8th April, 2015.
During the meeting, the Committee heard the Secretary and other officers of the Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways. The Committee also examined other budget (2015-16) documents of the
Ministry and the reply furnished by the Ministry to the questionnaire.

8. The reasons submitted by the Ministry for under-utilization of funds under some
schemes/programmes are of routine nature. The Committee feels that proper planning, timely
monitoring and taking preventing steps anticipating the routine bottlenecks would ensure
timely completion of schemes/projects and programmes. The Committee desires that
shortcomings with regard to implementation of projects may be identified in consultation with
the stakeholders involved in road projects so that such things are not repeated in future. The
Committee hopes that the spending pattern of the Ministry will see an improvement in the
coming years.
9. The Committee finds that the Ministry was not able to utilize Rs. 22.20 crore provided
from the Central Road Fund for State roads in Delhi for the year 2014-15. Though this fund
is non-lapsable, the reasons submitted by the Ministry for non-utilization due to less number
of proposals received from the Delhi Government are not impressive. The Committee hopes
that the Ministry should impress upon the State Governments in such cases to send their
proposals in time so that the allocated funds could be spent fully.
10. To a specific query on the under-utilization of funds on some schemes, the Secretary while
tendering his evidence before the Committee, informed that the majority of expenditure is incurred
during the last quarter of the financial year, as winter months are the main months for road
construction. However, Ministry of Finance imposed restrictions for ceiling of expenditure by 33%
for the last quarter of the financial year which is a major roadblock for incurring expenditure by the
Ministry.
11. The Committee appreciates the Ministry's concern in this regard. However, the
Committee notes that the Ministry did not actively pursue the matter with the Ministry of
Finance as could be understood from the reply furnished by the Ministry to the
recommendations made by the Committee in its 193rd Report in this regard. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should pursue the issue of removal of ceiling of expenditure
for the last quarter with the Ministry of Finance vigorously. The Committee urges upon the
Ministry of Finance to consider the removal on ceiling of expenditure for road projects during
the last quarter. It will help the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to spend the
allocation fully and also to complete the projects in time without cost overrun.

45. When asked about the major initiatives taken by the Ministry in the road sector, the Committee
was informed that a Hybrid Model for the Highways Sector - Annuity Mode with Construction Period
Capital Support has been introduced during the last year. As per the model, 40% of the Total Project
cost (TPC) is to be provided by the Authority to the concessionaire during the construction period
in the form of 'Construction Support'. The 'Construction Support' is to be disbursed in five equal
installments of 8% each and the timing of each such payment shall be linked to percentage of project
cost spent by the concessionaire. The concessionaire would be required to bear the balance 60% of
the project cost through a combination of its equity contribution and debt raised from the market.
Further, the 60% of the project cost borne by the concessionaire during the construction period is
to be recovered from the Authority in terms of annuity payments spread over a period of ten/twenty
years. In addition to annuity payments, there shall be separate provisions for payment of Operation
& Maintenance (O&M) payments subject to a predetermined limit and interest on outstanding balance
also to the concessionaire. The concessionaire remains responsible for O&M of the project highway
till the expiry of the concession period. The project gets transferred to the Authority after completion
of the concession period.

Ministry informed that a website on Toll Information System to make available in public domain,
information of public interest concerning toll plazas on National Highways/ Expressways operating
under Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and NHAI viz., the applicable User fee rates for
various categories of vehicles on any Toll Plaza, helping road users to ascertain the exact toll amount
for a particular plaza or a select route between two locations was launched on 31.10.2014. Updated
information to public/ road users about the concessions/discounts applicable for local and frequent
users etc. on any Toll Plaza is made available. The web portal is user friendly and public can access
the information through mobile phones and SMS.
47. The Committee after scrutinizing the information provided by the Ministry, expresses

of National Highways in the country. NHAI was able to spend Rs. 6,208 crore only out of Rs.

when the private players are withdrawing from National Highways projects due to
non-availability of equity and loan to carry forward the projects, NHAI was able to spend just
26% of the allocated fund. The Committee feels that with this spending trend, NHAI would
not be in a position to achieve its targets in the coming years.

III to VII are progressing at a snail's pace and there are no takers for projects under NHDP

at various stages of NHDP which was once considered as an ambitious project for providing
road connectivity even to the remote places of the country.

project stretches, the Government had to resort to Engineering, Procurement and
Construction (EPC) mode also for the construction of National Highways apart from Public
Private Partnership (PPP) mode. The Committee notes that out of 7980 Km length of National

52. Another important issue brought before the Committee was the poor design and
planning of National Highways. It was informed that many habitations in the country have
been divided by the National Highways and in the absence of underpasses and subways, people
residing on one side of the National Highway are not able to move to the other side freely.
Such bad planning results in high number of accidents in such places. Some Members of the
Committee raised the issue of 'blind spots' and lack of proper designing of the National
Highways. The Committee recommends that all the black spots be identified and road
designing be given due importance in construction of National Highways in future.
53. The Committee also notes that during rainy seasons, underpasses and subways
constructed on National Highways are flooded with rain water resulting in disturbance of
traffic movement in the absence of proper drainage system. The Committee is of the view that
while designing a national highway, drainage system on national highways should not be
ignored in the name of cost cutting. The Committee recommends that the Ministry as well
as NHAI, should ensure that in all the projects for development of national highways,
provision of drainage system should be made part of the concessionaire agreement.
54. When the issue of traffic congestion at Toll plazas was raised, the Secretary informed
the Committee that with the implementation of Electronic Toll Collection System in the
country, toll collection at toll plazas will be streamlined and the traffic will be regulated. The
Committee strongly feels that persons who are manning the toll gates throughout the country
should be imparted training on how to behave, general etiquette and civic sense, to deal with
the public, as clashes between toll operators and users on petty issues has been rising.
55. The issue of non-availability of wayside amenities and carriageways for light vehicles
was also brought to the attention of the Committee. Non-availability of neon signs on the
National Highways is another cause of concern. Absence of proper directions and signage on
the national highways do not help the user of NHs to reach his destination in time. The
Committee hopes that an exclusive lane will be earmarked on the tolled national highways for
Passive Radio Frequency Identification Card users. Also, there should be a separate lane for

14
emergency operations on the national highways in the country. If it is not possible do so on
the existing national highways, necessary provision may be incorporated in the Concessionaire
Agreements for future projects. The Committee feels that adequate number of Nitrogen
Filling Stations may be provided on national highways for those who prefer Nitrogen gas filling
rather than the regular air for their vehicles.
56. The Committee desires that NHAI would look into these issues seriously and make the
travel on National Highways a comfortable one and that the apprehensions expressed by the
Members on the achievement of targets during the current fiscal will be duly taken care of

Road Safety
91. There are four aspects of road safety, viz.,  Engineering, Enforcement, Education and
Emergency care which are also known as four Es of Road Safety. The engineering related aspects
are being taken care of at the design stage of the NH itself. The Enforcement aspect of the Road
Safety is vested with the respective States/Union Territories. The Education aspect of Road Safety
is taken care by Ministry of Road Transport & Highways through campaigns in print and electronic
media.
92. The following are the details of various activities undertaken by the Ministry under this
scheme:–
Publicity and Awareness
93. Publicity campaign is one of the best means of raising awareness and bringing about additional
changes about road safety among citizens. These campaigns aim at prevention of road accidents and
fatalities. These are being carried out by the Ministry through electronic/print media in the following
manner:–
i) Observance of road safety week throughout the country;
ii) Media campaign through visual and print media with special emphasis on the road
safety;
iii) Printing and distribution of road safety material in Hindi, English and regional languages
across the country in order to raise awareness on road safety;
iv) Organization of conference/seminar/workshop on road safety;
v) Organizing meetings of National Road Safety Council, to periodically review the action
being taken and share the best practices in the field of road safety;
vi) Inclusion of a chapter on road safety in the text books of Central Board of Secondary
Education syllabus;
vii) Identification of top 25 black spots in 13 states which account for 90% of road
accidents in India; and
viii) Installation of proper reflectors on bicycles to minimize road accidents.
94. The Committee was informed that 25000 video spots and 40000 radio spots will be telecasted/
broadcasted on television and radio channels during the current year. Around 20,000 video spots will
also be telecasted/broadcasted in 3000 cinema halls. Road safety messages and road safety material
will also be sent to different stakeholders for creating awareness about road safety.
95. The Committee is at a loss to see the allocation and expenditure pattern in respect of
several core activities of the Ministry i.e., strengthening/improving road transport and road
safety in a country of continental dimension; just Rs. 200 crores for the entire country and
that too is not utilized fully. Further, the component wise allocations under transport sector
appear to be just national. In other words, transport and safety on roads in our country it
appears is treated as notional and that is why we are one of those countries having highest
number of road accidents and deaths etc. Highway accident relief got just Rs. 25 crores and
only about Rs. 15 crores could be utilized; Road safety and pollution testing just Rs. 5 crores
for entire country but only about Rs. 15 Lakh was spent; Data collection, Research and

23
Development- just Rs. 2.00 crores, even that could not be spent at all based on which our
policies/programmes for improving road safety are formulated. We do not, therefore, still
have an authentic/dependable data on the critical issue of road transport. Our existing data
is highly unauthentic which shows 'driver's fault' as the main reason for road accidents in
more than 78% cases. The Committee finds it highly unbelievable as it indicates that poor
drivers are out to die on the road and not for earning their livelihood. It also raises doubt
if this is not an attempt to cover up the real reason as most of these drivers die and therefore,
are not available to tell the truth. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends to
strengthen and expand the Road Safety Department with adequate resources and manpower
with a view to create a visible impact in this area. The Committee would like to have a White
Paper on the condition of road safety in India and steps proposed in this regard.
96. The Committee feels that another major impediment for road safety in the country is
the non-enforcement of road safety Rules/regulations. Union Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways appears to be helpless because it has no enforcement powers. Multiplicity of
agencies under Central Government as well as State Governments is another problem in this
regard. The Committee feels that successful implementation of road safety Rules/regulations
can be achieved only with a close co-ordination with the State Governments as they are the
implementing agencies. Central Motor Vehicle Rules, Carriage by Road Rules remain till
today merely on paper without being enforced actually. Pulls and pressures from obvious
quarters having vested interest in not enforcing these Rules/regulations and nexus with the
enforcement agencies are mainly responsible for this state of affairs. The dynamics behind
this is very well known but nothing could be done so far in breaking this deep entrenched
nexus.
97. Two important legislations for strengthening road safety viz., amendments to Central
Motor Vehicles Act. for enhancement of penalties for violations of road safety rules and a Bill
to create National Road Safety and Traffic Management Board, have not been introduced in
the Houses of Parliament till date for reasons better known to the Ministry. The Committee
feels that in addition to educating school children on road safety, proper displays and notices
should be installed on the National Highways where violation of road safety rules have become
a common phenomenon. The Committee may be apprised on the delay in the introduction of
mandatory fitment of Auto Dipper as required by Rule 106 of Central Motor Vehicles Rules
1989 and Section 110(1)(j). The Committee also feels that installation of dividers on National
Highways with proper design and height will play an important role in reducing road accidents
in the country.

Computer System and National Database
113. The Committee was informed that with a view to computerizing all the Regional Transport
Offices (RTOs) in the country and bringing about uniformity in the Driving License and Vehicle
Registration documents issued by the Regional Transport Offices, a project was conceived and has
been under implementation since 2001. The objective of the scheme is to introduce information
technology in the road transport sector. The back-end computerization envisages incorporation of
details of existing driving license, registration certificates and permit details on standard common
software at Regional Transport Office level and with essential linkage at state level and later national
level. The front-end operation involves issue of smart card based driving licenses and registration
certificates of motor vehicles based on common smart card operating system for transport application
specifications.
114. On the issue of status of digitization of records of RTOs in the country, the Committee was
informed that the Ministry had sanctioned a project for creation of National Register and State
Register of Driving Licenses and Registration Certificate of Motor Vehicle at an estimated cost of Rs.
148 crore. National Informatics Center (NIC) was entrusted with the design, development,
computerization roll-out and maintenance of the project across all the States and UTs. Two
applications - V AHAN and SARATHI were conceptualized to capture the functionalities as mandated
by Central Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 as well as State motor vehicle Rules with customization in the
core product to suit the requirements of 36 States and UTs.
115. As of now, NIC has achieved almost 100% success in terms of deployment of core Schema/
product for Vehicle Registration (VAHAN) and for Driving Licenses (SARATHI) across the country.
Subsequently to consolidate the database, State Registry (SR) for all the States and National Register
(NR) were established. Almost all the sites in 36 States/UTs except the recently added ones are
connected. More than 16 crore Vehicle records and 6 crore License records are available in National
Register repository. State Transport departments and enforcement agencies have been provided
access to data on National Register to facilitate instant verification of all driving licenses (DLs)/
Registration Certificate (RCs) and the digitalized data is also made accessible through Mobile by
sending SMS from their registered number.
116. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry was able to spend the entire
allocation of Rs. 25.16 core (RE) during 2014-15 for national database, which reflects its
commitment towards computerization of RTOs in the country. The Committee feels that this
as a welcome measure to counter the multiple license issue menace in the country. The
Committee also hopes that introduction of passive Radio Frequency Identification based toll
collection will minimize the long queues on toll plazas in the country. The Committee would
also like to have the feedback received from the users of National Highways on the Electronic
Toll Collection (ETC) system being implemented by NHAI on fifty-one toll plazas on public
funded projects.

Road Transport and Highways collects, analyses and disseminates data relating to roads, road
transport and road safety. TRW renders assistance in terms of data inputs and economic analysis to

sector and road transport sectors. The major publications brought out by RW covering the road and

118. The Committee noted that an amount of Rs. 10 crore was allocated under the 'Other
Expenditure' in B.E. 2014-15 which was reduced to Rs. 7 crore at R.E. stage. Now the Ministry has
been allocated with Rs. 10 crore. When it was asked about the details of projects/schemes for which
the Ministry would utilize Plan outlay for the next fiscal and whether the allocated amount will be
sufficient enough to carry out the Development and Planning activities in road sector, it was informed
by the Ministry that allocation has been reduced mainly on account of non-sanction of schemes under

thrust of Research and Development (R and D) in the road sector is to build a sustainable road

improvement in road design, (ii) modernization of construction techniques, (iii) introduction of

generally 'applied' in nature, which, once completed, are adopted by user agencies in their work in

etc. Under this head, provision towards training and publicity are also made. Taking note of the

119. The Committee noted that Rs 2 crore allocated under this head for 2014-15 at BE and RE
levels remained unused. When it was asked about the non-utilization of the allocated fund, the

country is not able to move forward in implementing latest technologies in the construction of road
as in the western countries. The concessionaires of projects have been given clearance to bring any

technology is available globally, there is no need to do too much research in this sector at public cost.
121. The Committee finds that uniform design and technology for National Highways is not
possible in the country due to its topography and varying climatic conditions. The Committee
would like to know whether any study has been conducted to assess the cost-benefit analysis
of concrete and bitumen roads. The Committee also feels that time has come to introduce
international technologies in the Indian road construction sector.

Setting up of Inspection and Certification Centers
122. Under Section 59 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, Central Government has powers to fix the
age of motor vehicles of different categories. However, this Section has not been invoked so far. The
'age' of certain categories of vehicles for the purpose of tourist permit and national permit only has
been fixed, under rules 82 and 88 of Central Motor Vehicle Rules, 1989. The Ministry's stand has
been that a well maintained older vehicle can be less polluting than an ill maintained newer vehicle.
A vehicle can play on the road as long as it meets the requirements of the Motor V ehicles Act, 1988
and Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 with regard to safety, emission and fitness norms. The
Ministry, in its outcome Budget, has stated that fixation of age of vehicle would also be not advisable,
keeping in view the socio-economic condition of the country.
123. An outlay of Rs. 30 crore has been provided for setting up of Inspection and Certification
Centers during 2015-16.
124. When it was asked about the details of Inspection and Certification Centers set up in the
country for the enforcement of strict inspection and maintenance of motor vehicles during 2014-15,
the Committee was informed that the safety and emissions requirements of in-use vehicles can be
achieved if the vehicles go through a fitness test after regular intervals. Therefore, it was decided
to put in place a suitably designed Inspection and Maintenance System for vehicles.
125. MoRTH sanctioned 10 model automated I and C Center one each in the States of Andhra
Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh,
U.P and Delhi on a pilot basis. Under the scheme, the land is made available by the concerned States.
The total cost for setting up one such centre is around Rs. 1440 lakh.
